report:
# Batch 8 adversarial sweep — operator report

**Every one of the 15 confirmed defects is in the sourcing and attribution layer around the arguments; not one is a defect in the reasoning, the physics, or a verdict — which on a project whose product *is* provenance is the worst place for them to be.**

---

## 1. Did the new rules work?

Partly. The rule that was written down and mechanically checkable held perfectly. The rules that depend on the writer's judgement did not.

| | Sweep 1 (23 targets) | Sweep 8 (12 targets) |
|---|---|---|
| Raised | 214 (9.3/target) | 111 (9.25/target) |
| Confirmed | 45 (1.96/target) | 15 (1.25/target) |
| Confirmation rate of raised | 21.0% | 13.5% |
| Hedge-rule failures | 9 of 21 | **0 of 12** |
| Criticals surviving at critical | 0 | 0 |

**Confirmed defects per target fell 36%.** That is real improvement, not noise: the raise rate per target is essentially identical (9.3 vs 9.25), so the reviewers were looking just as hard and finding less that survived a refutation attempt.

The hedge rule is the unambiguous win: 9 of 21 → 0 of 12, and it held under adversarial pressure — D11, B06, B08 and R03 all answer their sources' own strongest text rather than the list's fragments, and two entries (D08, R04) reach genuine kernel-tier steelmen.

The new rules are the honest disappointment: **4 of 12 targets (33%) failed them** — D04, D13, A07, R04 — and the failure mode is instructive. In every case the unscoped absence claim had *migrated into a field the ratcheting test does not scan*: `compression.note` (A07, D13), a cluster note (B06), a whole-literature claim phrased as "nobody has produced" (R04), "did not treat" (D04). The test scans `tldr`, `refutation`, `untraceable`, `passage.gloss` and matches a "does not contain / never mentions / is absent from" regex. Writers have learned the regex, not the rule. Two mechanical fixes follow: extend `_blocks` to `compression.note` and the cluster `note` field, and add `\bnobody (?:has|in)\b`, `\bno one has\b`, `\bdid not treat\b` to `_ABSENCE`.

Also worth noting on severity: 9 of the 15 confirmed were raised as major and downgraded to moderate on verification. The raise-then-verify loop is doing calibration work, not just filtering.

---

## 2. Fix order, weighted by reader impact

**Tier 1 — rendered before a reader expands anything (TLDR, cluster note, meta line, published dataset). Fix these first regardless of severity label.**

1. **D13 gloss** — "Rick DeLano produced the film with Sungenis, who co-wrote it". False about a named living man's authorship; Variety's credit block, which we cite three inches away, reads *Screenplay by Rick DeLano*, Sungenis executive producer. Fix the gloss and the `_b8_D13.py` docstring in the same pass. Do **not** apply the proposed `originator` change on this evidence.
2. **A07 `clusters.py` note** — publishes the "$20,000" figure the gloss says it is deliberately withholding, and frames Knodel's shielding run as refusal while the refutation credits it as a control. Self-contradiction about a living person on the most screenshottable line on the board. Minimal fix: strike `$20,000`, keep the rest; do not adopt the proposed replacement, which states the shielding-run outcome unhedged where the body hedges it.
3. **A09 TLDR** — "pressure on the Pacific sea floor". Gross 2000 does not contain the word "Pacific". Invented geographic specific adjacent to a named citation, in the field most readers never expand past. Two-word fix; the entry's own verdict paragraph already has the correct wording.
4. **D11 TLDR** — "a table he copied from an encyclopaedia". False, one click from our own source list, and repeated in `people.py`, `_b6_B01.py`, `_b6_B04.py` and `clusters.py`. Fix corpus-wide. Do not take the proposed "at the same canal" clause; the 1849 pamphlet's venue is the New Bedford, the 1881 book's Experiment 1 is the Old Bedford.
5. **B06 `clusters.py` record** — `year="1849"` publishes into five dataset rows (items 47, 223, 382, 383, 395) that the treatment rendered directly below contradicts twice. Anchor the edit on the cluster key, never on the `originator=` line — that line is byte-identical across B02, B06, B07 and D12, which is exactly how the E01/E03 misfile was manufactured. Hedge the item-383/Carpenter inference; use the house title form *Earth Not a Globe*.
6. **B08 gloss** — "the northern half of the cluster is inherited" positively asserts the southern half is not. Rowbotham 1881 (za48.htm, "Motion of Stars North and South") carries the southern-pole denial, the simultaneity objection in Dubay's own comparative form, and the perspective reply. Genealogy is the deliverable; this is the field a defender quotes. Add PER-ROWBOTHAM to `people`.
7. **D02 gloss, opening paragraph** — "the Sun some 93 million miles off" inside "everything Galileo's model contained". First paragraph after the quote. Take the nine-word strike, not the proposed three-sentence excursus on the history of the astronomical unit.

**Tier 2 — body prose, real but reached only by readers who expand.**

8. **D11 §3(c)** — sun at 3,000 miles (it is <4,000 in 1865, 700 in 1881) and the Britannica misattributed as the source of the 8-inch table (its actual citation is refraction, at p. 34 — the ARG-B07 hinge). Both proposed replacements need editing: the first double-predicates; the second asserts Rowbotham took his coefficient from Britannica, which ARG-B07 itself refutes.
9. **C08 `untraceable`** — the false absence claim about Hall's solar chapter, sitting in the block that invites readers to check us. Correct the docstring slug sta12 → sta11. Strike the Dupuis attribution from the proposed replacement; Hall credits an anonymous Balliol treatise.
10. **R04 gloss** — the 2006/2013 chapter mapping is wrong and contradicts our own ARG-E13. 2006 Vol. I ch. 10 → 2013 Vol. II ch. **9**; 2013 Vol. II ch. 10 is a different chapter descending from 2006 ch. 12.
11. **D02 §4 and sources[5]** — the "globe placed in the centre of the heavens" sentence is Jowett's introduction, not the *Phaedo*. Drop the proposed claim that Perseus is robots-blocked; it is reachable.
12. **D02 §6 / gloss §3** — Schadewald is a critic of geocentrism; his equivalence sentence is not an inside-the-tradition concession, and "two of them from inside the tradition" is false. Fix both fields plus the preceding clause.
13. **D08 §7** — "revolving heavens" is asserted by both models; our own corpus carries "Precession from dome rotation". The same defect recurs at §9 and in `why_it_doesnt_save_claim`; fixing §7 alone leaves the knockdown available.
14. **A07 `compression.note`** — "nobody in its own lineage is on record obtaining", contradicted by our own gloss and our own steelman. Rescope using the entry's existing formula ("the sequences the press transcriptions cover"), not the proposed "not in the film".

---

## 3. Patterns — where the 65 unwritten arguments will break

These repeat across enough targets to be predictive:

**A. Secondary sources retro-fitted onto primary ones.** The single largest class. Rowbotham's sun height taken from a modern flat-earth figure via Wikipedia (D11); Sungenis's screenplay credit from Wikipedia's loose prose against a credit block (D13); Jowett's editorial summary quoted as Plato (D02); a debunker's assessment quoted as the movement's concession (D02); the Britannica credited for the wrong thing (D11); Manly Hall's chapter cited by the wrong slug (C08). **Predicted failure in unwritten entries: any claim about what a primary source says that was not verified against the specific edition named in the locator.**

**B. Rowbotham's 1881 third edition is the systematic blind spot.** B06 (1849 vs 1865), B08 (southern strand present in 1881), D11 (two editions conflated, both misquoted), and the already-logged A05/B04/B01 corrections. Any B- or D-lane entry touching *Zetetic Astronomy* should be assumed edition-confused until checked. za48.htm and the General Index at za68.htm settle most of it in minutes.

**C. `clusters.py` renders into the entry and contradicts it.** B06 (year), A07 (the `$20,000` note), B08 (`people[]`, `originator`), R03 (`real_source=None`), D04 (stale docstring claiming an unfixed field). The writing agents do not own that file, report the defect to the parent, and the parent does not apply it. This is the E03 pattern — "recorded, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" — for at least the fourth time. It is a process failure, not a writing failure, and it is the highest-leverage thing to fix, because those fields render into the summary line next to the verdict chip.

**D. TLDRs written from memory of the argument.** A09 ("points the same way everywhere" is true of the globe too), A07 (asserts an axis-dependent match the body says it cannot establish), R04 ("whole content is the word *local*" vs the body's "both *operative* clauses"), D04, C08. The TLDR is systematically stronger than the body it summarises.

**E. Fields the ratchet does not scan absorb the banned constructions.** See §1. Structural, and cheap to close.

---

## 4. What this did not cover

- **65 of 98 arguments have no treatment at all.** These twelve plus the first sweep's 23 are 33 of 98. Nothing here says anything about the other two-thirds.
- **17 of 19 biographies are stubs.** Untouched. The B08 finding (PER-ROWBOTHAM missing from a cluster whose argument he originated) is exactly the kind of defect that lives in that gap.
- **Moderate and minor findings went unverified.** Roughly 80 entries in the leads array. They are leads, not conclusions — treat the recommended replacement text in them as a starting draft, not a patch. Verification changed the recommended fix in most of the 15 that *were* checked.
- **Per-target summaries name defects that are not in the confirmed set.** B06's summary asserts a major about a galileolied.com calculation; R03's asserts two majors (van der Kamp's actual position, a question-begging §7); A09's sets `holds=false` on a verdict challenge. None of those appear in the confirmed list. They either failed verification or were never put through it. Do not treat the summaries as findings.
- **Verification was one adversarial pass per finding.** It killed roughly 87% of what was raised, which is a good sign for the survivors, but nothing here has been checked twice.
- **A09's verdict is live.** The reviewer filed a verdict challenge (the six items do not share a fate; the seven-orders-of-magnitude calculation refutes 56 and 113 but 214 is a 2006 attribution for a claim about consumer drones) and the auditor endorsed it. That needs a decision, and it is the only verdict on this board that is contested.

---

## 5. Are these twelve in good shape?

Yes, with one qualification I would not soften.

The arguments are sound. Twelve for twelve on the hedge rule, two kernel-tier steelmen, and under sustained attempts at refutation not a single verdict fell and not a single piece of reasoning or physics was shown wrong — the arithmetic that was re-derived (B08's geometry, A09's seven orders of magnitude and drone numbers, R04's 0.13 m and 27 orders, A07's 348.6 Hz Sagnac beat) all held. Compared with sweep 1 this is a different quality of work.

The qualification: **10 of 12 carry at least one confirmed defect, and every one of those defects is a provenance error.** Wrong number attributed to a named primary source. Editor's summary quoted as the author. Critic quoted as adherent. Wrong chapter, wrong edition, wrong screenplay credit, wrong basin, invented encyclopaedia. On any other project these would be footnote-grade. On this one they are the product failing at the exact thing it convicts its subject of, and each is checkable by a hostile reader in under two minutes from a link we ourselves supply.

Neither of the two clean targets is unambiguously clean either: D04 failed the new rules, and R03's per-target summary claims two majors that did not survive to the confirmed list.

So: ship-quality reasoning, not-yet-ship-quality citation hygiene. Tier 1 is seven edits and closes the reader-facing exposure. The pattern work in §3 — particularly the `clusters.py` application gap and the Rowbotham edition audit — is what stops sweep 9 from reading like this one.

confirmed.quoted_phrase: the item asserts the geometry it is meant to refute
confirmed.description: §7 claims that item 440, "Temple architecture mirroring revolving heavens", asserts the geometry it is meant to refute, because revolving heavens are "the motion of a sphere". That is false, and it is refuted by our own page. The modern flat model has revolving heavens: a firmament turning about the vertical axis through the north pole. Our own corpus carries the list item "Precession from dome rotation" (scripts/corpus.py:49), ARG-B08 describes the model as "the stars carried round on a dome that turns about the vertical axis through it" (scripts/_b8_B08.py:203), and deep_batch2 answers "Day-night cycle from firmament rotation" and "Precession from dome rotation" as mechanism claims of that same model. So "revolving heavens" discriminates between nothing, and item 440 is not self-refuting. The paragraph half-notices this three sentences later and contradicts itself: "either way it is a question about motion, not about shape". This is load-bearing, because verdict_challenge justifies SELF-CONTRADICTED on "items asserting concentric heavens and revolving heavens, which are the geometry of a sphere" (line 64) — with 440 removed, the internal contradiction rests on item 127 plus §5's Josephus nest alone. It survives, but the stated reasoning overstates its support, and a defender knocks this plank down in one sentence.
confirmed.recommendation: Replace the two sentences beginning "It is a real phenomenon" with: "It is a real phenomenon and it is what the builders watched. On its own it does not decide the shape question, and we are not going to pretend it does: a firmament turning over a plane also carries stars round a pole, and the list says so itself — 'Precession from dome rotation' and 'Day-night cycle from firmament rotation' are items in the same corpus. What decides it is that the turn has two centres, one in each hemisphere, which no single axis through a disc delivers; that is argued at B08 and not re-run here. What item 440 does is concede that the heavens revolve, which is a claim about motion; whether the sphere or the observer turns is the geocentric question, belonging to lane A and to D02." And amend verdict_challenge line 64 to read "alongside it, an item asserting concentric heavens — which, in the Latin-European art it names, are drawn around a globe", dropping the appeal to revolving heavens.
confirmed.short_summary: §7 wrongly says "revolving heavens" is sphere-only geometry
confirmed.failure_scenario: A defender replies: "Our model has revolving heavens — the firmament turns over the disc; your own site lists 'Precession from dome rotation' as one of our claims and your B08 argument spells out the turning dome. Item 440 asserts nothing about shape, and your own next sentence admits it is 'a question about motion, not about shape'. You have counted a non-contradiction into a SELF-CONTRADICTED verdict." The rebuttal costs nothing to make and lands on a plank the verdict_challenge names.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to knock this down and could not. Verdict: it survives, but at moderate, not major.

1. The phrase is in the live text. /home/claude/spinning-ball-review/scripts/_b8_D08.py line 321 (mirrored in data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json:5515): "Filed as evidence for a flat stationary earth, the item asserts the geometry it is meant to refute." The preceding sentence is "It is a real phenomenon, it is what the builders watched, and it is the motion of a sphere." Both are exactly as quoted in the criticism.

2. The criticism is factually right, and the corroboration is in our own repo. corpus.py:41 "Celestial sphere rotation about observer.", :44 "Day–night cycle from firmament rotation.", :49 "Precession from dome rotation." — all list items of the model D08 is arguing against. _b8_B08.py:203 describes that model as "the stars carried round on a dome that turns about the vertical axis through it", and deep_batch2.py:172 treats firmament/dome rotation as the flat model's own mechanism claims. External check agrees this is the standard modern flat model (spacecentre.nz: "Most flat-earthers agree on a general model that puts the stars in a dome above the Earth with the North Star (Polaris) at the top"; the enclosed-cosmology substack states the firmament rotates to move the stars). So "revolving heavens" is asserted by both models and discriminates between nothing. Item 440's four words do not assert a globe; §7 supplies the gloss "daily rotation of the celestial sphere about its poles" and then treats the gloss as if the item had said it. The step that would actually discriminate — two centres of rotation, one per hemisphere, which one axis through a disc cannot deliver — is argued at B08 and is absent from §7.

3. The paragraph does contradict itself three sentences later ("either way it is a question about motion, not about shape"). Worse for the text, §8 immediately after refuses this exact move on item 163 — "the same sightlines are available under either model. We are not going to pretend otherwise in order to win an item." §7 commits the error §8 declines. That internal inconsistency is the strongest form of the finding and the criticism understates it.

4. Load-bearing extent, which is why I mark it down from major: the defect does not touch the TLDR, and it does not move the verdict. SELF-CONTRADICTED still rests on item 127 (Sacrobosco concentric heavens drawn about a sphere, §6) and on §5's Josephus key (seven planetary courses, zodiac circle, nested spheres), both independently argued. verdict_challenge is challenged=False, so nothing is being overturned; only the stated reasoning at line 63-64 overstates its support. Per the repo rubric (review/curmudgeon.md:176-183), this is "the argument works but could be stronger... weaker framing than available" = moderate. It is not critical: it is a bad inference, not a claim about what a source says.

5. The replacement is a net improvement and introduces no new problem — no overclaim, no sneer, no religion adjudication, no living-person motive, no unscoped absence, no third-party quotation at all (it quotes only our own corpus items, so the 60-word fair-use cap is not engaged). Its B08 cross-reference and its two corpus quotations are accurate. Two caveats for whoever applies it: (a) it uses a hyphen in "Day-night" where corpus.py:44 has an en dash; (b) it does not fix the two other places carrying the same defect — refutation §9 ("A proof set that contains 'concentric heavens', 'revolving heavens' and 'a dome above a flat earth'... is holding two geometries at once", line 345) and why_it_doesnt_save_claim ("nothing for 440, whose revolving heavens are the daily turn of that sphere", line 219). Fixing §7 and the verdict reasoning while leaving those two would leave the same knockdown available.

confirmed.quoted_phrase: the 3,000-mile height he assigns the sun, which is computed from measured angles and
confirmed.description: Wrong number, attributed to a named primary source. Rowbotham does not assign the sun a height of 3,000 miles in either edition this entry cites. The 1881 third edition, ch. V "The True Distance of the Sun" (sacred-texts za23.htm, pp. 99-104), reads "the distance of the sun over that part of the earth to which it is vertical is only 700 statute miles" and "the under edge of the sun is considerably less than 700 statute miles above the earth", with all luminaries "within a vertical distance of 1000 statute miles". The 1865 first book edition (Project Gutenberg #69892, the 1865 London Simpkin, Marshall text) reads "the actual distance of the Sun from the Earth is less than 4,000 miles" and puts the firmament within 6,000 miles; Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 1, gives the same "less than 4,000 miles" for Earth Not a Globe. 3,000 miles is the modern (Dubay-era) figure, not Rowbotham's. This is live in docs/index.html. The point of the sentence - that the figure is computed from angles and cannot be looked at - survives the correction intact and is in fact better documented, since Rowbotham reaches both figures by plane trigonometry from London/Brighton altitudes.
confirmed.recommendation: Replace with: "So is the height he assigns the sun - “less than 4,000 miles” in the 1865 edition and “only 700 statute miles” by chapter V of the 1881 third edition - a figure he reaches by plane trigonometry from measured altitudes at two stations, and one nobody can look at."

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not.

(1) The phrase is live. /home/claude/spinning-ball-review/scripts/_b8_D11.py line 192, refutation section 3(c): "So is the 3,000-mile height he assigns the sun, which is computed from measured angles and cannot be looked at." It also appears once in docs/index.html, so it is published.

(2) The criticism is confirmed by three independent checks. Sacred-texts za23.htm, the 1881 third edition ch. V "The True Distance of the Sun", gives "the distance of the sun over that part of the earth to which it is vertical is only 700 statute miles" and puts all luminaries "within a vertical distance of 1000 statute miles". Project Gutenberg #69892, the 1865 first book edition, gives "the actual distance of the Sun from the Earth is less than 4,000 miles" (from London/Brighton, 51 miles apart, and from stations 800 miles apart at altitudes 45 and 38 degrees) and the firmament "within the distance of 6,000 miles"; 3,000 occurs in that text only in the perspective/vanishing-point discussion, not for the sun. Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 1 (Behrend e-text, cantab.net), on the 1865 edition: "Using reported observations of the sun's angular altitude, he calculated its actual height as less than 4,000 miles." No edition this entry cites assigns the sun 3,000 miles.

(3) Provenance of our error. The Flat Earth Society wiki's "Distance to the Sun" attributes ~3,000 miles to Thomas Winship's Zetetic Cosmogony, not Rowbotham; Wikipedia's "Zetetic Astronomy: The Earth not a Globe" asserts uncited that "the Sun and Moon were 3,000 miles (4,800 km) above Earth", the likely proximate source. That makes the error worse in context: the entry already cites WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1865 for its passage and the 1881 sacred-texts transcription in its locator, so both checkable editions were in hand, and the printed figure is a later flat-earth number retro-attributed to the origin source, the precise confusion this project exists to undo.

(4) The replacement is an improvement and introduces no new problem: about nine quoted words, far under the 60-word fair-use cap; "plane trigonometry from measured altitudes at two stations" is accurate for both editions; no overclaiming, sneering, religious adjudication, living-person motive claim, or unscoped absence assertion; and the paragraph's point (the figure is inferred, not observed) is better documented after the fix. Two caveats for the editor rather than reasons to reject: the proposed sentence double-predicates awkwardly after "So is" and should be tightened (e.g.: So is the height he assigns the sun: "less than 4,000 miles" in the 1865 edition, "only 700 statute miles" by chapter V of the 1881 third edition - reached by plane trigonometry from measured altitudes at two stations, and not a thing anyone can look at.); and the criticism's side remark that 3,000 is "the modern (Dubay-era) figure" is loosely attributed (the traceable source is Winship 1899 and the later Flat Earth Society) and should stay out of the page text, as the proposed replacement already does.

Severity major, not critical: a wrong number attributed to a named primary source, live in published output, off by a factor of four or more from either edition, in a source-tracing review - but confined to one clause, with the surrounding argument intact.

confirmed.quoted_phrase: took the formula, on trust, out of the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on
confirmed.description: Misattributed provenance for the eight-inch table, on a page whose product is provenance. In the 1881 third edition the curvature rule and its table stand in ch. II at p. 10 (sacred-texts za05.htm, "a curvature or declination of 8 inches in the first statute mile", the table running 1 mile/8 inches to 120 miles/9,600 feet), and the only authority Rowbotham gives for it is a footnote reading "Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination." The Britannica appears exactly once in the book's General Index - "Levelling, quotation from the Encyclopaedia Britannica [34]" - and at p. 34 (za14.htm) he quotes that article on refraction, not on curvature: "For though the refraction may at a mean compensate for about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth, it sometimes exceeds one-fifth, and at other times does not amount to one-fifteenth." Searched: za04-za15 and za20, za23, and the General Index za68 of the 1881 sacred-texts transcription. So we have credited the Britannica with the one thing it is not cited for while missing the thing it is cited for - which is the refraction coefficient, i.e. exactly the ARG-B07 hinge the same paragraph points at. The corrected version is a stronger instance of taking a number on trust, not a weaker one.
confirmed.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "and Rowbotham takes it on trust from nobody in particular: the table at p. 10 opens “If the earth is a globe, and is 25,000 English statute miles in circumference”, and the only authority offered for the declination is a footnote reading “Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination.” The one encyclopaedia he does quote - the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling, at p. 34 - he quotes for refraction, which he reports as compensating “at a mean” about one-seventh of the curvature but “sometimes” exceeding one-fifth and sometimes not reaching one-fifteenth. That is where his coefficient comes from, and it is where the dispute lives (see ARG-B07)."

verdict.reasoning: I tried to kill this and could not. It holds on all three checks. 1. PHRASE IS LIVE. /home/claude/spinning-ball-review/scripts/_b8_D11.py line 190, in refutation section 3(c): "...and Rowbotham took the formula, on trust, out of the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling." The same error is upstream in the tldr, line 26: "the curvature both are measured against comes off an arithmetic table he copied from an encyclopaedia." A fix to 3(c) alone leaves the tldr wrong. 2. THE CRITICISM IS FACTUALLY RIGHT, confirmed independently at the 1881 sacred-texts transcription the entry itself cites as its edition: - za05.htm (ch. II, p. 10): chapter opens "IF the earth is a globe, and is 25,000 English statute miles in circumference, the surface of all standing water must have a certain degree of convexity--every part must be an *arc of a circle*"; the declination sentence is "From the summit of any such arc there will exist a curvature or declination of 8 inches in the first statute mile", with the table running from 8 inches at 1 mile. The only authority given is the footnote "Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination." No Britannica anywhere on that page. - za68.htm (General Index): the sole Britannica entry is "Levelling, quotation from the Encyclopædia Britannica [34]"; the sole curvature entry is "Curvature in statute miles, table of the [10]". Two different pages, two different subjects. - za14.htm (p. 34): "The following remarks from the Encyclopædia Brittanica--article, 'Levelling'--bear on the question" introduces a passage entirely about refraction — visual ray incurvated by refraction, no fixed allowance possible, "the refraction may at a mean compensate for about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth, it sometimes exceeds one-fifth, and at other times does not amount to one-fifteenth." It contains no curvature table and no 8-inch figure; it refers to "the foregone formulæ" without reproducing them. The decisive point is that the review contradicts ITSELF. /home/claude/spinning-ball-review/docs/index.html, in the ARG-B07 material, already states correctly: "Rowbotham reprints the Encyclopædia Britannica article 'Levelling' in the same chapter as his lighthouse table... 'the refraction may at a mean compensate for about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth.' One-seventh is k = 0.143..." So the published site says Britannica = refraction in one place and Britannica = the 8-inch curvature formula in another. On a page whose entire product is provenance, and in a paragraph whose whole force is "he took a number on trust", crediting the wrong source is the one error that cannot be waved off. Anyone who opens the linked transcription finds it in thirty seconds. Major. 3. THE PROPOSED REPLACEMENT SHOULD NOT BE PASTED IN AS WRITTEN. It fixes the error and then commits a fresh one of the same species: - "That is where his coefficient comes from" is wrong, and the review's own ARG-B07 is the refutation: Rowbotham does not adopt Britannica's one-seventh, he substitutes his own rule, "one-twelfth the altitude of the object observed", which B07 shows is the wrong quantity in the wrong place (refraction scales with distance squared, not target height; hence 13 feet deducted from a ~641-foot curvature term at Cape Bonavista). He quotes the one-seventh passage to argue that NO fixed allowance can be made, not to source a coefficient. Replacing a false provenance claim with a second false provenance claim in the same clause is not an improvement. - Minor imprecision: "the table at p. 10 opens 'If the earth is a globe...'" — that sentence opens ch. II (the entry's own locator puts ch. II at p. 9); the table is at p. 10. Say "the chapter opens", not "the table opens". - Quote volume: it adds roughly 35 further words of quotation from Rowbotham/Britannica to an entry that already carries a long ENAG passage block, and the one-seventh / one-fifth / one-fifteenth string is already quoted verbatim under ARG-B07. Duplicative against the fair-use budget for a single work. The safe minimal edit is to drop the false attribution and keep the argument, which is unharmed and slightly strengthened: replace "and Rowbotham took the formula, on trust, out of the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling" with something like "and Rowbotham takes it on trust: the only authority offered for the declination is a footnote reading 'Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination.'" Then fix the tldr's "copied from an encyclopaedia" to match. Add the Britannica/refraction pointer only if the editors want it, and if so it must say he quotes the one-seventh figure and rejects it in favour of his own one-twelfth rule (cross-reference ARG-B07), not that his coefficient came from it. No new problems of the other kinds: no religion adjudicated, no living-person motive claim. The absence assertion is properly scoped by the General Index plus the two page checks, which is the right scoping for this book.

confirmed.description: The same misattribution as hole 2, in the field readers meet first and may never expand past. The eight-inch table is not copied from an encyclopaedia in either text checked: its stated authority in the 1881 third edition, ch. confirmed.quoted_phrase: the Sun some 93 million miles off
confirmed.description: Galileo's heliocentric model did not contain a Sun 93 million miles away, and the sentence says explicitly that these are the things "Galileo's model contained". The scale of the solar system in 1632 was the inherited ancient one: Copernicus used about 1,142 Earth radii for the solar distance and Tycho about 1,150 (liquisearch.com/astronomical_unit/history), roughly 4.5 million miles, about a twentieth of the true value. The first roughly modern determination is Cassini and Richer's Mars-parallax work of 1672 — forty years after the Dialogue — which gave 87 million miles (thegreatestsciencediscoveries.wordpress.com, which also notes that "Before Cassini, most scientists believed that stars were only a few million miles away"). This is the one factual error in the treatment that a defender can check in a minute, and it sits in the first paragraph a reader meets after the quote. The argument is untouched by the fix — the point is that a model preserving Galileo's proportions preserves a globe of definite size in a Sun-centred planetary system, whatever the era's numbers were.

The substantive point is right and worth keeping - "doctrine" does convert a comparative category into a shared teaching - but it needs no imputation of concealment to land, and the entry is otherwise notably clean on this: it names the unfalsifiable without ridicule and says in terms that it takes no position on anyone's religion.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "sharing one is what the word supplies, and it is supplied without argument."

unverified.quoted_phrase: the archive.org transcription we fetched terminated in ch. 6, so that chapter is recorded here as unread rather than characterised.
unverified.description: Not an error in this sentence - it is the model of how to scope a reading, and I verified the transcription does stop in ch. 6 with the omphalos chapter listed in contents but absent. The hole is what the gloss omits. Section 1 renders under the fixed heading "The claim in its own words" over an Eliade quotation, and the entry's own compression note says plainly that no author stands beside any of the six items and that Eliade and Guénon are this review's reconstruction of the vocabulary's origin. That disclosure renders after the refutation, in a block a skim-reader never opens. On a site whose product is provenance, the strongest self-limiting finding we have should not sit three sections downstream of the attribution it limits.
unverified.recommendation:
Append to the end of the gloss: "

One limit on all of this, stated here rather than left to a later section. The specimen attributes these six items to nobody: the full text retrieved from it on 2026-08-09 was searched and carries no author or work beside any of them. Eliade and Guénon are named here as the origin of the vocabulary, on this review's reconstruction, and not as a citation the compiler made. What follows answers what they wrote; it does not claim they were read.

"

unverified.quoted_phrase: nobody reads them as claims about topology
unverified.description: Backwards. A schematic transit diagram is precisely a topological claim - connectivity and ordering are preserved exactly, and it is the metric geometry (distance, scale, direction) that is discarded. The analogy still works; the noun is wrong, and it is the sort of slip a technically literate defender quotes to suggest we are careless elsewhere.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "nobody reads them as claims about distance or direction".

unverified.quoted_phrase: twelve witnesses are lying and there is no principled way to pick the twelfth
unverified.description: Two problems in one clause. "Lying" imputes bad faith where the argument needs only error, and the entry elsewhere is careful to distinguish being wrong from lying (it grants that Guénon's position is "held by serious people" and that Eliade "meant it"). And "pick the twelfth" does not parse: on the geographical reading you are picking which single site is right and which twelve are wrong, so there is no twelfth to pick.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "twelve of the thirteen are mistaken, and there is no principled way to say which twelve".

unverified.quoted_phrase: “The Omphalos and Sacred Stones”
unverified.description: The chapter title is quoted with a word missing. The contents of the archive.org transcription we cite give ch. 9 as "The Omphalos and the Sacred Stones". Trivial in effect, but it is a titled citation inside quotation marks on a page whose subject is whether people reproduce their sources accurately.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "“The Omphalos and the Sacred Stones”".

unverified.quoted_phrase: and all of it follows from a spinning ball
unverified.description: Section 6 is headed "The one point of contact with measurement", which is where precision is worth most. Precession does not follow from rotation alone: it requires an oblate spinning body plus the gravitational torque of the Sun and Moon on the equatorial bulge. A perfectly spherical spinning Earth would not precess. Everything else in the paragraph checks out - sigma Octantis at magnitude 5.47, the ~25,772-year cycle, Thuban near the pole in the third millennium BCE, Polaris closest around 2100 CE, Vega in roughly twelve thousand years.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "and all of it follows from a spinning ball once its shape is included — precession is the Sun's and Moon's pull on the equatorial bulge of a rotating, slightly flattened Earth, which is a chain of consequences a pole erected in a plane does not begin".

unverified.quoted_phrase: the same source records the movement's own summary of what its Tychonic variant does
unverified.description: Second instance of the Schadewald misattribution flagged above, in a different field and needing its own replacement text. The sentence "can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system" is not "the movement's own summary"; it is the assessment of a critic documenting the movement, and the closing gloss "That is the equivalence concession again, from the other end of the lineage" compounds the error by treating an outsider's description as a concession from inside.
unverified.recommendation: Replace "and the same source records the movement's own summary of what its Tychonic variant does: it “can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system.” That is the equivalence concession again, from the other end of the lineage." with: "and the same source — written by a critic of geocentrism, not an adherent — records what the movement's Tychonic variant does: it “can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system.” That is the same equivalence, stated from outside the movement by the man who documented it."

unverified.quoted_phrase: and there is no hedge here to drop
unverified.description: The block argues against itself and the drift_type is the weaker of the two available readings. (a) This clause denies there is a qualification to drop, while the paragraph immediately above it is headed "The clause that does not travel is the one that decides the case" and makes a dropped governing qualification — "while adhering to all the proportions and motions that were in Galileo's heliocentric model" — the whole point of the assessment. A reader can see both statements without scrolling. (b) force_upgraded is defined in deep.py as "a concession or permission is re-used as a proof", and nothing in the source sentence marks it as a concession. Read in place (I fetched the Vol. I scan), Sungenis and Bennett are asserting, in a book arguing that geocentrism is true, that Urban VIII already had a scientifically adequate alternative to Galileo. Using that as an evidence item is close to the authors' own use of it, which is what drift_type "none" describes. The R01 parallel invoked at the end of the paragraph does not carry: van der Kamp flagged his own sentence as a concession ("forcing an open door"); this sentence contains no such marker, and "how easy it is to envision" is the authors praising the model's virtue, not hedging it. As written we make the source weaker than it is, which is the hedge rule's failure mode running in the other direction.
unverified.recommendation:
Replace the third paragraph of the note with: "

What the drift is, and what it is not. We record this as force_upgraded and the reading has to be defended, because the source is not conceding anything: read in place, the authors are asserting — in a book arguing that geocentrism is true — that Urban VIII already had a scientifically adequate alternative to Galileo. What moves is not the wording and not the author's confidence but the governing clause. The sentence buys its Tychonic model at a stated price, “while adhering to all the proportions and motions that were in Galileo's heliocentric model”, and the price does not travel: items 22 and 123 carry the model and leave the clause behind. Readers who prefer hedge_dropped for that pattern have a case, and the two labels point at the same missing words. What we did not find is any qualification of confidence — no “may”, no “on this reading” — so the refutation meets the sentence at full strength rather than treating it as tentative. We also considered unsourced_addition for items 120, 121 and 122, since we did not locate the authors' own appeals to Plato, Aristotle or Ptolemy in the parts of either scan we could read. That was rejected as unsupportable: our fetch tool truncated the Volume I scan at about p. 26–30 and the Volume II scan at about p. 30, both works run past a thousand pages, and the Volume II table of contents plainly advertises a chapter called Hildegardian Geocentrism: Aristotelian Cosmology Meets Modern Science. Unreached is not the same as absent, and no claim of the second kind is made here.

"

unverified.quoted_phrase: smuggled in under the same numbering
unverified.description: "Smuggled" imputes deliberate concealment to whoever compiled the list — a living person about whom this project may make no motive or bad-faith claim — and it is the first word in the harness's own list of loaded language to scan for (curmudgeon.md, holistic check 3: "smuggled, pretend, dishonest, deliberate, quietly, merely"). It is also unnecessary: the sentence's force comes from the mismatch between a Tychonic cosmology and a flat-Earth list, and that mismatch is fully carried by a neutral verb. This is the only loaded word in our own voice anywhere in the file; "credulous" and "clever and empty" both occur inside quoted or role-played positions.
unverified.recommendation: Replace "It is a rival cosmology to the one the list is defending, smuggled in under the same numbering." with: "It is a rival cosmology to the one the list is defending, carried under the same numbering."

unverified.quoted_phrase: Item 122 invokes Ptolemy's spheres
unverified.description: Section 5 is described in the docstring as the one thing D02 adds that A22 has no reason to say, so it carries weight, and as written it is open to a one-line reply: the spheres of the Almagest — the text A22 quotes and the text a reader will assume is meant — are mathematical devices, deferents and epicycles, and a comet passing through a geometrical construction refutes nothing. The collision is real, but it needs the right Ptolemaic text named. Ptolemy's physical cosmos of nested solid shells is in the Planetary Hypotheses, where he "goes beyond the mathematical models of the Almagest to present a physical realization of the universe as a set of nested spheres" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy) and computes the dimensions of the universe from them. Naming it closes the escape route and makes the section stronger, not weaker.
unverified.recommendation: Replace "Item 122 invokes Ptolemy's spheres — the nested celestial orbs of the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic cosmos." with: "Item 122 invokes Ptolemy's spheres. Be precise about which spheres, because it decides the point: the Almagest's deferents and epicycles are geometry, and geometry is not broken by a comet. The solid ones are Ptolemy's too — the Planetary Hypotheses goes beyond the Almagest's mathematics to give a physical universe of nested spheres and computes its dimensions from them, and that is the cosmos the medieval and early-modern tradition inherited under his name."

unverified.quoted_phrase: His argument against a moving Earth in the same chapter is empirical, not metaphysical
unverified.description: Overstated as a definite description, and checkable in the chapter we cite. In De caelo II.14 (classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/heavens.2.ii.html) Aristotle gives several arguments against a moving Earth, and the first is exactly the kind this sentence denies: any motion of the Earth would be forced rather than natural, and "the movement could not be eternal. But the order of the universe is eternal." The natural-motion-to-the-centre argument ("the natural movement of the earth, part and whole alike, is the centre of the whole") comes before the stellar one as well. The observational argument we quote is genuinely there and genuinely his, but it is one of four, and saying "his argument... is empirical, not metaphysical" invites a defender to open the chapter and produce the metaphysics in the first paragraph. Scoping it costs three words and loses nothing, since the point being made is only that he nominated a falsifier.
unverified.recommendation: Replace "His argument against a moving Earth in the same chapter is empirical, not metaphysical: if the Earth moved," with: "He gives four arguments against a moving Earth in that chapter, and three of them are what you would expect — forced motion cannot be eternal, earth's natural movement is towards the centre, a stone thrown up comes back to where it started. The fourth is not metaphysics at all. If the Earth moved,"

unverified.quoted_phrase: the same chapter of De caelo that this cluster relies on
unverified.description: The cluster does not rely on that chapter. Item 121 is "Aristotle's unmoved mover", which our own refutation section 3 correctly locates in Metaphysics XII.7-8; De caelo II.14 is a text WE bring to the argument, not one the cluster invokes. Small, but it contradicts section 3 of the same entry, and the straw_man block renders on the page (render.py line 240).
unverified.recommendation: Replace "the estimate of 400,000 stades for the Earth's circumference is passed on in the same chapter of De caelo that this cluster relies on." with: "the estimate of 400,000 stades for the Earth's circumference is passed on in De caelo II.14, the chapter that carries both of those arguments."

unverified.quoted_phrase: the same wording runs through the film's promotional copy
unverified.description: Checked and it does not. The synopsis sentence is located in exactly one press release, carried on two channels: the PRWeb item of 8 December 2015 and its identical FrontGate Media posting. The second source we cite for it — "earlier distributor release carrying the same synopsis (In Ohm Entertainment, PR Newswire, 25 March 2015)" — does not contain either the "explores the significance of the Earth's place within the Cosmos" sentence or the "are we significant within the structure of the Universe?" passage; it carries different copy, and that different copy is what ARG-E01 quotes. So the label states something the linked document does not support, and the locator generalises one release into a body of promotional copy.
unverified.recommendation: Change the locator to: "Official distributor synopsis, issued through PRWeb by FrontGate Media with the home-video release, 8 December 2015, and reproduced on FrontGate's own site the same week; this is the one release we located carrying it. Quoted from the press text, not from the film's soundtrack, which we were not able to view in this pass." Change the sources[1] label to: "The Principle — earlier distributor release (In Ohm Entertainment, PR Newswire, 25 March 2015). It carries the same thesis in different words — “Are we significant or just a cosmic accident?”, “unexpected evidence of a preferred direction in the cosmos”, “aligned with our supposedly insignificant Earth” — and is the release ARG-E01 quotes."

unverified.quoted_phrase: single values holding at every point of spacetime
unverified.description: False for two of the six numbers named in the same sentence, in the paragraph the entry calls decisive. In Rees's list, Ω is the density parameter, which evolves with cosmic time in any FLRW model and is quoted as a present-day value; Q is the amplitude of density fluctuations, i.e. a statistical property of a field that by definition is not the same at every point — that is what fluctuations are. The following sentence compounds it: "A constant is a scalar; a scalar has no gradient and no preferred direction." Scalar fields routinely have gradients; only uniform ones do not. A cosmologist defending the film gets a free hit on the decisive paragraph, and the argument does not need the overreach: what defeats "Earthward" is spatial uniformity at a given epoch, which is true of all of them.
unverified.recommendation: Replace both sentences with: "Rees's six numbers — N, ε, Ω, λ, Q, D — and the rest of the standard list are properties of the universe as a whole, not of places in it. Λ is a constant in the strict sense, the same at every point of spacetime. Ω and Q are cosmological quantities that change with cosmic epoch, but at any given epoch they take the same value everywhere, and Q describes fluctuations that are statistically identical in every direction. Either way there is no spatial gradient to follow, and a uniform scalar has no preferred direction to give."

unverified.quoted_phrase: and nowhere states it, because stating it invites the check
unverified.description: The "because" clause attributes a reason for not stating a premise: that its authors leave it unstated to avoid scrutiny. That is a claim about the intentions of living, named people — Sungenis and DeLano — and nothing in the entry supports it. It is also probably wrong on the ordinary reading: unstated premises are usually unstated because their holders take them to be obvious, not because they are being concealed. The site's own standard is that unfalsifiable claims are named, not ridiculed, and that we distinguish being wrong from being evasive.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "and none of the five states it. That is not a concealment — it is the mark of a premise its holders take to be obvious. Stated out loud it becomes checkable, and it does not survive the check."

unverified.quoted_phrase: states the puzzle as a value, never as a bearing
unverified.description: An unscoped absence claim across three works — Weinberg's 1989 review, Rees's Just Six Numbers and Barnes's 77-page 2012 survey — asserting what none of them ever does. This is the sweep's dominant failure mode and the writing rule in deep.py forbids it in terms. It escapes the ratcheting test only because the test scans tldr, refutation, untraceable and passage.gloss, and does not scan compression.note; the rule is not scoped to what the test happens to read. (Note that the neighbouring absence claim in section 2 — "it is not in the distributor synopsis quoted above" — is correctly scoped and should be the model.)
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "states the puzzle as a magnitude. In the abstract and body of Weinberg 1989, in Rees's six numbers, and in Barnes's 2012 review, the fine-tuned quantity is always a value; no statement of it as a direction is located in the three texts read for this pass."

unverified.quoted_phrase: that we are 'a cosmic accident', of 'utter insignificance'
unverified.description: One of the three phrases is interrogative in the source and is quoted here as a proposition. The 25 March 2015 release reads "Are we significant or just a cosmic accident?" — a question. "relegates us to utter insignificance" (PRWeb, 8 December 2015) and "our supposedly insignificant Earth" are assertive and are fairly used. Converting a question into an assertion is the precise move this entry convicts the list of two blocks earlier, in the compression note, and a defender who checks one citation will find us doing it in the paragraph headed Straw man identified.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "that we are ‘just a cosmic accident’ — the copy puts it as a question, and the assertive versions sit alongside it: the principle ‘relegates us to utter insignificance’, and an Earth described in its own publicity as ‘supposedly insignificant’."

unverified.quoted_phrase: Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal and papal legate, wrote in De docta ignorantia II.12 in 1440
unverified.description: Anachronistic rank. De docta ignorantia was completed on 12 February 1440; Cusa was created cardinal in December 1448 (published 1449) and served as papal legate from 1450. The appositive is doing rhetorical work — a churchman, before Copernicus, from inside the Church — and the date is the load-bearing part, so the easiest defence is to keep both and lose the anachronism. The quotation itself checks out verbatim against Hopkins §162.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "Nicholas of Cusa — a churchman who would be made cardinal eight years later — wrote in De docta ignorantia II.12 in 1440"

unverified.quoted_phrase: the same way about that one centre. Southern trails close in the opposite handedness
unverified.description: Consequence (ii) rests on handedness, and handedness alone is answered by the source's own closing sentence in proof 101 (direction of motion depends on which way you face) - a reply we never quote and never answer, because we place the perspective defence entirely in proof 102. The reply has real force at this step: apparent handedness genuinely does reverse when you look at the opposite end of a single axis, and a northern observer who turns to face south does see the southern sky run the other way across his field of view. What the disc cannot deliver is not the reversal but the second centre with closed circles at altitude equal to latitude - which is (i) and section 4, not (ii). As written, (ii) is the one consequence in the list of five that a well-read defender can dispose of with a sentence from the source we are refuting.
unverified.recommendation: Replace consequence (ii) with: '(ii) One sense of rotation — and a centre in the other half of the sky. Handedness on its own settles nothing, and proof 101 says so in its last sentence: face the opposite end of any axis and the same rotation reverses its apparent sense. That is true. It is why the southern datum has to be stated as a second centre and not as a reversal: from a southern site the trails do not merely run the other way, they close into complete circles about a point due south at an altitude equal to the observer’s latitude, in one sidereal day. Turning to face south from a northern site produces no such point, on a disc or on a globe. Only crossing the equator does.'

unverified.quoted_phrase: stars all rotate … Unlike Polaris, however,
unverified.description: The ellipsis drops the source's own words 'around the opposite direction' - i.e. the clause in which Dubay states the very claim our TLDR headlines - and the quote then stops before the two sentences that close the proof: 'There is legitimate speculation regarding whether Sigma Octantis even exists. Either way, the direction in which stars move overhead is based on perspective and the exact direction you're facing, not which hemisphere you are in.' The gloss's count, 'there are four claims here, not one', is therefore short: there are five in the printed proof, and the fifth (existence doubted outright) is both the most striking illustration of our thesis and the one the harness says must be NAMED as unfalsifiable rather than ridiculed. Restoring the four elided words keeps the quote at 56 words, inside the 60-word in-copyright cap the test enforces.
unverified.recommendation: Set passage.quote to: 'Sigma Octantis is claimed to be a Southern central pole star similar to Polaris, around which the Southern hemisphere stars all rotate around the opposite direction. Unlike Polaris, however, Sigma Octantis can NOT be seen simultaneously from every point along the same latitude, it is NOT central but allegedly 1 degree off-center, it is NOT motionless.' (56 words; 'rotate around the opposite direction' is the source's own phrasing, sic.) In the gloss, replace 'So there are four claims here, not one' with 'So there are five claims here, not one' and, after the telescope clause, add: 'and closes by doubting that the star exists at all. That last one is worth naming plainly rather than mocking: a claim that an object visible to the unaided eye from half the planet may not exist is not a claim any observation offered here can settle for a reader who will not look.'

unverified.quoted_phrase: Sigma Octantis is a convenience for a navigator, not the
unverified.description: Our own cited source says the opposite. The Wikipedia Sigma Octantis article, which we list as source 5 for the magnitude, states: 'At magnitude +5.42, Sigma Octantis is barely visible to the naked eye, making it unusable for navigation, especially by comparison with the much brighter and more easily visible Polaris.' A defender who follows our own footnote finds our sentence contradicted, and it is the kind of small unforced error that discredits the paragraph around it - which is otherwise the strongest thing in the entry. The correction strengthens us: the star's uselessness as a navigational marker is further evidence that the southern pole is fixed by the trails, not by the star.
unverified.recommendation: Replace 'Sigma Octantis is a convenience for a navigator, not the evidence.' with: 'Sigma Octantis is a marker, and a poor one: at magnitude 5.42 it is barely a naked-eye object and of little practical use for navigation, which is why southern navigators find the pole by projecting the long axis of the Southern Cross instead. It is not the evidence.'

unverified.quoted_phrase: the official rationale for putting it there is that it is small,
unverified.description: The citation does not support the phrase, and 'official' overstates it. Our source 10 is the Wikipedia Flag of Brazil article, credited in its label with exactly this rationale; the article in fact says Sigma Octantis represents the Federal District because 'its unique position in the sky of the southern hemisphere represents the stability of the Federal District in the Brazilian union', and the 'dimmest star on any national flag' point is on the Sigma Octantis page, not the flag page. The 'all the other stars turn around it' formulation is documented, but by a Brazilian astronomy source rather than by a government: Zenite, 'O ceu da bandeira' - 'Do nosso ponto de vista, e em torno dela que giram todas as demais estrelas do firmamento.' Everything else in this sentence checks out (flag adopted 19 November 1889; the star numbered 7 represents the Federal District; 1889 to 2015 is 126 years), which is why the unsupported clause is worth fixing rather than dropping.
unverified.recommendation: Replace 'and the official rationale for putting it there is that it is small, but all the other stars turn around it' with: 'chosen for the Federal District, in the flag’s own symbolism, for its “unique position in the sky of the southern hemisphere” — and that position is the pole itself: from anywhere in Brazil it is the point the rest of the sky turns around (Zenite, “O ceu da bandeira”: “e em torno dela que giram todas as demais estrelas do firmamento”)'. Add https://zenite.nu/o-ceu-da-bandeira to sources and rewrite the Flag of Brazil source label to claim only the adoption date and the Federal District attribution.

unverified.quoted_phrase: Fitting each latitude separately
unverified.description: A stronger consequence is available and missing, and it is the one that answers the advocate's best move. Section 3 tests the disc on Polaris's altitude and on the southern pole; both require the reader to accept our arithmetic or to fly south. The disc also fails on the two items the treatment hands back as uncontested - item 16 'Perfect circular star trails around Polaris' and item 213 'Perfect star circles'. Under a dome of finite height h, an off-centre observer is at a different distance from each star at each hour, so every star would sweep faster near its closest approach and slower at its farthest, and its projected path would be a conic rather than a circle sharing a centre with every other star's. Observed trails are concentric circles at a uniform 15.04 degrees per hour. Perfect circularity is therefore not a datum the flat model gets for free; it is a datum only stars at effectively infinite distance about one axis can produce - and unlike the southern pole, a northern reader can test it in one night with the camera they already own. Our advocate rates the 'you have offered no observation I can make from where I am standing' objection at 4 and answers it with a southbound flight; this answers it without one.
unverified.recommendation: Add as a sixth consequence in section 3: '(vi) Circles that close, at one rate. Items 16 and 213 report that the trails are perfect circles, and they are right — which is the difficulty. On a dome of finite height the observer’s distance to each star changes through the night, so every star would run fastest near its closest approach and slowest at its farthest, and its path across the sky would be a conic rather than a circle about the same point as everyone else’s. Every long exposure ever taken shows concentric circles closing at a uniform 15.04 degrees per hour. That is the signature of stars at effectively unlimited distance turning about one axis, and it needs no flight: one camera, one tripod, one clear night in the northern hemisphere.' Then amend the advocate `preemptive` to cite (vi) as the no-travel answer to the argument-from-authority objection.

unverified.quoted_phrase: when the same sums run the other way
unverified.description: The never-rises condition is mis-stated, and our own steelman states it correctly two paragraphs earlier ('a star of declination d stays below the horizon for a northern observer at latitude f only when d < f - 90'). Read as written, 'the same sums run the other way' gives 'f + d < -90 in the north' - but for a northern observer at 40 N a star never rises when d < -50, i.e. f + d < -10, which is nowhere near -90. On no reading of 'the same sums' does the sentence produce the correct condition, which is f - d > 90 in the north. This sits in the paragraph where we tell the reader the globe's rule is the rule that generates the source's own correct latitude bands, so it is the first line a defender with a star chart will test.
unverified.recommendation: Replace 'a star never sets when φ + δ > +90° in the north or φ + δ < −90° in the south, and never rises when the same sums run the other way' with: 'a star never sets when |φ| + |δ| > 90° and latitude and declination share a sign, and never rises when |φ| + |δ| > 90° and their signs are opposite. At 34 degrees south that means everything south of declination −56° is permanently up and everything north of +56° never rises at all'.

unverified.quoted_phrase: one apparent centre per observer, and it lies in the direction of that axis
unverified.description: On a plane the rotation axis is vertical, and every vertical on a plane is parallel to every other - so 'the direction of that axis' is the zenith, for everybody, not the north. What our own section 3(iii) actually models is the direction to the point where the axis meets a dome of finite height h, which is northward at altitude arctan(h/r). The clause that follows, 'northward, everywhere on the disc', is right and rescues the meaning, but the stated reason contradicts it and a physicist-defender will say so.
unverified.recommendation: Replace 'and it lies in the direction of that axis — northward, everywhere on the disc' with: 'and on a plane it lies where that axis meets the dome — northward and elevated for every observer on the disc, because every vertical on a plane is parallel to every other, so no one on it can be tilted away from the axis'.

unverified.quoted_phrase: are the only items in the cluster that assert something about history
unverified.description: A quantifier that our own compression block contradicts. The compression note argues that items 143 and 267 ('Constant constellations', 'Constellation stability') are two-word fragments 'that a reader will take as a claim about time, that the constellations do not change'. Section 5 then says items 17 and 145 are the only items asserting anything about history. Both fields are defensible on their own reading - section 5 reads 143/267 the source's spatial way, the compression note reads them as the circulating fragment does - but the two are a short scroll apart on the rendered page and a critic compiling self-contradictions will pick this up. The hedge rule's second clause is also relevant: the circulating temporal reading is the one readers arrive with, and precession answers it.
unverified.recommendation: Replace 'are the only items in the cluster that assert something about history' with: 'are the two items that assert history on their face — and precession settles them, along with the temporal misreading of “Constant constellations” that the compression note below describes'.

unverified.quoted_phrase: full-text reproduction, 31 July 2018; proofs 98–108 read here
unverified.description: For a project whose product is provenance, the source list reaches proof 101 through a third-party WordPress reproduction and a SlideShare scan but omits the author's own posting of the same text (ericdubay.wordpress.com, 8 July 2018), which is where the full wording of proof 101 - including the two closing sentences our quote stops before - was confirmed during this review. The rexynotes copy is dated three weeks after it.
unverified.recommendation: Add to sources: dict(label='Dubay, 200 Proofs — the author’s own posting of the full text, 8 July 2018; proof 101 quoted from here', url='https://ericdubay.wordpress.com/2018/07/08/200-proofs-earth-is-not-a-spinning-ball-english/') and change the rexynotes label to '— third-party reproduction of the same text, 31 July 2018; used to locate proofs 98–108'.

unverified.field: scripts/clusters.py ARG-B06 note (renders as the summary line of the Refutation section)
unverified.quoted_phrase: Rowbotham's own '8 inches per mile squared' is lifted from a surveying text
unverified.description: An unverified provenance claim, published as the basis line on a page whose entire product is provenance. Our own module docstring records that the mechanism is unconfirmed: at 1881 ch. II p. 9 Rowbotham introduces the figure flat, with no sourcing located on the page, and the prose below the basis line deliberately retreats to the narrower, checkable statement (8 in/mile is D^2/2R for one statute mile, and Simms's levelling treatise uses it). "Lifted from a surveying text" asserts a transmission route we did not establish - and the one text we can show he actually reprints is the Encyclopaedia Britannica "Levelling" article, which is not where the 8 inches comes from in his book. I confirmed the Metabunk listing does support Simms (1875) using the 8-inch approximation, so the arithmetic claim is safe; only the word "lifted" is not.
unverified.recommendation: Replace the note with: "Rowbotham's '8 inches per mile' is D^2/2R for one statute mile - 0.2032 m - the first-mile value of the difference between the true and the apparent level that his own century's levelling literature tabulates. He reprints an Encyclopaedia Britannica article on levelling for its refraction sentence and discards the curvature the same article's formulae supply, then calls the Ordnance Survey as his witness seven years after it published the figure of the earth derived from the Principal Triangulation."

unverified.quoted_phrase: no copy or transcription of the sixteen-page 1849 pamphlet could be reached at all, and the same was recorded when ARG-B01 went looking for it
unverified.description: Two problems in one sentence, and they undercut the gloss's bolded conclusion. (1) It misstates ARG-B01's record. B01 did not record that nothing could be reached; it built a whole passage block on WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1849 out of the title page plus "the one body sentence Robert Schadewald reproduces verbatim", and used Schadewald's quotation as evidence when reattributing item 384. So a partial witness to the pamphlet's contents exists, was used by a sibling entry, and is neither consulted here nor listed in this entry's COULD NOT REACH block. (2) The dating inference over-concludes. The Standing Order is dated to the Session of 1862 only in the 1881 third edition; the 1865 text quotes it undated, citing only "No. 6" (Lords) and "No. 44" (Commons) - I verified this on the Gutenberg text. Standing Orders requiring deposited plans and sections with a datum line long predate 1862 (unchecked - the Parliamentary Archives research guide redirected and the Norfolk record office page is robots-disallowed), so an 1849 pamphlet could have quoted the order then in force. The 1862 date fixes a terminus post quem for the text we can read, not for the argument, which is a weaker claim than "So this is a claim of the 1860s".
unverified.recommendation: Replace the quoted clause with: "no copy or transcription of the sixteen-page 1849 pamphlet could be reached here, and ARG-B01 reached it only through its title page and the one body sentence Robert Schadewald reproduces - six theodolite experiments on the Bedford Level, with nothing about railway sections in what he quotes." And soften the paragraph's closing sentence from "So this is a claim of the 1860s, sharpened in the 1880s." to "So the earliest text of it we can read is of the 1860s, and it was sharpened in the 1880s; whether a version stood in the pamphlet is not something the sources we could reach can settle." Add Schadewald's chapter to sources[].

unverified.quoted_phrase: The argument needs horizontal datum line to mean plane. In surveying it does not.
unverified.description: We miss the strongest answer available, and it is inside his own quotation - which is doubly costly because the treatment's whole rhetorical strategy is that the answer is inside his own quotation. The clause immediately BEFORE the datum clause he prints is: "That the section be drawn to the same horizontal scale as the plan; and to a vertical scale of not less than one inch to every one hundred feet". Two independently specified scales on the two axes means a railway section is not a picture of the ground at all - it is a graph of height against chainage, with the vertical exaggerated by roughly an order of magnitude. Curvature is not merely ignored in such a drawing, it is unrepresentable in it, and the straightness of the baseline carries no geometric information whatever. We spend the section on the gravity meaning of "horizontal" and on Ordnance Datum, both correct, and never make the point a reader is most likely to reach unaided.
unverified.recommendation: Insert immediately after the quoted sentence: "It also needs a section to be a picture of the ground, and the clause before the datum clause - in the same quotation - says it is not. The section is drawn “to the same horizontal scale as the plan; and to a vertical scale of not less than one inch to every one hundred feet”. Two different scales on the two axes make it a graph of height against chainage, with the vertical exaggerated by roughly an order of magnitude, and on a graph the curvature of the ground is not merely ignored, it is unrepresentable. A straight baseline under a distorted profile is a drawing convention, not a measurement of the earth."

unverified.field: refutation, section 1 (and advocate.best_defense, which never attacks this move)
unverified.quoted_phrase: That fixed point is a benchmark, and British ordnance benchmarks of the 1860s carried heights above Ordnance Datum Liverpool
unverified.description: The load-bearing move of the whole entry - the TLDR bets on it - rests on an unstated step. The order requires only that the datum "be referred to some fixed point stated in writing on the section"; it does not require an Ordnance Survey benchmark, and a railway datum is arbitrary in height and frequently a purely local mark. Our chain runs fixed point -> ordnance benchmark -> Ordnance Datum Liverpool -> mean sea level, and only the last two links are sourced (I verified the Wikipedia Ordnance datum text: "tidal observations were taken at the Victoria Dock, Liverpool, over a short period in 1844"). A defender goes here first: "a section datum is an arbitrary plane the engineer picks; nothing ties it to a tide gauge." Worse, advocate.best_defense never raises it - it attacks the curvature off-switch, the balanced-sight reinterpretation, survey closure and the correction lines, all of which section 3 and section 6 already answer - so the one move that is genuinely exposed is the one the steelman of our critics leaves alone. The fix is to stop needing the sea: what defeats the plane inference is that the datum defines a LEVEL surface, because it is set out with a spirit level, whatever its height.
unverified.recommendation: Replace the quoted clause with: "That fixed point is a physical mark on the ground, and the order does not say what height it sits at - a railway datum is arbitrary in height and often purely local. What is not arbitrary is the surface it defines. The datum is carried along the work with a spirit level, and a spirit-levelled surface is perpendicular to the plumb line at every point on it, so the constant datum the order demands is a level surface by construction, whatever number is written against it. Where the fixed point is an ordnance benchmark the number is referred to Ordnance Datum Liverpool, from tidal observations at Victoria Dock in 1844; where it is not, his own Experiment 14 shows what else it tends to be - a section diagram labelled “the datum line—the Trinity high water mark”." Change the following sentence "The datum is the sea." to "The datum is a level surface, and where it is tied to a gauge it is the sea." Then add to advocate.best_defense, in their voice: "Your datum argument is a bait and switch. The order I quote requires a fixed point, not a tide gauge; engineers pick a convenient datum below the lowest cutting and it is a plane on the drawing by definition." - so that the preemptive answer above is visibly earned.

unverified.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, first case (and the parallel sentence in refutation section 3)
unverified.quoted_phrase: the combined curvature-and-refraction term enters at 0.0675D² metres with D in kilometres
unverified.description: Attributes the full curvature-and-refraction term to any imbalance. The residual after an unbalanced setup is 0.0675(Db^2 - Df^2), not 0.0675D^2: a 20 per cent imbalance at a kilometre leaves 0.0675(1.0^2 - 0.8^2) = 24 mm, not the 68 mm we quote. The figures we give are the full-imbalance bound, which is the right order of magnitude and the right rhetorical point, but a working surveyor - the reader this section is explicitly written to keep on side - will spot it, and section 3 repeats the same form ("Break the balance and the term reappears at 0.0675D² metres"). The underlying constants check out: 0.0785D^2 curvature minus one-seventh gives 0.0673-0.0675, and 0.7 mm at 100 m and 6.8 cm at 1 km follow.
unverified.recommendation: "the combined curvature-and-refraction term stops cancelling and leaves 0.0675(Db² − Df²) metres for sight lengths in kilometres — at most 0.7 mm where a 100 m sight is wholly unmatched, at most 6.8 cm at a kilometre". Make the same change in refutation section 3: "Break the balance and the term reappears in proportion to the difference of the squared sight lengths: sub-millimetre at a hundred metres, up to 6.8 cm at a kilometre."

unverified.field: sources[] label for the Principal Triangulation Wikipedia entry

unverified.description: The label credits that page with two things it does not carry. On fetching it: it gives the survey dates (1791-1853), the 1858 report's full title, and a loose statement that surveyors allowed for "the spherical nature of the earth (meaning there were more than 180 degrees in a triangle)" - but it does not state the 289-station count, and does not mention the Airy ellipsoid. The 289 figure and both ellipsoid results are on the Alexander Ross Clarke entry, which we also cite and which confirms our numbers exactly: "a=20,927,005 ft., inverse flattening c=299.33" from British data alone, and 289 stations. So the facts are all sound; the pointer is aimed at the wrong one of our own two sources, and the Airy-ellipsoid reduction (true, and catalogued by The National Archives as "Latitudes and longitudes of the Principal Stations on Airy's 1830 Figure") is currently uncited.

unverified.quoted_phrase: Items 56 and 113 replace the inertial deflection with an electromagnetic one.
unverified.description: Sections six and seven refute items 56, 113 and 214 as though they were the credited originator's claims, with no scoping sentence, under a card whose meta line names Sungenis and Bennett as the source. The scoping does exist - it is in the compression block, which renders in a separate collapsed <details> after the refutation. The corrections entry of 2026-08-05 fixed exactly this in R08 by moving the disclosure to a heading ahead of the refutation. The same fix has not been applied here.
