We could not locate either claim in the Sungenis text we were able to search - the Vol. I archive rendering truncates inside chapter 1 and the Vol. II scan part-way through - so what follows answers a claim of unknown authorship that circulates in the list, not an argument of the cluster's credited authors, whose own version (below) contradicts it."

unverified.quoted_phrase: the measured parameter matches complete dragging to the precision of ring-laser gyroscopy
unverified.description: This is the quantitative hinge of our reply to the strongest form of the geocentric case, and it carries no citation - there is no ring-laser source in `sources`. It is also stated harder than the literature supports: the figure comes from large-ring-laser work where 1 part in 10^9 is a threshold recently reached, not a routine accuracy. The G Wettzell analysis (arXiv:2208.09134) opens "The absolute measurement of the Earth angular rotation rate with ground-based instruments becomes challenging if the 1 part in 10^9 of precision has to be obtained" and reports that "the Allan deviation drops below 1 part in 10^9 after an integration time of about 10^4 s". "Better than one part in 10^9" reads as an established margin; it is an integration-limited Allan deviation at the edge of the art. The argument survives comfortably at 1 part in 10^8, so the fix costs nothing.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "the measured parameter matches complete dragging to the limit of the best mechanical measurements of Earth's rotation - the large ring laser at Wettzell reaches an Allan deviation below one part in 10^9 after about 10^4 s of integration, and finds no discrepancy with the astronomical rate." Add to `sources`: {label: "Absolute measurement of Earth's angular rotation rate with the G Wettzell ring laser - Allan deviation below 1 part in 10^9 after ~10^4 s", url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09134"}.

unverified.quoted_phrase: Hans Thirring showed in 1918 that inside a rotating mass shell the inertial frames are dragged
unverified.description: Thirring 1918 is the single citation the STANDARD PHYSICS verdict rests on, it is named five times across the entry, and it appears nowhere in `sources`. We cite the 1985 repair and the 1966 extension - both of which I verified (Pfister & Braun, Class. Quantum Grav. 2(6):909-918, 1985, title exact; Brill & Cohen, Phys. Rev. 143:1011, 1966, title exact) - but not the paper being repaired. The Gravity Probe B numbers in the steelman are likewise uncited; they are correct (Everitt et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 106:221101, 2011: measured -37.2 +/- 7.2 mas/yr against -39.2 mas/yr predicted), but on a page whose product is provenance, an unsourced number in a steelman is the first thing a hostile reader tests. Worth adding: Thirring published a correction to the 1918 paper in 1921, which strengthens our "that result was imperfect" sentence rather than weakening it.
unverified.recommendation: Add to `sources`: {label: "Thirring, 'Uber die Wirkung rotierender ferner Massen in der Einsteinschen Gravitationstheorie', Physikalische Zeitschrift 19:33-39 (1918), with the author's own correction at Phys. Z. 22:29-30 (1921) - the rotating-shell result this argument rests on, and its first repair", url: "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lense%E2%80%93Thirring_precession"} and {label: "Everitt et al., 'Gravity Probe B: Final Results of a Space Experiment to Test General Relativity', Phys. Rev. Lett. 106:221101 (2011) - frame-dragging drift -37.2 +/- 7.2 mas/yr against -39.2 predicted", url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.3456"}.

unverified.quoted_phrase: about 300 miles or five degrees, and it has stayed there
unverified.description: Three problems in one clause, and the second is the one a defender uses. (i) NOAA AOML says "the storm must be at least 300 miles from the equator", not "about"; and 300 miles is 4.3 degrees of latitude, not five. (ii) "it has stayed there" is an empirical stability claim with nothing behind it - NOAA's FAQ is a rule of thumb, not a time series, and we have not shown the cyclogenesis exclusion latitude is stable to better than a few degrees. (iii) The comparison is therefore between quantities of the same size: Yizengaw's migration, which I verified verbatim ("latitudinal swath reaches ~3.85 degrees latitude in about twenty years or at the displacement rate of 0.2 degrees per year" at 47W), is 3.85 degrees against an exclusion belt of ~4.3 degrees whose empirical width is surely larger than that. The far stronger argument is static and we do not use it: at any single epoch the dip equator sits many degrees from the geographic equator across the South American and Atlantic sector, yet the calm belt tracks the geographic line - no time series required.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "The line first, and the decisive version needs no history: at any single epoch the magnetic dip equator departs from the geographic equator by many degrees of latitude across the South American and Atlantic sector, while the belt in which cyclonic organisation fails tracks the geographic line - NOAA's hurricane researchers state it as a distance from the equator, at least 300 miles. The dip equator also migrates, about 0.2 degrees of latitude per year over Brazil, some 3.85 degrees in twenty years; the calm belt does not follow it."

unverified.quoted_phrase: because its rotation axis points the same way everywhere on it
unverified.description: The stated reason does not distinguish the two cases, so as written it explains nothing. A rotation axis is a single direction; the Earth's axis also "points the same way everywhere on it". The fact that does the work - and which the steelman states correctly ("only the component of the rotation vector along the local vertical enters the horizontal deflection") - is that on a flat disc the local vertical is parallel to the axis at every point, so the projection never changes sign. Anyone who knows the physics will spot that the TLDR's reason is vacuous, and the TLDR is the field most likely to be quoted back at us.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with "because on a flat disc the local vertical is parallel to the rotation axis everywhere, so the component that does the deflecting never changes sign."

unverified.quoted_phrase: That qualification is not modesty, it is accurate physics history
unverified.description: We quote Sungenis's hedge and then supply our own account of what it means, skipping the sentence in which he says what it means. The full passage reads: "...but not exactly. He discovered that the gravitational field inside the rotating universe was above zero. He discovered that these 'above zero' forces are caused by the centrifugal and Coriolis forces, the very ones that are deemed 'fictitious' in the Newtonian system and thus would measure zero." On his reading the inexactness is the point - it is what makes the forces real rather than fictitious - which is a claim, not an admission. Our gloss is compatible with the text but is not the only reading, and quoting the intervening sentence makes our own finding sharper, not weaker: Pfister and Braun's repair removes precisely the anomalous interior term he is celebrating.
unverified.recommendation: After "...says so twice in one sentence: very much like, and but not exactly." insert: "He then says what the inexactness is - the gravitational field inside the rotating universe was above zero - and reads that as showing the Coriolis and centrifugal terms are real rather than fictitious. Note what follows: the 1985 repair removes the anomalous interior term, so the modern literature does not vindicate his qualification, it deletes it."

unverified.quoted_phrase: Transcribed here from two press accounts of the film — Newsweek, 15 February 2019, for the first sentence, and JOE.co.uk for the second — which differ in small ways.
unverified.description: Three problems in the one provenance statement, on a page whose product is provenance. (1) The Newsweek article at the URL we cite carries a byline of "Feb 25, 2019 at 05:04 PM EST" (updated 3 March 2019), not 15 February 2019. The wrong date appears twice — in this locator and in the sources label. (2) The split attribution is wrong: Newsweek prints BOTH quoted sentences verbatim, including "We obviously were not willing to accept that, and so we started looking for ways to disprove it was actually registering the motion of the Earth." JOE.co.uk was not needed for the second sentence, and the two accounts do not differ on it at all; they differ only on the first (JOE prints "What we found is, when we turned on that gyroscope, we found...", dropping the "is, is" stutter and hyphenating "15-degree"). (3) The sources label puts a paraphrase inside quotation marks: the headline is "'Behind the Curve' Ending: Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves With Own Experiments in Netflix Documentary", not "Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves in Behind the Curve". Quote length is fine — 53 words, under the 60-word cap.
unverified.recommendation: Locator: "Bob Knodel speaking on camera in the ring laser gyroscope sequence. Transcribed here from Newsweek's account of the film, 25 February 2019, which carries both sentences verbatim; JOE.co.uk prints the same sequence with light copy-editing to the first sentence. No timecoded viewing of the film was made for this entry and the surrounding edit was not verified." Sources label: "Newsweek, “‘Behind the Curve’ Ending: Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves With Own Experiments in Netflix Documentary”, 25 February 2019 — transcription of the gyroscope quote and the closing light-through-holes experiment".

unverified.quoted_phrase: Jay L. Wile's contemporaneous review of the film describes the follow-up
unverified.description: The Wile post is not contemporaneous with the film and is not from 2019. Its own dateline reads 8 August 2023, and the Goodreads syndication of the same post reads "August 08, 2023 04:27" — two independent surfaces agreeing. The film premiered April 2018 and reached Netflix in February 2019, so this is a review written four and a half years later, and "contemporaneous" is the word carrying its evidential weight in a paragraph we lean on for the entire shielding narrative (the magnetic enclosure, the dome-of-stars hypothesis, the bismuth chamber). The substance checks out — the post does read "Thus, they repeated the experiment, this time putting the gyroscope in a container that excludes magnetic fields" and "they got the same result" and "a chamber made out of bismuth" — so only the dating and the reliability signal are wrong.
unverified.recommendation: Gloss: "Jay L. Wile's review of the film, posted 8 August 2023, describes the follow-up". Sources label: "Jay L. Wile, “A Really Good Flat Earth Documentary” (8 August 2023) — secondary account, written some years after the film, of the magnetic enclosure, the dome-of-stars hypothesis and the proposed bismuth chamber".

unverified.quoted_phrase: built the first gyroscope in 1852
unverified.description: Not supported by the source we cite for it, and wrong on the standard account. The Wikipedia "Foucault's gyroscope" page we list credits Foucault with naming the instrument ("I propose to name gyroscope the sole instrument which has served me to observe them") and makes no first-builder claim; Wikipedia's "Gyroscope" article gives the priority to Johann Bohnenberger, "who first wrote about it in 1817", with Walter R. Johnson's disc version in 1832. This is a free hit for a defender in the paragraph headed "where the evidence actually is" — the paragraph whose whole job is to be unimpeachable, since it is where the entry relocates the case so that it does not rest on the film. The argument is untouched: Foucault did build his in 1852 expressly to demonstrate the Earth's rotation and did coin the name.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "Léon Foucault built his gyroscope in 1852 as a follow-up to his pendulum, for the express purpose of demonstrating the Earth's rotation, and coined the word for it — the rotating-mass instrument itself goes back to Bohnenberger in 1817, but the name is Foucault's, from gyros and skopein, to view the rotation."

unverified.quoted_phrase: Position is externally updated; heading is not.
unverified.description: Overstated, and overstated in exactly the place the advocate is strongest. In an aided (GPS/INS) system the Kalman filter estimates and corrects attitude and heading errors as well as position — heading error becomes observable under horizontal acceleration and is trimmed from GPS velocity. A reader with avionics knowledge answers this sentence in one line and takes the section with it. The true and much stronger claim is about INITIAL alignment: gyrocompassing derives true north from the sensed horizontal component of the Earth's rotation vector with nothing fed in, which is precisely the operation the next clause already invokes.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "Position is externally updated, and in an aided system the filter trims heading error along with it. What is not supplied from outside is the initial heading: a strapdown platform obtains true north during gyrocompass alignment by sensing the horizontal component of the Earth's rotation vector, with no satellite and no star in view — the same operation a gyrotheodolite performs underground."

unverified.field: clusters.py A07 note (renders in the section 3 summary)
unverified.quoted_phrase: exactly 360°÷24h
unverified.description: The gloss is careful to say the opposite: "the sidereal rate — the one a gyroscope actually senses, because it measures rotation with respect to the local inertial frame rather than with respect to the Sun — is Ω = 7.292115 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹, or 15.041° per hour... The figure as spoken carries two significant figures and cannot separate them, so nothing here claims that this apparatus resolved sidereal from solar." The word "exactly" in the visible summary claims the match to the solar-day rate that the body declines to claim, and it points at the wrong quantity: what the instrument senses is 360° per sidereal day, not per 24 hours. Same field as the major finding above; separable defect, and separable in its consequences, because this one is a physics slip a specialist reader catches rather than a tone problem.
unverified.recommendation: Within the replacement note, use: "— the rate a rotating Earth produces to two significant figures (sidereal 15.041°/hour)" in place of "— exactly 360°÷24h".

unverified.quoted_phrase: The reversal is carried by item 12 alone, and the cluster is named after it.
unverified.description: drift_type="reversed" renders under the heading "The list overstates its own source" and the label "The item states the opposite of its source" — both of which assert that the 2018 film is the text item 12 was compressed from. Our own evidence says otherwise: the sources list dates a circulating mechanical-gyroscope version of the argument to a Metabunk thread opened 20 March 2016 (verified: thread start date 20 March 2016), two years before the film, and the entry's own answer to item 112 leans on that same 2016 artefact. The note is honestly scoped in one clause ("The only source text available to hold it against is..."), but the section header, the drift label and this sentence together leave a reader with a provenance claim the entry cannot support. This is the genealogy, which is the product; it also overlaps the year="2018" issue the writer reported to the parent, which the published prose does not carry.
unverified.recommendation: Insert after the quoted sentence: "One caveat on what is being compared. The film is not demonstrably the text the list compressed: a mechanical-gyroscope version of the claim was already circulating and being picked apart on Metabunk by 20 March 2016, two years before the film, and no earlier text of item 12's own is in our records. The filmed statement is the best source text we can hold the item against, and the reversal is stated on that footing rather than as a claim about descent."

unverified.quoted_phrase: which is the rate a rotating Earth predicts and the rate a stationary one puts at zero
unverified.description: The TLDR states flat what the body is careful to qualify — the recurring failure of writing the TLDR from memory of the argument. The refutation says: "the axis geometry is unresolved: a three-axis unit reports the magnitude of the rotation vector, the full 15.041° per hour at any latitude, whereas a single-axis unit with its input axis vertical reads only Ω sin φ. Nothing in this treatment depends on which it was." But the TLDR does depend on it: 15°/hour is "the rate a rotating Earth predicts" only for a unit reading the full vector. For a vertical single-axis unit at the filming latitude (San Diego, ~32.7°N) the prediction is about 8.1°/hour, and a 15°/hour reading would then NOT be the predicted value. The verdict survives either way — any non-zero reading contradicts a prediction of zero — but the headline sentence claims a match the entry elsewhere says it cannot establish.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "which is the magnitude of the rotation rate a turning Earth produces and the rate a stationary one puts at zero".

unverified.quoted_phrase: Navigation-grade units of this class are specified at bias uncertainties better than 0.01
unverified.description: "of this class" quietly assigns the filmed instrument to a grade the very next sentence says we cannot establish ("No make, model, input-axis orientation or uncertainty is given in the sequences the press transcriptions cover"). The 1,500× comparison is doing rhetorical work — implying the reading is too large to be bias — on an assumption the entry disclaims one sentence later. Self-limiting, hence minor, but it is the kind of sentence the advocate's "you promoted a spoken number to an experimental result" charge feeds on.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "Navigation-grade ring lasers are specified at bias uncertainties better than 0.01° per hour, some fifteen hundred times smaller than the figure reported here — though nothing available to us establishes that the filmed unit was of that grade."

unverified.quoted_phrase: If the Earth held still, that subtraction would be a fiction
unverified.description: Overstated against the model actually held. The barycentric correction removes the observer's velocity RELATIVE to the Solar-System barycentre. A neo-Tychonic cosmos - Sun circling a fixed Earth, stellar sphere carried with it, which is exactly what van der Kamp needed to keep aberration and parallax - reproduces the same relative velocity by construction, so the same correction applies with the attribution reversed and nothing is a fiction. Our own next paragraph concedes precisely this ('They are measurements of motion relative to matter'), so the sentence is not just exposed, it is contradicted two lines later by our own text, and it sits inside the paragraph the advocate block identifies as the page's most vulnerable.
unverified.recommendation: Replace 'If the Earth held still, that subtraction would be a fiction, and the fiction would have to be the reason exoplanet signals stay coherent across years of observation.' with: 'The correction is not optional and not a convention: leave it out and exoplanet signals decohere across a season. unverified.quoted_phrase: the earliest datable person to read the practice as solar was an outsider who was told he had misread it
unverified.description: Section 2 conflates two different propositions and credits Tertullian with denying the wrong one. Apology 16 (New Advent / ANF, checked 2026-08-09) reads: "Others, again, certainly with more information and greater verisimilitude, believe that the sun is our god ... The idea no doubt has originated from our being known to turn to the east in prayer." The next sentence is a tu quoque, not a denial: "But you, many of you, also under pretence sometimes of worshipping the heavenly bodies, move your lips in the direction of the sunrise." What the outsiders assert is that the sun is the Christians' god; what Tertullian denies is that. He does not deny — and cannot deny, since east is defined by sunrise — that the practice is keyed to the sun's rising, which is all item 446 ("Liturgical eastward orientation assumes sun's path") actually says. So "he was told he had misread it" overstates: he was told his conclusion did not follow, not that his description was wrong. The treatment's own `preemptive` field already warns against exactly this hardening ("do not let §2 harden into 'the eastward turn has nothing to do with the sun'"), which is evidence the writer saw the risk and the body sentence drifted past it anyway. The point survives intact once stated precisely, and stated precisely it is stronger — the structural parallel is that a directional practice is being used to read off a doctrinal commitment.
unverified.recommendation: Replace from "and the earliest datable person" to the end of the paragraph with: "and that the earliest datable reading of the practice as evidence of a solar commitment was an outsider's, answered on the spot. Tertullian concedes the description — Christians are “known to turn to the east in prayer” — and denies only the conclusion drawn from it, that the sun is the Christians' god; his reply is that pagans too “under pretence sometimes of worshipping the heavenly bodies, move [their] lips in the direction of the sunrise”. He is not denying that east is where the sun comes up. He is denying that facing it tells you what a man holds to be true — which is the inference this cluster needs and does not make."

Wikipedia's Computus article, which is our source, puts it exactly that way: the Alexandrian Easter "still placed the vernal equinox on 21 March, although Bede had already noted its drift in 725". A defender who checks the one citation attached to the claim finds a man who is not a designer, and the quantifier in a TLDR is the first thing a hostile reader tests (sweep pattern 2). The substantive point — the drift was recorded and not corrected for eight centuries — is true and is better served by saying that.

Refutation §4: replace "The designers knew the approximation was drifting and recorded it:" with "The tradition that ran it recorded the drift rather than correcting it:".

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Passes, and passes properly. The refutation is aimed at Hall's own chapters, not at the list fragment: every phrase attributed to Hall in the passage, gloss and compression block was checked verbatim against the sacred-texts transcriptions and all of it is there — sta12 ("a band of fixed stars about sixteen degrees wide, apparently encircling the earth"; "The plane of the zodiac intersects the celestial equator at an angle of approximately 23° 28'"; the 72/2,160/25,920 precession numbers; "The oldest circular zodiac known is the one found at Tentyra, in Egypt"; Cole's four-feet-nine medallion inside a seven-feet-nine square with the constellations "represented in a spiral"), sta32 (the Egyptian temples "miniature representations of the universe" sentence and all four Josephus clauses — land and sea, the seven lamps "referred to the course of the planets, of which that is the number", the twelve stones and "that circle which the Greeks call the Zodiac", the girdle that "signified the ocean"), sta14 (Ephesus "designed as a miniature of the universe") and sta09 (the four cardinal angles, the Eliphas Levi elemental gloss, "the perfect emblem of the microcosm and the macrocosm"). The second clause of the hedge rule is also honoured rather than gestured at: §2 and §3 answer the circulating dome reading on the object's own merits while §5 answers Hall's version, and the compression block says so explicitly. drift_type=unsourced_addition is the right call — the item's content word ("dome") is not in the chapter searched, and the note scopes the search to sta12 rather than to Hall's book. The new-rules check also passes: absence claims are scoped throughout ("not located in the text of that chapter as transcribed at sta12, which is the text we searched", "forty-one other chapters were not read", "in the descriptions we consulted", plus a volunteered gap for Cauville's 1997 monograph). One residual unscoped absence is flagged as a minor hole. No recommendation is shipped as published prose: the forward-looking editorial instructions all sit in `advocate`, which render.py does not render — which is itself the basis of hole 5.

holes.quoted_phrase: the item asserts the geometry it is meant to refute
holes.description: §7 claims that item 440, "Temple architecture mirroring revolving heavens", asserts the geometry it is meant to refute, because revolving heavens are "the motion of a sphere". That is false, and it is refuted by our own page. The modern flat model has revolving heavens: a firmament turning about the vertical axis through the north pole. Our own corpus carries the list item "Precession from dome rotation" (scripts/corpus.py:49), ARG-B08 describes the model as "the stars carried round on a dome that turns about the vertical axis through it" (scripts/_b8_B08.py:203), and deep_batch2 answers "Day-night cycle from firmament rotation" and "Precession from dome rotation" as mechanism claims of that same model. So "revolving heavens" discriminates between nothing, and item 440 is not self-refuting. The paragraph half-notices this three sentences later and contradicts itself: "either way it is a question about motion, not about shape". This is load-bearing, because verdict_challenge justifies SELF-CONTRADICTED on "items asserting concentric heavens and revolving heavens, which are the geometry of a sphere" (line 64) — with 440 removed, the internal contradiction rests on item 127 plus §5's Josephus nest alone. It survives, but the stated reasoning overstates its support, and a defender knocks this plank down in one sentence.
holes.recommendation: Replace the two sentences beginning "It is a real phenomenon" with: "It is a real phenomenon and it is what the builders watched. On its own it does not decide the shape question, and we are not going to pretend it does: a firmament turning over a plane also carries stars round a pole, and the list says so itself — 'Precession from dome rotation' and 'Day-night cycle from firmament rotation' are items in the same corpus. What decides it is that the turn has two centres, one in each hemisphere, which no single axis through a disc delivers; that is argued at B08 and not re-run here. What item 440 does is concede that the heavens revolve, which is a claim about motion; whether the sphere or the observer turns is the geocentric question, belonging to lane A and to D02." And amend verdict_challenge line 64 to read "alongside it, an item asserting concentric heavens — which, in the Latin-European art it names, are drawn around a globe", dropping the appeal to revolving heavens.
holes.short_summary: §7 wrongly says "revolving heavens" is sphere-only geometry
holes.failure_scenario: A defender replies: "Our model has revolving heavens — the firmament turns over the disc; your own site lists 'Precession from dome rotation' as one of our claims and your B08 argument spells out the turning dome. Item 440 asserts nothing about shape, and your own next sentence admits it is 'a question about motion, not about shape'. You have counted a non-contradiction into a SELF-CONTRADICTED verdict." The rebuttal costs nothing to make and lands on a plank the verdict_challenge names.

holes.quoted_phrase: The kernel also reaches only two of the seven items.
holes.description: The count contradicts the enumeration that immediately follows it. The cluster has exactly seven items (74, 126, 127, 163, 430, 440, 456 — confirmed in data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json). The sentence then names six of them as items the kernel does nothing for: 127, 440, 74, 430, 126, and 163. Seven minus six is one, not two. This is failure pattern 2 from the harness — a quantifier written from memory of the argument rather than from the argument — and it appears in the section a reader opens second.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "The kernel reaches exactly one of the seven items — 456, the ceiling itself."
holes.short_summary: "only two of the seven" contradicts its own list of six
holes.failure_scenario: A reader counts: the sentence excludes 127, 440, 74, 430, 126 and 163, which is six of seven, leaving one. The published number is two. Anyone checking our arithmetic in the section where we are being most scrupulous finds us unable to count our own items.

holes.quoted_phrase: The relief is round, and it was fixed above a viewer’s head
holes.description: The relief is not round. It is a square sandstone slab carrying a circular composition. Our own passage quote says so in the words Hall chose to print — John Cole's medallion is "enclosed in a square, whose sides are seven feet nine inches long" — and the gloss makes the square frame a point of the argument ("A spiral on a flat medallion in a square frame is a draughtsman's solution"). The Wikipedia article we cite states that "the square of the overall sculpture is oriented to the walls of the temple". §2 concedes more than the object gives, and it concedes it against our own evidence two fields earlier.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "The carved sky-disc is round, and the slab it is cut into was fixed above a viewer’s head, so a person standing under it stood under a disc of stars set in a square frame."
holes.short_summary: "The relief is round" contradicts our own quoted square frame
holes.failure_scenario: A defender reads the gloss, where the square frame is evidence that the object is a draughtsman's map, then reads §2, where the object is round and therefore dome-like. Either the shape argument in the gloss is wrong or the concession in §2 is; the page asserts both within one screen.

holes.quoted_phrase: pronaos built under Tiberius
holes.description: The source label places "late Ptolemaic, c. 50 BCE" and "pronaos built under Tiberius" in one line about one object, which dates the relief's own pronaos sixty-five to ninety years after the relief. egypt-museum.com does say "The pronaos itself was constructed under the Roman emperor Tiberius", but that sentence conflates the main Hathor temple's pronaos (Tiberian, per the Dendera Temple complex article we also cite) with the pronaos of the roof chapel of Osiris, which is where the zodiac ceiling was and which is Ptolemaic. §1 of the refutation gets this right by writing "the hypostyle hall was added under Tiberius"; the source label repeats the conflation uncorrected, and source labels are rendered to readers by render.py.
holes.recommendation: Replace the label with: "Dendera Zodiac — Louvre inventory D 38 / E 13482 / CM 464; sandstone bas-relief; late Ptolemaic, c. 50 BCE; from the ceiling of the pronaos of the roof chapel of Osiris. (This page's sentence that 'the pronaos itself was constructed under the Roman emperor Tiberius' describes the main temple's pronaos, not the Osiris chapel's, and is not followed here.)"
holes.short_summary: Source label dates the relief's pronaos to Tiberius, c. 50 BCE relief
holes.failure_scenario: A defender reads the label and says: "By your own citation the pronaos this ceiling came from was built under Tiberius, so the ceiling is first-century AD, so your Cauville 50 BCE dating and your two eclipses are attached to the wrong room." The reply exists, but it is not on the page, and the contradiction we hand them is our own.

holes.quoted_phrase: Hall does the list’s work for it and then undoes it in the same paragraph
holes.description: advocate.survives is set to 4, and the schema in scripts/deep.py states that survives >= 3 obligates a concrete text change in `preemptive`. No text change was made. The preemptive is entirely a defence of text that already exists, and for the one move its own author calls "the one that must not be fudged" — the charge that Hall's "celestial equator" and "23° 28′" are 1928 astronomical vocabulary and not ancient testimony — the instruction is to keep the existing framing sentence and add nothing. render.py does not render the `advocate` field at all (it renders tldr, passage, steelman, refutation, compression, verdict_challenge when challenged, straw_man, related, people, sources), so the answer to the strongest move of the strongest defence is invisible to every reader. A grep of the rendered fields for "1928" and "vocabulary" finds the caveat nowhere. The existing framing does scope the geometry to Hall's chapter, which is why this is moderate rather than major — but the disclaimer the writer judged mandatory is not published.
holes.recommendation:
Add to the gloss, immediately after the framing sentence: "

One thing this section does not claim. Hall’s “celestial equator” and his 23° 28′ are the ordinary astronomical vocabulary of 1928 and they are not testimony about what the builders of Dendera believed. The point here is narrower, and it is about the proof set rather than about ancient Egypt: the list offers Hall’s chapters as its authority, so what those chapters say about the shape of the thing is a fact about the list’s own source.

"
holes.short_summary: survives=4 but preemptive makes no text change; advocate is unrendered
holes.failure_scenario: A defender writes: "Your star witness is Manly Hall's 1928 editorial prose, written in 1928 astronomy's vocabulary. Quoting his framing as though it were ancient testimony is compression — the offence your own hedge rule exists to catch." Our answer is written down, rated, and placed in a field render.py never emits, so the published page meets the charge with silence.

holes.quoted_phrase: A planisphere is a projection: a spherical sky flattened onto a plane by a stated rule
holes.description: The Dendera ceiling is not a ruled projection. Its constellations are laid out schematically — "represented in a spiral", in the description we ourselves print from Cole — and no projection rule produces a spiral. The sentence defines the word in a way the object does not satisfy, and then §3 leans on that definition to say the geometry "is visible whether or not it was named". The claim we actually need is weaker and true: it is a sky map on a flat surface whose contents are laid out as seen from a centre, with a zodiacal band around it. Wikipedia's own wording — "a planisphere or map of the stars on a plane projection" — supports the weaker claim, not the ruled-projection one.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "A planisphere is a sky map on a flat surface — in the reference accounts, “a planisphere or map of the stars on a plane projection”. Dendera’s is schematic rather than ruled; the constellations run in a spiral, as Cole’s description says, and no projection rule produces a spiral. What matters is not the rigour of the rule but what is being laid flat: the contents of the sky as seen from a centre, with the zodiacal band around it."
holes.short_summary: "projection by a stated rule" is not what the spiral layout is
holes.failure_scenario: A defender says: "You define a planisphere as a sphere flattened by a stated rule, then cite a description saying the constellations run in a spiral. Name the rule. You cannot, because there isn't one — the layout is symbolic, which is our whole point about the ceiling." Our own quoted evidence supplies the ammunition.

holes.quoted_phrase: Its first chapter argues that the earth is one
holes.description: Garbled clause. Sacrobosco's first chapter argues that the earth is a sphere, which is the point of the sentence and the point of §6; "the earth is one" states nothing, and it sits at the pivot of the paragraph, immediately after "Its title is the sphere". The five observational arguments listed after it were checked against the De sphaera mundi article and all five are there (stars rising sooner in the east, lunar eclipses timed differently by longitude, more northern stars visible as one travels north, seeing further from the masthead, water taking a round shape).
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Its first chapter argues that the earth is a sphere, from observations"
holes.short_summary: "the earth is one" should read "the earth is a sphere"
holes.failure_scenario: A reader reaches the sentence that carries §6 and cannot tell what Sacrobosco is being said to have argued. In a section whose whole job is that the concentric heavens are drawn around a ball, the word "sphere" is missing from the one clause that needed it.

holes.quoted_phrase: no ancient label on the stone says it
holes.description: An unscoped absence claim about an object whose inscriptions we did not read, in a treatment that scopes its absence claims carefully everywhere else ("not located in the text of that chapter as transcribed at sta12", "forty-one other chapters were not read", "in the descriptions we consulted"). The ratcheting test counts unscoped absence-claims and they may fall but never rise. The claim is almost certainly true and it is made as a concession in the defender's favour, which is why it is minor — but it is the one sentence in the entry that states a corpus-wide absence from a sample, and §2 already declares that Cauville's 1997 monograph, the publication that would settle what is written on the stone, was not read.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and no ancient label reading anything like ‘projection’ appears in the descriptions of the stone’s inscriptions we consulted — Cauville’s 1997 monograph, which would settle it, we did not read"
holes.short_summary: Unscoped absence about the stone's inscriptions, unread
holes.failure_scenario: The ratcheting unscoped-absence test picks this up, or a defender asks which publication of the Dendera inscriptions we searched — and §2 has already told them we did not read the one that catalogues them.

reviews.summary: D08 is one of the stronger entries in the lane and its analysis survives: every Hall quotation checks out verbatim against sta12, sta32, sta14 and sta09; the UCL zodiac-import quote, the Victorian Web account (Jean Lelorrain, explosives, Paris summer 1822, Louis XVIII's 150,000 francs, Champollion's autokrator, the Mosaic-chronology sentence), the Louvre numbers D 38 / E 13482 / CM 464, the Cauville–Aubourg 50 BCE dating with the 25 September 52 BCE lunar eclipse as an Eye of Horus locked in a circle and the 7 March 51 BCE solar eclipse as Isis holding a baboon by the tail, the four women and four falcon-headed pairs at 45°, the Sacrobosco facts (c. 1230, hundreds of manuscripts, Ferrara 1472, at least 84 editions in two centuries) and the Nut quotations all verify in the editions cited. The steelman is genuine KERNEL tier — it concedes the native Egyptian sky-over-flat-earth cosmology outright and then shows the zodiac is the one imported element — and the hedge rule is satisfied in both clauses. The verdict SELF-CONTRADICTED holds, but on narrower support than the entry claims: §7's argument that item 440's "revolving heavens" asserts sphere-only geometry is wrong, because the flat model posits a revolving firmament, as our own corpus item "Precession from dome rotation" and ARG-B08's turning dome both state, and the same paragraph then concedes it is "a question about motion, not about shape". Alongside that, seven smaller defects: the kernel's item count says two where its own enumeration leaves one; §2 calls a square slab round against our own quoted Cole description; a rendered source label dates the relief's pronaos to Tiberius beside a c. 50 BCE relief; advocate.survives=4 produced no text change, and the caveat the writer called mandatory sits in a field render.py never emits; §3 defines a planisphere as a ruled projection the spiral layout does not satisfy; "the earth is one" should read "the earth is a sphere"; and one unscoped absence about the stone's inscriptions. One divergence worth noting rather than flagging: Wikipedia names the mason Claude Lelorrain where the Victorian Web source we cite names him Jean — our text follows the source it cites.

holes.quoted_phrase: the 3,000-mile height he assigns the sun, which is computed from measured angles and
holes.description: Wrong number, attributed to a named primary source. Rowbotham does not assign the sun a height of 3,000 miles in either edition this entry cites. The 1881 third edition, ch. V "The True Distance of the Sun" (sacred-texts za23.htm, pp. 99-104), reads "the distance of the sun over that part of the earth to which it is vertical is only 700 statute miles" and "the under edge of the sun is considerably less than 700 statute miles above the earth", with all luminaries "within a vertical distance of 1000 statute miles". The 1865 first book edition (Project Gutenberg #69892, the 1865 London Simpkin, Marshall text) reads "the actual distance of the Sun from the Earth is less than 4,000 miles" and puts the firmament within 6,000 miles; Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 1, gives the same "less than 4,000 miles" for Earth Not a Globe. 3,000 miles is the modern (Dubay-era) figure, not Rowbotham's. This is live in docs/index.html. The point of the sentence - that the figure is computed from angles and cannot be looked at - survives the correction intact and is in fact better documented, since Rowbotham reaches both figures by plane trigonometry from London/Brighton altitudes.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "So is the height he assigns the sun - “less than 4,000 miles” in the 1865 edition and “only 700 statute miles” by chapter V of the 1881 third edition - a figure he reaches by plane trigonometry from measured altitudes at two stations, and one nobody can look at."

holes.quoted_phrase: took the formula, on trust, out of the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on
holes.description: Misattributed provenance for the eight-inch table, on a page whose product is provenance. In the 1881 third edition the curvature rule and its table stand in ch. II at p. 10 (sacred-texts za05.htm, "a curvature or declination of 8 inches in the first statute mile", the table running 1 mile/8 inches to 120 miles/9,600 feet), and the only authority Rowbotham gives for it is a footnote reading "Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination." The Britannica appears exactly once in the book's General Index - "Levelling, quotation from the Encyclopaedia Britannica [34]" - and at p. 34 (za14.htm) he quotes that article on refraction, not on curvature: "For though the refraction may at a mean compensate for about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth, it sometimes exceeds one-fifth, and at other times does not amount to one-fifteenth." Searched: za04-za15 and za20, za23, and the General Index za68 of the 1881 sacred-texts transcription. So we have credited the Britannica with the one thing it is not cited for while missing the thing it is cited for - which is the refraction coefficient, i.e. exactly the ARG-B07 hinge the same paragraph points at. The corrected version is a stronger instance of taking a number on trust, not a weaker one.
holes.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "and Rowbotham takes it on trust from nobody in particular: the table at p. 10 opens “If the earth is a globe, and is 25,000 English statute miles in circumference”, and the only authority offered for the declination is a footnote reading “Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination.” The one encyclopaedia he does quote - the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling, at p. 34 - he quotes for refraction, which he reports as compensating “at a mean” about one-seventh of the curvature but “sometimes” exceeding one-fifth and sometimes not reaching one-fifteenth. That is where his coefficient comes from, and it is where the dispute lives (see ARG-B07)."

holes.quoted_phrase: he copied from an encyclopaedia
holes.description: The same misattribution as hole 2, in the field readers meet first and may never expand past. The eight-inch table is not copied from an encyclopaedia in either text checked: its stated authority in the 1881 third edition, ch. II p. 10, is the footnote "Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination." A defender who opens sacred-texts za05.htm - one click from our own source list - finds this in under a minute, and the TLDR is where they will have started. Secondary muddle in the same sentence: "the 1849 experiments" and "the Bedford Level test" are set against each other as two venues when the 1849 pamphlet's theodolite experiments were themselves at the Bedford Level (Schadewald ch. 1: "A small boat was sent out 6 miles from the Theodolite").
holes.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "and the curvature both are measured against comes off an arithmetic table whose only stated authority is a footnote pointing at “any work on geometry or geodesy”" - and, in the same sentence, change "the 1849 experiments run on a surveyor's theodolite" to "the 1849 experiments run at the same canal on a surveyor's theodolite".

holes.field: passage.locator (and the same claim in passage.gloss)
holes.quoted_phrase: definition stands in the introductory section of the 1865 first book
holes.description: NOT the already-reported work-id issue (passage.work=WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1865 vs a cluster crediting 1849) - this is about what we tell the reader the 1865 text says. We publish that "a shorter form of the same definition" stands in the 1865 introductory section, and the gloss repeats that "the definition in words appears in the introductory section of the 1865 first book edition" (line 73). The 1865 text (Project Gutenberg #69892, p. 3) reads in full: "The term 'zetetic' is derived from the Greek verb zeteo; which means to search or examine—to proceed only by inquiry." It stops there. The clause this entire entry is built on - "to take nothing for granted, but to trace phenomena to their immediate and demonstrable causes" - is not in the 1865 sentence; it is an 1881 third-edition expansion. "Take nothing for granted" opens our TLDR, heads section 1, and is the source_wording in the compression block, so calling the 1865 form merely "shorter" understates by exactly the phrase that matters. This is recurring failure #3 (1865 vs the enlarged 1881 third edition) in its subtlest form: the 1865 edition exists, the passage exists, and the load-bearing words are still not in it.
holes.recommendation: Replace the locator sentence with: "The 1865 first book edition carries a shorter definition in its introductory section at p. 3 - “The term ‘zetetic’ is derived from the Greek verb zeteo; which means to search or examine—to proceed only by inquiry” - and stops there; the clause ‘to take nothing for granted, but to trace phenomena to their immediate and demonstrable causes’ enters with the expanded chapter I of the 1881 third edition." And in the gloss (line 73) replace "and the definition in words appears in the introductory section of the 1865 first book edition and in the expanded chapter I of the 1881 third edition" with "and the definition in words appears in the introductory section of the 1865 first book edition, though without the clause this entry turns on: ‘take nothing for granted’ is an 1881 addition."

holes.quoted_phrase: speculative—imaginary—not tangible,—scheming, but not proving. …
holes.description: Our ellipsis cuts the sentence that immediately follows the definition in both editions, and it is the single best piece of evidence for this entry's own thesis. Verified verbatim in the 1865 text (Gutenberg #69892, p. 3) and confirmed as the next sentence in the 1881 ch. I (sacred-texts za04.htm): "None can doubt that by making special experiments and collecting manifest and undeniable facts, arranging them in logical order, and observing what is naturally and fairly deducible, the result will be far more consistent and satisfactory than by framing a theory or system and assuming the existence of causes for which there is no direct evidence..." Rowbotham's own definition therefore asks for experiments, logical arrangement and deduction - inference, named as such, two lines after "theoretic" is ruled out. Leaving it out costs us twice: it is the cheapest possible proof that the observation-versus-theory dichotomy collapses inside his own paragraph and not merely inside his apparatus, and without it section 2's "The argument needs ‘take nobody's word for it’ to mean ‘trust your eyes’" reads as our compression of him rather than the list's, which is the one place in the entry a hedge-rule attack could land.
holes.recommendation: Extend the quoted passage so the ellipsis falls after this sentence rather than before it, adding: "None can doubt that by making special experiments and collecting manifest and undeniable facts, arranging them in logical order, and observing what is naturally and fairly deducible, the result will be far more consistent and satisfactory than by framing a theory or system and assuming the existence of causes for which there is no direct evidence..." - and add to section 3, before (a): "The dichotomy is not stable even in the definition. The sentence directly after it asks that facts be collected and then “arrang[ed] in logical order”, with the reader “observing what is naturally and fairly deducible”. That is inference, in his own voice, on the same page as the rule that is supposed to exclude it."

holes.quoted_phrase: about which observers count, not by a rule about which observations do.
holes.description: The closing sentence of the entry asserts a cause for which nothing in the entry supplies a referent. Nothing above it has discussed which observers were admitted or excluded - the preceding sentence is about Wallace's raised sightline and Oldham's three poles, which are rules about observations, not observers - so a reader cannot tell whether we mean Hampden's refusal of the 1870 referee's verdict, the movement's later handling of Wallace, or something about Rowbotham himself. As written it is an unsourced causal claim in the most quotable position in the entry, and it brushes against the standing constraint on motive claims without naming anyone.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "It was stopped one step before it would have answered. The step is small and specific - a sightline high enough to beat the refraction, and a marker at the midpoint so the bulge has somewhere to show - and when Wallace took it in 1870 and Oldham repeated it in 1901 with three poles at equal height, the middle pole stood about six feet above the outer two."

holes.field: clusters.py D11 note (renders as the published basis line)
holes.quoted_phrase: Rowbotham's founding move — 'observation is real, theory is imaginary'
holes.description: Quotation marks around words Rowbotham did not write, on a page whose entire product is establishing who wrote what. It is a fair summary - his actual wording at 1881 ch. I p. 1 is that the theoretic is "speculative—imaginary—not tangible,—scheming, but not proving" - but the punctuation presents a paraphrase as a quotation, and the same paraphrase circulates elsewhere on the page in the expanded form "trust nothing you have not seen", which is further from anything he wrote and sits oddly beside his own call to arrange facts and deduce from them. Cheap to fix and it costs nothing rhetorically.
holes.recommendation: Replace the note with: "Rowbotham's founding move, in his own words: the theoretic is “speculative—imaginary—not tangible,—scheming, but not proving”. It is the epistemology the whole genre rests on, and it is the thing actually being defended."

citation_failures: scripts/_b8_D11.py:190 - Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling cited as the source of Rowbotham's curvature formula. The article is quoted in the book (1881 3rd ed., p. 34, per General Index entry 'Levelling, quotation from the Encyclopaedia Britannica [34]') but on REFRACTION; the curvature table at p. 10 is footnoted 'Any work on geometry or geodesy will furnish proofs of this declination.'

scripts/_b8_D11.py:192 - '3,000-mile height he assigns the sun' matches neither cited edition: 1881 3rd ed. ch. V (za23.htm, pp. 99-104) says 'only 700 statute miles'; 1865 (Gutenberg #69892) says 'less than 4,000 miles'.

scripts/_b8_D11.py:35 and :73 - the 1865 introductory definition is characterised as 'a shorter form of the same definition'; the 1865 sentence ends at 'to proceed only by inquiry' and does not contain 'take nothing for granted', which is the phrase the entry is built on.
reviews.summary: The argument is sound and the verdict (NOT DEMONSTRATED) holds - section 7's defence of it is the best-argued paragraph in the entry, and the hedge rule is satisfied: the refutation answers Rowbotham's chapter and his own experiments, not the list's fragments. Everything wrong is in the layer around the argument, and it is the same three recurring failures. Three sentence-level factual patches are needed, two in reader-first fields: the sun's height is 700 statute miles in the 1881 third edition (ch. V, pp. 99-104) and 'less than 4,000 miles' in 1865, not 3,000; the eight-inch curvature table is footnoted to 'any work on geometry or geodesy', not copied from the Britannica, whose Levelling article Rowbotham quotes at p. 34 for refraction - the coefficient that is actually the ARG-B07 hinge; and the 1865 definition stops at 'to proceed only by inquiry', so 'take nothing for granted' - our headline, our section 1 and our compression source_wording - is an 1881 addition and cannot be described as merely a shorter form of the same sentence. Verified clean and better than it needed to be: the Bacon I.xli and I.l quotations, both Hooke Micrographia clauses, the Royal Society's own 1662 First Charter wording, Horace Epistles I.i.14, the Osiander Ad lectorem attribution and Rosen's 'calculus consistent with the observations', the Experiment 1 wording and the six-feet-at-the-centre arithmetic, Schadewald on the 16-page pamphlet and its six theodolite experiments, Wallace 1870 and Oldham 1901, and the Wettzell ring laser, whose cited paper is titled 'Overcoming 1 part in 10^9 of earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data' - the instrument, the site and the figure all match. Not re-raised, per the brief: the WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1865 passage.work, the cluster's 1849 credit, and the 87/183-belongs-in-R10 split, though the last has a reader-facing consequence worth noting to whoever resolves it - the published cluster NAME, 'Perception is reliable; the observer defines the centre', asserts of Rowbotham the very doctrine our own section 5 says is not his.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Against the source under refutation, the hedge rule is honoured and honoured unusually well. I pulled Eliade's own sentences and both quotes are verbatim: the numbered schema and "According to Indian beliefs, Mount Meru rises at the center of the world, and above it shines the polestar" are in The Symbolism of the Center exactly as we print them, and "The multiplicity, or even the infinity, of centers of the world raises no difficulty for religious thought. For it is not a matter of geometrical space..." is verbatim in The Sacred and the Profane ch. 1 (hermetics.net transcription, chapter-01 URL). Guénon's "This centre constitutes the fixed point known symbolically to all traditions as the 'pole' or axis around which the world rotates" is verbatim in ch. 2 of the archive.org King of the World transcription, and that transcription does terminate in ch. 6, as we say. The entry answers the source at its full strength: it quotes "the zone of absolute reality" against itself, refuses the "only symbolism" move, and grants the traditionalist kernel outright. drifted=true with category_shifted is the right call and is not a work-avoidance setting - the six item texts match the corpus character-for-character (160 "Axis mundi doctrine.", 173, 174, 451, 453, 454), and the shift really is of category rather than wording. The one place a hedge IS stripped is not the source under refutation but a supporting exhibit: the Flatlantis blurb, which is doubly hedged ("alleged", "ancient cultures... believed existed") and which we recast as a flat assertion about a physical object. That is finding 2, raised at major rather than critical because it is not the target of the refutation.
reviews.summary: The verdict (UNFALSIFIABLE) holds and every quotation checks out verbatim against the primary sources, including both Eliade passages, Guénon ch. 2, Pausanias 10.16.3 and the Sūrya Siddhānta's two-pole verse. Two defects need new prose: §3's Meru case answers only the siddhāntic tradition while asserting an unscoped negative about "the Sanskrit astronomical tradition", leaving the Purāṇic Meru - the centre of a lotus-plan Jambūdvīpa, and the far commoner referent of item 173 - unmentioned and available to a defender as a cherry-picking charge; and the compression note recasts a doubly-hedged publisher's blurb about a named living author as a flat assertion about a physical object. new_rules_ok is false on the first of those: "did not treat" evades the ratcheting test's regex but is exactly the unscoped-absence pattern the rule names.
citation_failures: Guénon, Le Roi du Monde ch. 9 is quoted in our gloss as "The Omphalos and Sacred Stones"; the contents of the archive.org transcription we cite read "The Omphalos and the Sacred Stones". A dropped article inside quotation marks around a chapter title.

The three Jonathan Z. Smith quotations at pp. 5, 8 and 10 are correct - I verified each against the Engstrom thesis - but they were read there, not in To Take Place. The sources block discloses this in a label; the refutation prose does not, and the same entry scrupulously scopes its Guénon reading in the gloss.

Unchecked, recorded as unchecked and not relied on: "Three Purāṇic Statements on the Shape of the Earth", History of Science in South Asia, is blocked by robots.txt. It would be the best scholarly citation for the Purāṇic/siddhāntic split in finding 1; the recommendation below uses the Wilson Viṣṇu Purāṇa on wisdomlib and the Mount Meru Wikipedia article instead, both of which I did reach.

holes.quoted_phrase: The Sanskrit astronomical tradition did not treat Meru as a mountain at the middle of a plane.
holes.description: This is the defender's first move and we have not preempted it. There are two Hindu Merus. The Purāṇic Meru sits at the centre of Jambūdvīpa, innermost of seven ring-continents in seven ring-oceans, and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa likens the arrangement to "the seed-cup of the lotus of the earth" (Wilson trans., wisdomlib, Book II ch. 2) - a plan, not a globe, and by far the more widely circulated Meru. Item 173 says only "Hindu Mount Meru axis" and does not name a text, so nothing entitles us to route it to the siddhānta. Worse, the Wikipedia Mount Meru article - a source in the same family as the one we cite - states that "The Suryasiddhanta mentions that Mt. Meru lies at the centre of the Earth ('bhuva-madhya') in the land of the Jambunad (Jambudvīpa)", so the very text we march out carries Jambūdvīpa language. The sentence quoted is also the unscoped-absence pattern in disguise: a negative claim about a whole corpus made from one text. It slips the ratcheting test in tests/test_provenance.py only because _ABSENCE does not include "did not treat". Everything else in the Meru paragraph verified: sphere, bhūgola, 1,600 yojanas, ch. 12 v. 43 two pole stars at zenith, geocentric - all confirmed on the Surya Siddhanta article we cite.
holes.recommendation:
Replace the opening two sentences of the Meru paragraph with: "

Meru (item 173). The item names no text, and Hindu tradition supplies two Merus. The one the flat reading needs is genuinely there and is conceded first: the Purāṇic Meru stands at the centre of Jambūdvīpa, innermost of seven ring-shaped continents set in seven ring-shaped oceans, and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa likens the whole arrangement to “the seed-cup of the lotus of the earth” — a plan seen from above, with a mountain 84,000 yojanas high at its middle. Nobody has to be argued out of that reading; it is the plain sense of the text. What has to be said next is that the same civilisation's computational astronomy, the tradition that had to predict eclipses and be checked against the sky, took the other option. The Sūrya Siddhānta holds that the Earth is a sphere — bhūgola, literally earth-ball — and gives it a diameter of 1,600 yojanas; its twelfth chapter, on cosmography, sets Meru on the axis of that sphere and states that on both sides of Meru, at the north and south poles of the earth, a polar star stands at the zenith." Then keep "Two poles." and the existing geocentrism concession unchanged.

holes.quoted_phrase: an assertion about a physical object at a physical place, which is precisely the step from symbol to geography this cluster turns on.
holes.description: We characterise a named living author's book from its publisher's blurb, and in doing so we strip the blurb's own hedges - the move this entire entry exists to catch. I fetched the Goodreads page: the description reads "Flatlantis is an exploration into the history of Flat Earth, the mythology of Atlantis, and the mystery of Mount Meru, the alleged magnetic mountain ancient cultures worldwide believed existed at the North Pole." Author, title and 2020 date all verified. But "alleged" and "ancient cultures... believed existed" put that sentence in exactly the reporting frame we praise Eliade for using two paragraphs earlier. Calling it "an assertion about a physical object at a physical place" reads the hedge off a living man's book description that we did not read past. The entry is otherwise scrupulous here - it says outright that a channel to the specimen is not established - which makes this sentence the odd one out.
holes.recommendation: Replace the em-dashed clause with: "— wording which is itself in reported form, saying what cultures are alleged to have believed rather than asserting the mountain is there, and which nonetheless names a magnetic mountain at a stated latitude. That is a kind of object Eliade's centre is not. The book was not read for this entry, so what it argues is recorded here as unchecked; the publisher's description is cited as evidence that a geographical reading of Meru circulates, not as a characterisation of its author's position, and" - then continue with the existing "Whether the specimen drew on that book is not established here...".

holes.quoted_phrase: where the traditions it names did astronomy, they answered the other way
holes.description: Recurring failure 2. The body insists on scoping this - "This section is scoped deliberately, because the material cuts unevenly and pretending otherwise would be the error this review exists to catch" - and then concedes in the same paragraph that the Sūrya Siddhānta is geocentric and therefore supports the Earth-at-rest half of the list. The TLDR carries neither that concession nor the Purāṇic complication of finding 1, and "the traditions it names" is plural and unqualified where the body reaches exactly one astronomical text. Our own advocate rates the geocentrism barb a genuine hit and rated the defence 4 for it; a reader who expands nothing meets the unhedged version first.
holes.recommendation: Replace the final clause of the TLDR with: "— and where the same traditions kept computational astronomy it went the other way on shape, the Sūrya Siddhānta setting Meru on the axis of a sphere with a polar star at the zenith of each of two poles, in a text that is itself geocentric and says so."

holes.quoted_phrase: A common corporate name for ancestors has been reinterpreted as the proper name of a single figure” (p. 5)
holes.description: Three quotations from To Take Place are printed with page cites in a way that reads as first-hand. They are accurate - I confirmed all three against the Engstrom thesis, including the p. 10 limiting sentence and the "typical narrative units" phrase at p. 8, and separately confirmed the terrestrial/chthonic line (p. 10) and "the language of 'center' is preeminently political and only secondarily cosmological" (p. 17) via the dreamflesh essay. But we read Smith through a University of Florida thesis, and the prose gives no sign of it. The sources block does disclose it in a label, which is why this is moderate and not major; the standard the entry sets for itself elsewhere is higher, since the very next section-worth of prose scopes the Guénon reading explicitly to a transcription that stopped at ch. 6. Our own corrections log (C02, 2026-08-09) treats quoting through an undisclosed intermediary as the exact move this site criticises.
holes.recommendation: After "and goes back to the ethnography." insert: "(Smith's sentences are quoted here as they are reproduced in Engstrom's University of Florida thesis, linked below, at the page numbers that thesis gives; the 1987 book itself was not consulted for this entry.)"

holes.quoted_phrase: clusters.py D04 and D05 record originator='Mircea Eliade (misapplied)' in a field
holes.description: The statement is no longer true and was already untrue when the file was finished. clusters.py D04 now reads originator=None with a dated comment block, D05 carries "Same correction as D04, 2026-08-09", and review/corrections.json logs the withdrawal under 2026-08-09 with named-originator and traced-item counts moved (20 to 19, 356 to 348). The module docstring carries the same stale claim under the heading "FOR THE PARENT - a record-level issue I could not fix". Neither field renders, so reader impact is nil and this is not the published-to-do failure the rules name; but it is a false statement about our own records inside our own review apparatus, on a project whose product is provenance, and the next agent who reads this file will go looking for a defect that has been repaired.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "clusters.py D04 and D05 formerly recorded originator='Mircea Eliade (misapplied)' in a field documented as naming the person who introduced the argument into the flat-earth canon. He did not. The field has since been set to originator=None with Eliade moved to real_source, where a genuine work being cited belongs, and the withdrawal is logged in review/corrections.json under 2026-08-09." Make the matching change to the docstring's "FOR THE PARENT" block, retitling it to record the fix as landed and leaving only the Guénon PER-* gap outstanding.

holes.quoted_phrase: sharing one is what the word smuggles in.
holes.description: This block renders on the page. "Smuggles" is on the harness's own list of loaded language to scan for, and here it attributes covert intent to a word choice made by the list's compiler, who is named in our corpus and is presumably living. The substantive point is right and worth keeping - "doctrine" does convert a comparative category into a shared teaching - but it needs no imputation of concealment to land, and the entry is otherwise notably clean on this: it names the unfalsifiable without ridicule and says in terms that it takes no position on anyone's religion.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "sharing one is what the word supplies, and it is supplied without argument."

holes.quoted_phrase: the archive.org transcription we fetched terminated in ch. 6, so that chapter is recorded here as unread rather than characterised.
holes.description: Not an error in this sentence - it is the model of how to scope a reading, and I verified the transcription does stop in ch. 6 with the omphalos chapter listed in contents but absent. The hole is what the gloss omits. Section 1 renders under the fixed heading "The claim in its own words" over an Eliade quotation, and the entry's own compression note says plainly that no author stands beside any of the six items and that Eliade and Guénon are this review's reconstruction of the vocabulary's origin. That disclosure renders after the refutation, in a block a skim-reader never opens. On a site whose product is provenance, the strongest self-limiting finding we have should not sit three sections downstream of the attribution it limits.
holes.recommendation:
Append to the end of the gloss: "

One limit on all of this, stated here rather than left to a later section. The specimen attributes these six items to nobody: the full text retrieved from it on 2026-08-09 was searched and carries no author or work beside any of them. Eliade and Guénon are named here as the origin of the vocabulary, on this review's reconstruction, and not as a citation the compiler made. What follows answers what they wrote; it does not claim they were read.

"

holes.quoted_phrase: nobody reads them as claims about topology
holes.description: Backwards. A schematic transit diagram is precisely a topological claim - connectivity and ordering are preserved exactly, and it is the metric geometry (distance, scale, direction) that is discarded. The analogy still works; the noun is wrong, and it is the sort of slip a technically literate defender quotes to suggest we are careless elsewhere.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "nobody reads them as claims about distance or direction".

holes.quoted_phrase: twelve witnesses are lying and there is no principled way to pick the twelfth
holes.description: Two problems in one clause. "Lying" imputes bad faith where the argument needs only error, and the entry elsewhere is careful to distinguish being wrong from lying (it grants that Guénon's position is "held by serious people" and that Eliade "meant it"). And "pick the twelfth" does not parse: on the geographical reading you are picking which single site is right and which twelve are wrong, so there is no twelfth to pick.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "twelve of the thirteen are mistaken, and there is no principled way to say which twelve".

holes.quoted_phrase: “The Omphalos and Sacred Stones”
holes.description: The chapter title is quoted with a word missing. The contents of the archive.org transcription we cite give ch. 9 as "The Omphalos and the Sacred Stones". Trivial in effect, but it is a titled citation inside quotation marks on a page whose subject is whether people reproduce their sources accurately.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "“The Omphalos and the Sacred Stones”".

holes.quoted_phrase: and all of it follows from a spinning ball
holes.description: Section 6 is headed "The one point of contact with measurement", which is where precision is worth most. Precession does not follow from rotation alone: it requires an oblate spinning body plus the gravitational torque of the Sun and Moon on the equatorial bulge. A perfectly spherical spinning Earth would not precess. Everything else in the paragraph checks out - sigma Octantis at magnitude 5.47, the ~25,772-year cycle, Thuban near the pole in the third millennium BCE, Polaris closest around 2100 CE, Vega in roughly twelve thousand years.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and all of it follows from a spinning ball once its shape is included — precession is the Sun's and Moon's pull on the equatorial bulge of a rotating, slightly flattened Earth, which is a chain of consequences a pole erected in a plane does not begin".

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Passes, with one qualification. The refutation's load-bearing section (6) answers the source's whole sentence including the governing clause "while adhering to all the proportions and motions that were in Galileo's heliocentric model" — I fetched the archive.org Vol. I scan and the sentence is there verbatim as quoted, so the rebuttal is aimed at the source's own wording and not at the five-noun-phrase fragment. Sections 1-5 argue against the items, but the treatment is explicit and repeated that the items contain no proposition (gloss 4, refutation 7), so it is not passing off a fragment-refutation as a source-refutation. Items 120, 121 and 122 have no located source passage at all and the compression note says so in scoped terms rather than asserting absence. The qualification is recorded as hole 5: the direction of the drift may be mischaracterised, and characterising Sungenis's sentence as a mere "possibility" arguably understates the source rather than overstating it — which is a hedge-rule error running the other way, and milder, but the same species.

holes.quoted_phrase: the Jowett Phaedo text at Project Gutenberg gives
holes.description: The quotation "a globe placed in the centre of the heavens... maintained there by the perfection of balance" is not Plato and not the Phaedo. Fetching https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1658/1658-h/1658-h.htm returns it from Jowett's INTRODUCTION, in the form "Now the whole earth is a globe placed in the centre of the heavens, and is maintained there by the perfection of balance" — Jowett's own nineteenth-century summary essay, not the translated dialogue. Our sources entry lists it under "Plato, Phaedo (Jowett)" as though it were the text. This matters more than a stray citation because it is the ONLY primary-text support the treatment offers for Plato holding the Earth to be a globe: the 33b quote in the same paragraph is about the WORLD/cosmos, not the Earth (confirmed against classics.mit.edu/Plato/timaeus.html: "he made the world in the form of a globe, round as from a lathe"), so once the Jowett sentence goes, the closing "Round Earth, round heavens, one centre" has nothing under its first two words — and both the TLDR ("All four men named here worked with a spherical Earth") and the cluster note ("Every one of them held the Earth to be a *sphere*") rest on it. The claim itself is true (Phaedo 108e-110b), but our own biography rule — quote provenance, not a paraphrase drifted through secondary literature — is the rule we broke. NOTE FOR THE PATCHER: our fetch tool truncates every online Jowett Phaedo I tried (Gutenberg, classics.mit.edu, LibreTexts) before the closing myth, and standardebooks is robots-blocked, so I could NOT verify Jowett's exact dialogue wording; the replacement below therefore describes the passage instead of quoting it, and the Stephanus range should be checked against a reachable edition before it is published.
holes.recommendation: In refutation section 4, replace from "What is not disputed" to the end of the paragraph with: "What is not disputed is the shape of Plato's cosmos: in the same dialogue the maker “made the world in the form of a globe, round as from a lathe, having its extremes in every direction equidistant from the centre” — a sentence about the universe, not about the Earth. For the Earth itself the text is the Phaedo, whose closing myth at 108e–110b has it round, resting at the middle of the heaven with no support but its own equipoise, and seen from above like a ball made of twelve pieces of leather. The often-quoted line about “a globe placed in the centre of the heavens… maintained there by the perfection of balance” is Jowett's summary in his introduction to that dialogue rather than Plato's own words, and is not relied on here. Round Earth, round heavens, one centre." And replace the sources[5] label with: "Plato, Phaedo (Jowett), Project Gutenberg ebook 1658 — the closing myth at 108e–110b, the Earth round and central and self-balancing. The sentence 'a globe placed in the centre of the heavens, and is maintained there by the perfection of balance' occurs in Jowett's introduction to the dialogue, not in Plato, and is not cited as Plato here; the Perseus edition is blocked to our fetch tool by robots.txt and was not consulted".

holes.quoted_phrase: Three independent statements of the same concession, two of them from inside the tradition being cited.
holes.description: The count is wrong and the attribution is wrong. I fetched the Schadewald appendix (cantab.net .../PlaneTruth/pages/Appendix_D.html) and pulled the full paragraph. The sentence "The variant of the Tychonian system advocated by the Association for Biblical Astronomy can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system" is Schadewald's own assertion, in his own voice, sandwiched between "All modern American geocentrists seem to be young-earth creationists who hold that the Bible compels them to reject Copernicus along with Darwin" and "This makes it far more coherent than Flood Geology... Nevertheless, most creationists seem embarrassed by geocentricity." Schadewald is a critic of geocentrism writing a debunker's appendix; he is offering the point as the reason the position beats flood geology, not conceding anything on the movement's behalf, and the movement is not quoted. So of the three statements, exactly ONE (the Sungenis-Bennett sentence) is from inside the tradition; Schadewald and Wikipedia are both outside it. A defender who checks the link finds us sourcing a movement 'concession' to its opponent, on a page whose product is provenance.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence with: "Three independent statements of the same equivalence, one from inside the tradition and two from outside it — the authors' own sentence above; Schadewald's account of what the Association for Biblical Astronomy's variant does, written by a critic of geocentrism who offers it as the reason the position is more coherent than flood geology; and the standard summary of the historical system."

holes.quoted_phrase: the Sun some 93 million miles off
holes.description: Galileo's heliocentric model did not contain a Sun 93 million miles away, and the sentence says explicitly that these are the things "Galileo's model contained". The scale of the solar system in 1632 was the inherited ancient one: Copernicus used about 1,142 Earth radii for the solar distance and Tycho about 1,150 (liquisearch.com/astronomical_unit/history), roughly 4.5 million miles, about a twentieth of the true value. The first roughly modern determination is Cassini and Richer's Mars-parallax work of 1672 — forty years after the Dialogue — which gave 87 million miles (thegreatestsciencediscoveries.wordpress.com, which also notes that "Before Cassini, most scientists believed that stars were only a few million miles away"). This is the one factual error in the treatment that a defender can check in a minute, and it sits in the first paragraph a reader meets after the quote. The argument is untouched by the fix — the point is that a model preserving Galileo's proportions preserves a globe of definite size in a Sun-centred planetary system, whatever the era's numbers were.
holes.recommendation: Replace "a globe some 7,900 miles across, five planets going round the Sun, the Sun some 93 million miles off, a Moon of measured distance and diameter" with: "a globe of a definite size, five planets going round the Sun, and a Sun and Moon at definite distances — the seventeenth century's figures, not ours. Copernicus and Tycho alike put the Sun at about 1,150 Earth radii, roughly a twentieth of the true distance, and the first approximately modern value came from Cassini and Richer's Mars parallax in 1672, forty years after the Dialogue. The point does not turn on the numbers: whichever era's proportions you take, taking them means taking a globe of a definite radius inside a Sun-centred planetary system."

holes.quoted_phrase: the same source records the movement's own summary of what its Tychonic variant does
holes.description: Second instance of the Schadewald misattribution flagged above, in a different field and needing its own replacement text.
