The sentence "can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system" is not "the movement's own summary"; it is the assessment of a critic documenting the movement, and the closing gloss "That is the equivalence concession again, from the other end of the lineage" compounds the error by treating an outsider's description as a concession from inside.
holes.recommendation: Replace "and the same source records the movement's own summary of what its Tychonic variant does: it “can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system.” That is the equivalence concession again, from the other end of the lineage." with: "and the same source — written by a critic of geocentrism, not an adherent — records what the movement's Tychonic variant does: it “can predict exactly the same relative motions between celestial bodies as the conventional system.” That is the same equivalence, stated from outside the movement by the man who documented it."

holes.quoted_phrase: and there is no hedge here to drop
holes.description: The block argues against itself and the drift_type is the weaker of the two available readings. (a) This clause denies there is a qualification to drop, while the paragraph immediately above it is headed "The clause that does not travel is the one that decides the case" and makes a dropped governing qualification — "while adhering to all the proportions and motions that were in Galileo's heliocentric model" — the whole point of the assessment. A reader can see both statements without scrolling. (b) force_upgraded is defined in deep.py as "a concession or permission is re-used as a proof", and nothing in the source sentence marks it as a concession. Read in place (I fetched the Vol. I scan), Sungenis and Bennett are asserting, in a book arguing that geocentrism is true, that Urban VIII already had a scientifically adequate alternative to Galileo. Using that as an evidence item is close to the authors' own use of it, which is what drift_type "none" describes. The R01 parallel invoked at the end of the paragraph does not carry: van der Kamp flagged his own sentence as a concession ("forcing an open door"); this sentence contains no such marker, and "how easy it is to envision" is the authors praising the model's virtue, not hedging it. As written we make the source weaker than it is, which is the hedge rule's failure mode running in the other direction.
holes.recommendation:
Replace the third paragraph of the note with: "

What the drift is, and what it is not. We record this as force_upgraded and the reading has to be defended, because the source is not conceding anything: read in place, the authors are asserting — in a book arguing that geocentrism is true — that Urban VIII already had a scientifically adequate alternative to Galileo. What moves is not the wording and not the author's confidence but the governing clause. The sentence buys its Tychonic model at a stated price, “while adhering to all the proportions and motions that were in Galileo's heliocentric model”, and the price does not travel: items 22 and 123 carry the model and leave the clause behind. Readers who prefer hedge_dropped for that pattern have a case, and the two labels point at the same missing words. What we did not find is any qualification of confidence — no “may”, no “on this reading” — so the refutation meets the sentence at full strength rather than treating it as tentative. We also considered unsourced_addition for items 120, 121 and 122, since we did not locate the authors' own appeals to Plato, Aristotle or Ptolemy in the parts of either scan we could read. That was rejected as unsupportable: our fetch tool truncated the Volume I scan at about p. 26–30 and the Volume II scan at about p. 30, both works run past a thousand pages, and the Volume II table of contents plainly advertises a chapter called Hildegardian Geocentrism: Aristotelian Cosmology Meets Modern Science. Unreached is not the same as absent, and no claim of the second kind is made here.

"

holes.quoted_phrase: smuggled in under the same numbering
holes.description: "Smuggled" imputes deliberate concealment to whoever compiled the list — a living person about whom this project may make no motive or bad-faith claim — and it is the first word in the harness's own list of loaded language to scan for (curmudgeon.md, holistic check 3: "smuggled, pretend, dishonest, deliberate, quietly, merely"). It is also unnecessary: the sentence's force comes from the mismatch between a Tychonic cosmology and a flat-Earth list, and that mismatch is fully carried by a neutral verb. This is the only loaded word in our own voice anywhere in the file; "credulous" and "clever and empty" both occur inside quoted or role-played positions.
holes.recommendation: Replace "It is a rival cosmology to the one the list is defending, smuggled in under the same numbering." with: "It is a rival cosmology to the one the list is defending, carried under the same numbering."

holes.quoted_phrase: Item 122 invokes Ptolemy's spheres
holes.description: Section 5 is described in the docstring as the one thing D02 adds that A22 has no reason to say, so it carries weight, and as written it is open to a one-line reply: the spheres of the Almagest — the text A22 quotes and the text a reader will assume is meant — are mathematical devices, deferents and epicycles, and a comet passing through a geometrical construction refutes nothing. The collision is real, but it needs the right Ptolemaic text named. Ptolemy's physical cosmos of nested solid shells is in the Planetary Hypotheses, where he "goes beyond the mathematical models of the Almagest to present a physical realization of the universe as a set of nested spheres" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy) and computes the dimensions of the universe from them. Naming it closes the escape route and makes the section stronger, not weaker.
holes.recommendation: Replace "Item 122 invokes Ptolemy's spheres — the nested celestial orbs of the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic cosmos." with: "Item 122 invokes Ptolemy's spheres. Be precise about which spheres, because it decides the point: the Almagest's deferents and epicycles are geometry, and geometry is not broken by a comet. The solid ones are Ptolemy's too — the Planetary Hypotheses goes beyond the Almagest's mathematics to give a physical universe of nested spheres and computes its dimensions from them, and that is the cosmos the medieval and early-modern tradition inherited under his name."

holes.quoted_phrase: His argument against a moving Earth in the same chapter is empirical, not metaphysical
holes.description: Overstated as a definite description, and checkable in the chapter we cite. In De caelo II.14 (classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/heavens.2.ii.html) Aristotle gives several arguments against a moving Earth, and the first is exactly the kind this sentence denies: any motion of the Earth would be forced rather than natural, and "the movement could not be eternal. But the order of the universe is eternal." The natural-motion-to-the-centre argument ("the natural movement of the earth, part and whole alike, is the centre of the whole") comes before the stellar one as well. The observational argument we quote is genuinely there and genuinely his, but it is one of four, and saying "his argument... is empirical, not metaphysical" invites a defender to open the chapter and produce the metaphysics in the first paragraph. Scoping it costs three words and loses nothing, since the point being made is only that he nominated a falsifier.
holes.recommendation: Replace "His argument against a moving Earth in the same chapter is empirical, not metaphysical: if the Earth moved," with: "He gives four arguments against a moving Earth in that chapter, and three of them are what you would expect — forced motion cannot be eternal, earth's natural movement is towards the centre, a stone thrown up comes back to where it started. The fourth is not metaphysics at all. If the Earth moved,"

holes.quoted_phrase: the same chapter of De caelo that this cluster relies on
holes.description: The cluster does not rely on that chapter. Item 121 is "Aristotle's unmoved mover", which our own refutation section 3 correctly locates in Metaphysics XII.7-8; De caelo II.14 is a text WE bring to the argument, not one the cluster invokes. Small, but it contradicts section 3 of the same entry, and the straw_man block renders on the page (render.py line 240).
holes.recommendation: Replace "the estimate of 400,000 stades for the Earth's circumference is passed on in the same chapter of De caelo that this cluster relies on." with: "the estimate of 400,000 stades for the Earth's circumference is passed on in De caelo II.14, the chapter that carries both of those arguments."

citation_failures: sources[5] Plato, Phaedo (Jowett), Gutenberg 1658 — FAILED. The quoted sentence is in Jowett's introduction, not in Plato's dialogue. Verified by direct fetch of the Gutenberg page, which returns it as "Now the whole earth is a globe placed in the centre of the heavens, and is maintained there by the perfection of balance" from the introduction section; the top web-search hit for the phrase is 'Phaedo (Jowett)/Introduction' on Wikisource.

sources[10] Schadewald, The Plane Truth, Appendix D — the citation EXISTS and the quoted words are exact, but our characterisation of them fails. The label and refutation section 6 present the sentence as the movement's own statement; the fetched paragraph shows it as Schadewald's assertion in a critic's appendix.
Not a source-list failure but a citation-grade error: the gloss attributes to Galileo's model a solar distance of 93 million miles, a value first approximated by Cassini and Richer in 1672.
reviews.summary: Verdict holds — NOT DEMONSTRATED is right and section 7's reasoning for declining SELF-CONTRADICTORY is sound. I verified every classical citation against the editions named and they check out exactly: De caelo II.13 and II.14 (Timaeus/'rolled', eclipse shadow, Egypt and Cyprus, 400,000 stades, 'passings and turnings of the fixed stars'), Metaphysics XII.7 and XII.8 (fifty-five and forty-seven spheres), Timaeus 40b and 33b, the Wikipedia Tychonic-system sentences, the HAO Tycho page, Graney arXiv:1004.4034, the ESA parallax figures to the decimal, and the Sungenis sentence at p. 26 of the Vol. I archive scan word for word. Three things fail. The Plato sphericity claim rests on a sentence from Jowett's introduction cited as Plato's Phaedo, and with it removed the treatment has no primary text for a round Earth in Plato — which the TLDR and the cluster note both assert. The Schadewald equivalence line is a critic's assessment presented twice as the movement's own concession, making section 6's 'two of them from inside the tradition' false. And the gloss puts a 93-million-mile Sun inside Galileo's model, a value first measured forty years after the Dialogue. Six smaller holes follow, including 'smuggled' — the one loaded word in our own voice, and the first word on the harness's own watchlist.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The refutation is NOT aimed at the five-word fragment. It answers the teleological question first, then the cumulative Bayesian form (section 7), and only then the fragments — and it says so. That is the rule satisfied. But the baseline it measures drift against is not the source: `compression.source_wording` and the rendered "The source says" blockquote are distributor publicity issued via PRWeb 8 December 2015, fourteen months after release, for a film the writer states was not viewed. The drift verdict (category_shifted, question→assertion) is therefore a comparison of the list item against a marketing blurb, not against the film. This does not make the refutation land on the fragment — Hartnett's eyewitness review is used to establish where the film's positional argument actually sits, which is the right move — so hedge_rule_ok stays true. It does mean the published drift finding is weaker than the block presents it as, and the corroborating source cited for "the same wording runs through the film's promotional copy" does not carry that wording at all (checked: the 25 March 2015 In Ohm / PR Newswire release contains "Are we significant or just a cosmic accident?" and "our supposedly insignificant Earth", not the synopsis). Two holes below.
citation_failures: sources[1] — "The Principle — earlier distributor release carrying the same synopsis (In Ohm Entertainment, PR Newswire, 25 March 2015)": the release exists and is correctly attributed to In Ohm Entertainment, but it does not carry the synopsis. Two separate fetches return no occurrence of "The Principle explores the significance of the Earth's place within the Cosmos" or the "are we significant within the structure of the Universe?" passage. It carries different copy — "Are we significant or just a cosmic accident?", "unexpected evidence of a preferred direction in the cosmos", "aligned with our supposedly insignificant Earth" — which is the copy ARG-E01 quotes.

gloss — "Rick DeLano produced the film with Sungenis, who co-wrote it": contradicted by the film's credits in three places, including a source we ourselves cite. Variety's credit block reads "Screenplay by Rick DeLano"; Letterboxd and TV Guide both give Writer: Rick DeLano; the film's own 25 March 2015 distributor release gives "Producer/Writer Rick DeLano" and "Executive Producer Robert Sungenis". No source located credits Sungenis as writer.

gloss — Hartnett's position on the redshift shells is stated more strongly than he states it. He writes "Whether or not these shell are centred on the earth in real space requires some assumptions and interpretation of the evidence" and "It may only be a redshift space effect."
reviews.summary: The analysis is sound and the verdict holds: the refutation answers the strongest (Bayesian) form of the argument, concedes fine-tuning at full strength, adjudicates nothing about God or purpose, and does not sneer. Every physics citation checked out verbatim — Barnes's "I do not attempt to defend any conclusion", Laskar's ±1.3° about 23.3° and the 0°–85° chaotic zone, Cusa's Hopkins §162 sentence word for word, Variety's "a baby's smile" and "the crescendo of a symphony", the PRWeb synopsis in full. The defects are all in the layer around the argument, exactly as the sweep predicts: a screenplay credit given to the wrong living man, distributor publicity labelled as the film's own statement of thesis, a corroborating source that does not corroborate, a named living physicist's hedge compressed away in a treatment whose subject is compressed hedges, and a verdict-justifying count in section 8 that the compression block contradicts.

holes.quoted_phrase: Rick DeLano produced the film with Sungenis, who co-wrote it
holes.description: The film's writing credit is Rick DeLano's, not Sungenis's, and Sungenis's producing credit is executive producer. Variety's own credit block — a source we cite on this entry — reads "Screenplay by Rick DeLano"; Letterboxd and TV Guide both list Writer: Rick DeLano; the film's 25 March 2015 distributor release, also cited here, reads "Producer/Writer Rick DeLano" and "Executive Producer Robert Sungenis". No located source credits Sungenis with the screenplay. This is a claim about a named living man's authorship, on a page whose product is attribution, and it is the basis on which the cluster records originator="Robert Sungenis", originator_work="The Principle (film)" — the same failure shape as the D04 and C02 originator corrections. works.py WRK-PRINCIPLE-2014 carries it too ("Produced by Rick DeLano and Robert Sungenis"), and that record is linked from this passage block.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Rick DeLano wrote and produced the film — Variety's credit block reads Screenplay by Rick DeLano — and Robert Sungenis is its executive producer and appears in it on screen; Sungenis and Bennett's Galileo Was Wrong supplies the CMB material that the film's positional half rests on, which is treated at ARG-E01." Then amend WRK-PRINCIPLE-2014's imprint to "Written and produced by Rick DeLano; executive producer Robert Sungenis; directed by Katheryne Thomas; narrated by Kate Mulgrew. Released 24 October 2014.", and log the originator field in review/corrections.json as reported-not-yet-resolved: the cluster credits Sungenis for a film he did not write, and the field's own definition is the person who introduced the argument, not the person who financed the artefact.

holes.quoted_phrase: which is the film's own statement of its thesis and the text we were able to check
holes.description: It is not the film's own statement of its thesis. It is publicity copy issued through PRWeb by FrontGate Media on 8 December 2015, fourteen months after the film's release, for the home-video launch — and the locator on the same entry states we were unable to view the film. The rendered compression block heads this text "The source says", so a reader meets a marketing blurb presented as the source's own words, and the entire drift verdict (interrogative and teleological vs declarative and positional) is derived from it. This is the ARG-E03 correction shape — pointing readers at the artefact carrying the least of the argument — arriving one level down, in the label rather than the work record.
holes.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "which is the distributor's statement of the film's thesis, issued for the home-video release on 8 December 2015, and the only statement of it we were able to check in this pass". In compression.note, open the second paragraph with: "One scoping caveat, and it cuts against us: the wording compared here is distributor publicity, not the film's soundtrack, which we were not able to view. What the film asserts on screen is characterised below from John Hartnett's review, by a physicist who sat for its interviews and watched the result."

holes.quoted_phrase: he reads it as placing us near the centre of the visible universe
holes.description: Hartnett is a named living physicist and he does not read the shells that way. His review is explicit that the redshift-space centring is trivial because we observe from here, and that real-space centring is not established: "Whether or not these shell are centred on the earth in real space requires some assumptions and interpretation of the evidence", "Once certain assumptions are made about the Universe, allowing for what we can't see and cosmic variance, the result may well be that we can't conclude that it is real space cosmic structure", "It may only be a redshift space effect." His positional view he states separately and in his own terms — "(near) galactocentric", and "The planet Earth is in a special place in the Universe, which is not the same thing as being absolutely geocentric." Welding his shells work to a centrality conclusion he expressly declines to draw from it is the drop-the-hedge move this entry exists to convict the list of, performed by us on our own best witness.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "the concentric-shell structure in redshift space is his own work and he is careful about what it shows — the shells are centred on us in redshift space because that is where we observe from, and whether they are “centred on the earth in real space requires some assumptions and interpretation of the evidence”; it “may only be a redshift space effect”. His own position he states separately: the Earth is “in a special place in the Universe, which is not the same thing as being absolutely geocentric”, a view he calls (near) galactocentric. The “axis of evil”, he writes, “defines an axis in the cosmos, an anisotropy axis” — “But it does not point at the planet Earth.”" Carry the same correction into refutation section 2, which currently says he "does think we occupy a special place" without noting the special place is the galaxy's, not the Earth's.

holes.quoted_phrase: four of these five items make claims about significance, purpose and meaning
holes.description: The count is contradicted twice inside this entry, and it is the sentence that justifies the UNFALSIFIABLE verdict, so a reader who checks it finds the page arguing against itself. The compression block says of item 184: "The list item is declarative and positional: fine-tuning favors centrality." Section 3 opens "This is the decisive point for items 184 and 288" — i.e. it treats 184 as one of the two items the no-address argument is aimed at, which is only coherent if 184 is positional. And item 85, "Universe ordered around observer", is answered in section 5 by Cusa's observer passage as a claim about what every observer perceives — perceptual and geometric, not a claim about significance. On the entry's own readings the meaning-claims are 185 and 187, two of five, not four. Recurring failure 2 from the harness: a quantifier written last, from memory of the argument rather than from the argument.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence and the one after it with: "It records something specific. Two of these five items — “teleological seasons fit Earth” and “infinite universe removes meaning of center” — are claims about significance and meaning, and no observation settles those either way, not ours and not theirs. The other three are positional, and each fails for its own reason rather than for want of evidence: “cosmological constant fine-tuned Earthward” because a constant is the wrong kind of object to point anywhere, “fine-tuning favors centrality” because the connective is the list's own and no tuned quantity carries a location, and “universe ordered around observer” because that is what every observer everywhere sees, as Cusa set out in 1440. The cluster is filed UNFALSIFIABLE because the premise all five need — that centrality is what significance would consist in — is not the kind of claim an observation can settle in either direction."

holes.quoted_phrase: the same wording runs through the film's promotional copy
holes.description: Checked and it does not. The synopsis sentence is located in exactly one press release, carried on two channels: the PRWeb item of 8 December 2015 and its identical FrontGate Media posting. The second source we cite for it — "earlier distributor release carrying the same synopsis (In Ohm Entertainment, PR Newswire, 25 March 2015)" — does not contain either the "explores the significance of the Earth's place within the Cosmos" sentence or the "are we significant within the structure of the Universe?" passage; it carries different copy, and that different copy is what ARG-E01 quotes. So the label states something the linked document does not support, and the locator generalises one release into a body of promotional copy.
holes.recommendation: Change the locator to: "Official distributor synopsis, issued through PRWeb by FrontGate Media with the home-video release, 8 December 2015, and reproduced on FrontGate's own site the same week; this is the one release we located carrying it. Quoted from the press text, not from the film's soundtrack, which we were not able to view in this pass." Change the sources[1] label to: "The Principle — earlier distributor release (In Ohm Entertainment, PR Newswire, 25 March 2015). It carries the same thesis in different words — “Are we significant or just a cosmic accident?”, “unexpected evidence of a preferred direction in the cosmos”, “aligned with our supposedly insignificant Earth” — and is the release ARG-E01 quotes."

holes.quoted_phrase: single values holding at every point of spacetime
holes.description: False for two of the six numbers named in the same sentence, in the paragraph the entry calls decisive. In Rees's list, Ω is the density parameter, which evolves with cosmic time in any FLRW model and is quoted as a present-day value; Q is the amplitude of density fluctuations, i.e. a statistical property of a field that by definition is not the same at every point — that is what fluctuations are. The following sentence compounds it: "A constant is a scalar; a scalar has no gradient and no preferred direction." Scalar fields routinely have gradients; only uniform ones do not. A cosmologist defending the film gets a free hit on the decisive paragraph, and the argument does not need the overreach: what defeats "Earthward" is spatial uniformity at a given epoch, which is true of all of them.
holes.recommendation: Replace both sentences with: "Rees's six numbers — N, ε, Ω, λ, Q, D — and the rest of the standard list are properties of the universe as a whole, not of places in it. Λ is a constant in the strict sense, the same at every point of spacetime. Ω and Q are cosmological quantities that change with cosmic epoch, but at any given epoch they take the same value everywhere, and Q describes fluctuations that are statistically identical in every direction. Either way there is no spatial gradient to follow, and a uniform scalar has no preferred direction to give."

holes.quoted_phrase: and nowhere states it, because stating it invites the check
holes.description: The "because" clause attributes a reason for not stating a premise: that its authors leave it unstated to avoid scrutiny. That is a claim about the intentions of living, named people — Sungenis and DeLano — and nothing in the entry supports it. It is also probably wrong on the ordinary reading: unstated premises are usually unstated because their holders take them to be obvious, not because they are being concealed. The site's own standard is that unfalsifiable claims are named, not ridiculed, and that we distinguish being wrong from being evasive.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and none of the five states it. That is not a concealment — it is the mark of a premise its holders take to be obvious. Stated out loud it becomes checkable, and it does not survive the check."

holes.quoted_phrase: states the puzzle as a value, never as a bearing
holes.description: An unscoped absence claim across three works — Weinberg's 1989 review, Rees's Just Six Numbers and Barnes's 77-page 2012 survey — asserting what none of them ever does. This is the sweep's dominant failure mode and the writing rule in deep.py forbids it in terms. It escapes the ratcheting test only because the test scans tldr, refutation, untraceable and passage.gloss, and does not scan compression.note; the rule is not scoped to what the test happens to read. (Note that the neighbouring absence claim in section 2 — "it is not in the distributor synopsis quoted above" — is correctly scoped and should be the model.)
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "states the puzzle as a magnitude. In the abstract and body of Weinberg 1989, in Rees's six numbers, and in Barnes's 2012 review, the fine-tuned quantity is always a value; no statement of it as a direction is located in the three texts read for this pass."

holes.quoted_phrase: that we are 'a cosmic accident', of 'utter insignificance'
holes.description: One of the three phrases is interrogative in the source and is quoted here as a proposition. The 25 March 2015 release reads "Are we significant or just a cosmic accident?" — a question. "relegates us to utter insignificance" (PRWeb, 8 December 2015) and "our supposedly insignificant Earth" are assertive and are fairly used. Converting a question into an assertion is the precise move this entry convicts the list of two blocks earlier, in the compression note, and a defender who checks one citation will find us doing it in the paragraph headed Straw man identified.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "that we are ‘just a cosmic accident’ — the copy puts it as a question, and the assertive versions sit alongside it: the principle ‘relegates us to utter insignificance’, and an Earth described in its own publicity as ‘supposedly insignificant’."

holes.quoted_phrase: Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal and papal legate, wrote in De docta ignorantia II.12 in 1440
holes.description: Anachronistic rank. De docta ignorantia was completed on 12 February 1440; Cusa was created cardinal in December 1448 (published 1449) and served as papal legate from 1450. The appositive is doing rhetorical work — a churchman, before Copernicus, from inside the Church — and the date is the load-bearing part, so the easiest defence is to keep both and lose the anachronism. The quotation itself checks out verbatim against Hopkins §162.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Nicholas of Cusa — a churchman who would be made cardinal eight years later — wrote in De docta ignorantia II.12 in 1440"

reviews.hedge_rule_note: PASS, with one qualification. The refutation is aimed squarely at the source, not at the list fragment: it answers proof 101 clause by clause, and its opening move concedes the latitude bands of proofs 103-105 rather than disputing them. Verified: proof 101 reads verbatim (ericdubay.wordpress.com, 8 July 2018 posting) "Sigma Octantis is claimed to be a Southern central pole star similar to Polaris, around which the Southern hemisphere stars all rotate around the opposite direction. Unlike Polaris, however, Sigma Octantis can NOT be seen simultaneously from every point along the same latitude, it is NOT central but allegedly 1 degree off-center, it is NOT motionless, and in fact cannot be seen at all using publicly available telescopes! There is legitimate speculation regarding whether Sigma Octantis even exists. Either way, the direction in which stars move overhead is based on perspective and the exact direction you're facing, not which hemisphere you are in." Our quote, gloss and clause-by-clause section all track the first four claims accurately. The compression block is honest and unusually good: drifted=true, and it records a WEAKENING (the seven list items keep only the uncontested northern half) which the seven-value enum cannot name, exactly as the harness permits. drifted is not being used to avoid work. The qualification is that our reading of the passage stops one sentence too early and so mischaracterises the source as declining to explain the southern sky (holes 2 and 4) - a source-fidelity defect, but not the fragment-refuting failure the hedge rule exists to catch. new_rules_ok: no unscoped absence claims - every negative is scoped ("not located in the text read", "Not checked against the 2018 print edition", "the one this pass could place least confidently"). No recommendation is shipped as published prose; the four self-criticisms live in the module docstring addressed to the parent, not in ENTRY.

holes.quoted_phrase: in 2015 is the engagement with Sigma Octantis; the northern half of the cluster
holes.description: The genealogy is half-traced, and the half it misses is the half the treatment says is new. Our gloss traces the northern strand to Carpenter 1885 (verified: Gutenberg 55387, title page '5th Edition: 6th Thousand', Baltimore 1885; proofs 71 and 80 quoted correctly) and then says the southern engagement is what 2015 adds. It is not. Rowbotham's Zetetic Astronomy 3rd ed., 1881 has a section titled 'Motion of Stars North and South' (sacred-texts transcription za48.htm) whose opening sentence is the claim itself - 'IT has often been urged that the earth must be a globe, because the stars in the southern hemisphere move round a south polar star' - and which answers 'There is no southern pole, no south pole star, and no southern circumpolar constellations.' Dubay's simultaneity objection is there in the same comparative form: 'The Southern Cross is not at all times visible from every point of the southern hemisphere, as the Great Bear is from every point in the northern.' So is the facing reply: 'If we stand with our backs to the north, on the high land known as Arthur's Seat...' Our own WRK-DUBAY-2015 record already notes Dubay names Rowbotham in 17 of the 200 items and closes at #200 with a Rowbotham quotation, and PER-ROWBOTHAM's record already links this edition. On a project whose product IS the genealogy, B08 credits the flagship southern claim to 2015 and lists people=[PER-DUBAY, PER-CARPENTER] with the originator of the argument absent.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence 'What is new in 2015 is the engagement with Sigma Octantis; the northern half of the cluster is inherited.' with: 'What is new in 2015 is the naming of Sigma Octantis. The argument around it is not. Rowbotham’s Zetetic Astronomy (3rd ed., 1881) gives the southern sky a section of its own, “Motion of Stars North and South”, which opens on this exact claim — “IT has often been urged that the earth must be a globe, because the stars in the southern ‘hemisphere’ move round a south polar star” — and answers it with a flat denial: “There is no southern pole, no south pole star, and no southern circumpolar constellations.” Proof 101’s simultaneity objection is there in the same comparative form (“The Southern Cross is not at all times visible from every point of the southern hemisphere, as the ‘Great Bear’ is from every point in the northern”), and so is its closing perspective reply, which Rowbotham stages by asking the reader to “stand with our backs to the north” on Arthur’s Seat and watch the zenith stars recede north-west. Quoted from the 1881 third edition; not checked against the 1865 first book edition. Both halves of this cluster are inherited, and the southern half is the older of the two.' Add the sacred-texts za48.htm URL to sources. RECORD CHANGES, not prose: add PER-ROWBOTHAM to `people`; the clusters.py B08 record still reads originator='Eric Dubay', 2015, real_source=None, which understates the descent found here and in the writer's own docstring note about Carpenter - it needs real_source set and the originator question settled by the parent, and this subsumes the sweep's note at review/curmudgeon-sweep-raw.json line 550.

holes.quoted_phrase: proof 101 goes after whether the star can be observed at all rather than
holes.description: We tell the reader the source declines to explain the southern sky and only attacks observability, and that its positive claim lives outside the book ('The positive claim is stated most plainly outside the book'). Proof 101's own closing sentence, four words after where our quote stops, is the positive claim: 'Either way, the direction in which stars move overhead is based on perspective and the exact direction you're facing, not which hemisphere you are in.' (verified verbatim at ericdubay.wordpress.com, 8 July 2018 posting of the same text our sources reproduce). The source does try to fit it in, in the very proof we are glossing. That is a claim about what a source says that the source does not say, in the field whose whole job is to characterise the passage accurately - and it is self-inflicted, because our own ellipsis and stopping point hide the sentence. It also costs us the best kernel available: the reason the facing reply is worth answering is that its premise is TRUE (look at the opposite end of any axis and the same rotation reverses its apparent sense), which is precisely why the southern datum has to be stated as a second CENTRE and not as a reversal of handedness.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'which is why proof 101 goes after whether the star can be observed at all rather than trying to fit it in.' with: 'which is why proof 101 spends most of its length on whether the star can be observed at all. It does offer an accommodation, in its last sentence: “the direction in which stars move overhead is based on perspective and the exact direction you’re facing, not which hemisphere you are in.” That sentence is the model’s positive account of the southern sky, its premise is true, and section 4 answers it.' In the following paragraph replace 'The positive claim is stated most plainly outside the book.' with 'The same positive claim is put more expansively outside the book.'

holes.quoted_phrase: rotation axis gives every observer exactly one centre of rotation
holes.description: The TLDR's stated reason does not discriminate between the two models, and on its most natural reading it is a property of ours. A globe also has a single rotation axis, and it also gives every observer exactly one visible centre of rotation - and it delivers precisely the two-opposite-centres observation the sentence says a single axis cannot produce. The premise that actually kills the disc is absent from the TLDR: on a plane every observer's horizon is parallel to every other's, so one axis over the centre puts the one centre north of everybody; it takes a curved surface to tilt a southern horizon until the other end of the axis rises. A charitable reading exists ('exactly one centre for all observers collectively'), but 'every observer' pushes the reader to the per-observer reading, which is shared by the globe. This is the recurring TLDR-quantifier failure: 'exactly one' written from memory of the argument rather than from it, in the highest-visibility field of the argument our own cluster note calls 'the item the flat model most clearly gets wrong'.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'because a single rotation axis gives every observer exactly one centre of rotation' with: 'because every observer on a plane shares the same horizon, so one axis over the centre puts the sky’s one centre to the north of all of them; it takes a curved surface to tilt a southern horizon far enough for the other end of that axis to rise'.

holes.quoted_phrase: the same way about that one centre. Southern trails close in the opposite handedness
holes.description: Consequence (ii) rests on handedness, and handedness alone is answered by the source's own closing sentence in proof 101 (direction of motion depends on which way you face) - a reply we never quote and never answer, because we place the perspective defence entirely in proof 102. The reply has real force at this step: apparent handedness genuinely does reverse when you look at the opposite end of a single axis, and a northern observer who turns to face south does see the southern sky run the other way across his field of view. What the disc cannot deliver is not the reversal but the second centre with closed circles at altitude equal to latitude - which is (i) and section 4, not (ii). As written, (ii) is the one consequence in the list of five that a well-read defender can dispose of with a sentence from the source we are refuting.
holes.recommendation: Replace consequence (ii) with: '(ii) One sense of rotation — and a centre in the other half of the sky. Handedness on its own settles nothing, and proof 101 says so in its last sentence: face the opposite end of any axis and the same rotation reverses its apparent sense. That is true. It is why the southern datum has to be stated as a second centre and not as a reversal: from a southern site the trails do not merely run the other way, they close into complete circles about a point due south at an altitude equal to the observer’s latitude, in one sidereal day. Turning to face south from a northern site produces no such point, on a disc or on a globe. Only crossing the equator does.'

holes.quoted_phrase: stars all rotate … Unlike Polaris, however,
holes.description: The ellipsis drops the source's own words 'around the opposite direction' - i.e. the clause in which Dubay states the very claim our TLDR headlines - and the quote then stops before the two sentences that close the proof: 'There is legitimate speculation regarding whether Sigma Octantis even exists. Either way, the direction in which stars move overhead is based on perspective and the exact direction you're facing, not which hemisphere you are in.' The gloss's count, 'there are four claims here, not one', is therefore short: there are five in the printed proof, and the fifth (existence doubted outright) is both the most striking illustration of our thesis and the one the harness says must be NAMED as unfalsifiable rather than ridiculed. Restoring the four elided words keeps the quote at 56 words, inside the 60-word in-copyright cap the test enforces.
holes.recommendation: Set passage.quote to: 'Sigma Octantis is claimed to be a Southern central pole star similar to Polaris, around which the Southern hemisphere stars all rotate around the opposite direction. Unlike Polaris, however, Sigma Octantis can NOT be seen simultaneously from every point along the same latitude, it is NOT central but allegedly 1 degree off-center, it is NOT motionless.' (56 words; 'rotate around the opposite direction' is the source's own phrasing, sic.) In the gloss, replace 'So there are four claims here, not one' with 'So there are five claims here, not one' and, after the telescope clause, add: 'and closes by doubting that the star exists at all. That last one is worth naming plainly rather than mocking: a claim that an object visible to the unaided eye from half the planet may not exist is not a claim any observation offered here can settle for a reader who will not look.'

holes.quoted_phrase: Sigma Octantis is a convenience for a navigator, not the
holes.description: Our own cited source says the opposite. The Wikipedia Sigma Octantis article, which we list as source 5 for the magnitude, states: 'At magnitude +5.42, Sigma Octantis is barely visible to the naked eye, making it unusable for navigation, especially by comparison with the much brighter and more easily visible Polaris.' A defender who follows our own footnote finds our sentence contradicted, and it is the kind of small unforced error that discredits the paragraph around it - which is otherwise the strongest thing in the entry. The correction strengthens us: the star's uselessness as a navigational marker is further evidence that the southern pole is fixed by the trails, not by the star.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'Sigma Octantis is a convenience for a navigator, not the evidence.' with: 'Sigma Octantis is a marker, and a poor one: at magnitude 5.42 it is barely a naked-eye object and of little practical use for navigation, which is why southern navigators find the pole by projecting the long axis of the Southern Cross instead. It is not the evidence.'

holes.quoted_phrase: the official rationale for putting it there is that it is small,
holes.description: The citation does not support the phrase, and 'official' overstates it. Our source 10 is the Wikipedia Flag of Brazil article, credited in its label with exactly this rationale; the article in fact says Sigma Octantis represents the Federal District because 'its unique position in the sky of the southern hemisphere represents the stability of the Federal District in the Brazilian union', and the 'dimmest star on any national flag' point is on the Sigma Octantis page, not the flag page. The 'all the other stars turn around it' formulation is documented, but by a Brazilian astronomy source rather than by a government: Zenite, 'O ceu da bandeira' - 'Do nosso ponto de vista, e em torno dela que giram todas as demais estrelas do firmamento.' Everything else in this sentence checks out (flag adopted 19 November 1889; the star numbered 7 represents the Federal District; 1889 to 2015 is 126 years), which is why the unsupported clause is worth fixing rather than dropping.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'and the official rationale for putting it there is that it is small, but all the other stars turn around it' with: 'chosen for the Federal District, in the flag’s own symbolism, for its “unique position in the sky of the southern hemisphere” — and that position is the pole itself: from anywhere in Brazil it is the point the rest of the sky turns around (Zenite, “O ceu da bandeira”: “e em torno dela que giram todas as demais estrelas do firmamento”)'. Add https://zenite.nu/o-ceu-da-bandeira to sources and rewrite the Flag of Brazil source label to claim only the adoption date and the Federal District attribution.

holes.quoted_phrase: Fitting each latitude separately
holes.description: A stronger consequence is available and missing, and it is the one that answers the advocate's best move. Section 3 tests the disc on Polaris's altitude and on the southern pole; both require the reader to accept our arithmetic or to fly south. The disc also fails on the two items the treatment hands back as uncontested - item 16 'Perfect circular star trails around Polaris' and item 213 'Perfect star circles'. Under a dome of finite height h, an off-centre observer is at a different distance from each star at each hour, so every star would sweep faster near its closest approach and slower at its farthest, and its projected path would be a conic rather than a circle sharing a centre with every other star's. Observed trails are concentric circles at a uniform 15.04 degrees per hour. Perfect circularity is therefore not a datum the flat model gets for free; it is a datum only stars at effectively infinite distance about one axis can produce - and unlike the southern pole, a northern reader can test it in one night with the camera they already own. Our advocate rates the 'you have offered no observation I can make from where I am standing' objection at 4 and answers it with a southbound flight; this answers it without one.
holes.recommendation: Add as a sixth consequence in section 3: '(vi) Circles that close, at one rate. Items 16 and 213 report that the trails are perfect circles, and they are right — which is the difficulty. On a dome of finite height the observer’s distance to each star changes through the night, so every star would run fastest near its closest approach and slowest at its farthest, and its path across the sky would be a conic rather than a circle about the same point as everyone else’s. Every long exposure ever taken shows concentric circles closing at a uniform 15.04 degrees per hour. That is the signature of stars at effectively unlimited distance turning about one axis, and it needs no flight: one camera, one tripod, one clear night in the northern hemisphere.' Then amend the advocate `preemptive` to cite (vi) as the no-travel answer to the argument-from-authority objection.

holes.quoted_phrase: when the same sums run the other way
holes.description: The never-rises condition is mis-stated, and our own steelman states it correctly two paragraphs earlier ('a star of declination d stays below the horizon for a northern observer at latitude f only when d < f - 90'). Read as written, 'the same sums run the other way' gives 'f + d < -90 in the north' - but for a northern observer at 40 N a star never rises when d < -50, i.e. f + d < -10, which is nowhere near -90. On no reading of 'the same sums' does the sentence produce the correct condition, which is f - d > 90 in the north. This sits in the paragraph where we tell the reader the globe's rule is the rule that generates the source's own correct latitude bands, so it is the first line a defender with a star chart will test.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'a star never sets when φ + δ > +90° in the north or φ + δ < −90° in the south, and never rises when the same sums run the other way' with: 'a star never sets when |φ| + |δ| > 90° and latitude and declination share a sign, and never rises when |φ| + |δ| > 90° and their signs are opposite. At 34 degrees south that means everything south of declination −56° is permanently up and everything north of +56° never rises at all'.

holes.quoted_phrase: one apparent centre per observer, and it lies in the direction of that axis
holes.description: On a plane the rotation axis is vertical, and every vertical on a plane is parallel to every other - so 'the direction of that axis' is the zenith, for everybody, not the north. What our own section 3(iii) actually models is the direction to the point where the axis meets a dome of finite height h, which is northward at altitude arctan(h/r). The clause that follows, 'northward, everywhere on the disc', is right and rescues the meaning, but the stated reason contradicts it and a physicist-defender will say so.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'and it lies in the direction of that axis — northward, everywhere on the disc' with: 'and on a plane it lies where that axis meets the dome — northward and elevated for every observer on the disc, because every vertical on a plane is parallel to every other, so no one on it can be tilted away from the axis'.

holes.quoted_phrase: are the only items in the cluster that assert something about history
holes.description: A quantifier that our own compression block contradicts. The compression note argues that items 143 and 267 ('Constant constellations', 'Constellation stability') are two-word fragments 'that a reader will take as a claim about time, that the constellations do not change'. Section 5 then says items 17 and 145 are the only items asserting anything about history. Both fields are defensible on their own reading - section 5 reads 143/267 the source's spatial way, the compression note reads them as the circulating fragment does - but the two are a short scroll apart on the rendered page and a critic compiling self-contradictions will pick this up. The hedge rule's second clause is also relevant: the circulating temporal reading is the one readers arrive with, and precession answers it.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'are the only items in the cluster that assert something about history' with: 'are the two items that assert history on their face — and precession settles them, along with the temporal misreading of “Constant constellations” that the compression note below describes'.

holes.quoted_phrase: full-text reproduction, 31 July 2018; proofs 98–108 read here

The rexynotes copy is dated three weeks after it.

ARITHMETIC, all independently recomputed and correct: 15.04 deg/hr from a 23h56m04s day; 8.6% of the sphere in a 34-degree cap; Polaris altitude arctan(h/r) with h=5000 km giving 36.9 / 29.4 / 26.6 degrees at 30N / 10N / equator; per-latitude fits 5,800 / 3,850 / 1,570 / 0 km; 19.4 degrees = ~39 lunar diameters; rim circumference ~126,000 km; 222 degrees of longitude and bearing separations 89 / 133 / 138 degrees for Santiago, Cape Town and Sydney; parallelism of the sight-lines to ~1 microarcsecond at 294 ly; Sigma Octantis circumpolar below ~1.1 deg S; Crux circumpolar south of 34 S with Acrux near -63 deg; precession 25,800 yr and ~1 deg per 72 yr; one zodiacal sign since Hipparchus. The only loose figure is 'about 13,800 km' for all three cities (Santiago computes to ~13,730 km); not worth a finding.
reviews.summary: The verdict (REFUTED) holds and the analysis is sound: the geometry, every number I recomputed, and the clause-by-clause answer to proof 101 all stand, and the compression block's recorded weakening - the list keeps only the uncontested northern half - is a genuine and well-handled counter-example to the page's usual drift pattern. The defects are in the layer around the argument, as the sweep predicted. Two are source-fidelity: our quote of proof 101 stops one sentence early, and the gloss consequently tells the reader the source declines to explain the southern sky when proof 101's closing sentence explains it (perspective and which way you are facing) - which also costs us the strongest kernel, since that premise is true and is why the datum must be stated as a second centre rather than as reversed handedness. One is genealogical and matters most for this project: the southern strand is not new in 2015: Rowbotham's 1881 third edition already carries the denial ("There is no southern pole, no south pole star, and no southern circumpolar constellations"), the simultaneity objection in the same comparative form, and the facing reply, in a book our own records already link. The TLDR's stated reason ("a single rotation axis gives every observer exactly one centre of rotation") is a property the globe shares and does not discriminate. Smaller: the never-rises condition is mis-stated in the opening concession, the Brazil flag rationale is not in the page we cite, "a convenience for a navigator" is contradicted by our own Sigma Octantis source, and the strongest no-travel argument (perfect concentric trails at a uniform 15.04 deg/hr are impossible under a finite dome for an off-centre observer) is missing - the one that answers the rated-4 advocate objection without a southbound flight. Tone and the hard constraints are clean: no religious adjudication, no motive or bad-faith claims about a living author beyond one structural "which is why", the unfalsifiable move is named rather than mocked, and the in-copyright quote stays inside the 60-word cap even after the recommended restoration (56 words).

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Passes, and passes well. The refutation is aimed at Rowbotham's own sentences at their own strength, not at the list fragment. I verified both load-bearing quotations independently: the 1865 first book edition (Gutenberg #69892) carries "Every survey of this and other countries, whether ordnance or otherwise, is now carried out in connection with a horizontal datum ... it is virtually an admission by all the most practical scientific men of the day that the Earth cannot be other than a plane!" and the "the very Government of the country has been obliged to interfere!" sentence verbatim at pp. 54-56; the 1881 third edition (sacred-texts za18) carries "Standing Orders of the Houses of Lords and Commons on Railway Operations, for the Session of 1862" at p. 56 and "In all these extensive surveys the doctrine of rotundity is, of necessity, entirely ignored" at p. 57. The source is markedly stronger than item 223 ("Surveying plane assumption."), and the treatment says so and answers the stronger version. It also refuses to refute items 47, 382, 383 and 395 as the source's claims, which is the correct move. The one hedge-adjacent defect is not in the refutation but in the compression block's enum choice: drift_type="unsourced_addition" renders as the bolded label "The source does not contain this", directly above a note that says we did not run a full-text search of either edition. That is filed as hole 7, not as a hedge-rule failure.

holes.quoted_phrase: The flat-earth site that runs this argument does the sum honestly and gets 20 m of “ignored curvature” across a 100-square-mile block
holes.description: We credit galileolied.com/plane-surveying with a calculation it does not perform. I fetched the page twice with different prompts. It quotes engineering texts for the limit ("Surveys covering an area up to 260 km2 may be treated as plane surveys", "Survey works up to 100 square miles (260 sq kilometers) are treated as plane", "Plane surveying is done of the area of survey is less than 250 km2") and reproduces one textbook curvature line that runs the OTHER way - "It is to be noted that the difference in length between the arc and the subtended chord on the earth surface for a distance of 18.2 km is only 0.1 m". No 20 m, 20.3 m, 65 ft or 16.1 km figure was located on it, and the second fetch reported explicitly that the author performs no original arithmetic. The 20 m is ours. This is the project's own signature error - attributing to a source something the source does not contain - committed inside the steelman, which is the one section whose whole job is to state the opponent's case as the opponent states it. It is also an attribution to a named living author (the site gives a contact, Steven J. Merrill), and the sources[] label repeats it: "quoting the 260 km2 plane-surveying limit and computing 20 m of 'ignored' curvature across it". Note that the site's own quoted arc-versus-chord line concedes 0.1 m, which is a weaker starting point than we hand them - so this misattribution makes our steelman generous in the wrong currency.
holes.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "The modern flat-earth statement of this argument quotes that limit and stops there: it reproduces the textbook lines, including “the difference in length between the arc and the subtended chord on the earth surface for a distance of 18.2 km is only 0.1 m”, and does no arithmetic of its own. So do it for them, because the honest version of the argument needs it: a 260 km² block is about 16.1 km on a side, and the drop from a tangent plane across it is 16,100²/(2 × 6,371,000) = 20.3 m." And change the sources[] label to: "The modern flat-earth statement of this argument, quoting the 260 km2 plane-surveying limit out of the engineering texts (the 20.3 m tangent-plane drop across a block that size is our arithmetic, not the site's)".

holes.field: scripts/clusters.py ARG-B06 originator_work / year, and the five published dataset rows derived from them
holes.quoted_phrase: "B06": dict(lane="B", name="Surveyors assume a plane and make no 'allowance'",
holes.description: The record and the treatment contradict each other in public. data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.csv publishes five rows - items 47, 223, 382, 383, 395 - each reading "Samuel Rowbotham, Zetetic Astronomy, 1849", and the argument card's meta line prints "first published by Samuel Rowbotham" for all five. The treatment rendered immediately below says the opposite twice: the passage block is headed "Earth Not a Globe, 1865", the gloss asserts in bold that the claim is not of 1849, and the compression note states that four of the five items are "of unestablished authorship", including item 383, which ARG-B01 already traced to Carpenter 1885 proof 4. This is the exact defect logged three times in corrections.json (R06, B01, E13) - cluster-level attribution applied item by item - and B01 has already established the house fix: its originator_work reads "Zetetic Astronomy (item 384: Carpenter 1885, proof 4)". The module docstring reports the year half of this to the parent, but not the item-attribution half, and neither was applied.
holes.recommendation: In scripts/clusters.py, anchor the edit on the cluster key "B06" and never on the originator line - that line is byte-identical across four clusters (B06, B07 and two others), which is precisely how the E01/E03 misfile was manufactured. Set: originator_work="Zetetic Astronomy (item 223; items 47, 382, 383 and 395 not located in the texts searched - item 383 restates Carpenter 1885, proof 4)", year="1865". Rebuild so the five dataset rows stop reading 1849, and append a corrections.json entry in the past tense once it lands.

holes.field: scripts/clusters.py ARG-B06 note (renders as the summary line of the Refutation section)
holes.quoted_phrase: Rowbotham's own '8 inches per mile squared' is lifted from a surveying text
holes.description: An unverified provenance claim, published as the basis line on a page whose entire product is provenance. Our own module docstring records that the mechanism is unconfirmed: at 1881 ch. II p. 9 Rowbotham introduces the figure flat, with no sourcing located on the page, and the prose below the basis line deliberately retreats to the narrower, checkable statement (8 in/mile is D^2/2R for one statute mile, and Simms's levelling treatise uses it). "Lifted from a surveying text" asserts a transmission route we did not establish - and the one text we can show he actually reprints is the Encyclopaedia Britannica "Levelling" article, which is not where the 8 inches comes from in his book. I confirmed the Metabunk listing does support Simms (1875) using the 8-inch approximation, so the arithmetic claim is safe; only the word "lifted" is not.
holes.recommendation: Replace the note with: "Rowbotham's '8 inches per mile' is D^2/2R for one statute mile - 0.2032 m - the first-mile value of the difference between the true and the apparent level that his own century's levelling literature tabulates. He reprints an Encyclopaedia Britannica article on levelling for its refraction sentence and discards the curvature the same article's formulae supply, then calls the Ordnance Survey as his witness seven years after it published the figure of the earth derived from the Principal Triangulation."

holes.quoted_phrase: no copy or transcription of the sixteen-page 1849 pamphlet could be reached at all, and the same was recorded when ARG-B01 went looking for it
holes.description: Two problems in one sentence, and they undercut the gloss's bolded conclusion. (1) It misstates ARG-B01's record. B01 did not record that nothing could be reached; it built a whole passage block on WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1849 out of the title page plus "the one body sentence Robert Schadewald reproduces verbatim", and used Schadewald's quotation as evidence when reattributing item 384. So a partial witness to the pamphlet's contents exists, was used by a sibling entry, and is neither consulted here nor listed in this entry's COULD NOT REACH block. (2) The dating inference over-concludes. The Standing Order is dated to the Session of 1862 only in the 1881 third edition; the 1865 text quotes it undated, citing only "No. 6" (Lords) and "No. 44" (Commons) - I verified this on the Gutenberg text. Standing Orders requiring deposited plans and sections with a datum line long predate 1862 (unchecked - the Parliamentary Archives research guide redirected and the Norfolk record office page is robots-disallowed), so an 1849 pamphlet could have quoted the order then in force. The 1862 date fixes a terminus post quem for the text we can read, not for the argument, which is a weaker claim than "So this is a claim of the 1860s".
holes.recommendation: Replace the quoted clause with: "no copy or transcription of the sixteen-page 1849 pamphlet could be reached here, and ARG-B01 reached it only through its title page and the one body sentence Robert Schadewald reproduces - six theodolite experiments on the Bedford Level, with nothing about railway sections in what he quotes." And soften the paragraph's closing sentence from "So this is a claim of the 1860s, sharpened in the 1880s." to "So the earliest text of it we can read is of the 1860s, and it was sharpened in the 1880s; whether a version stood in the pamphlet is not something the sources we could reach can settle." Add Schadewald's chapter to sources[].

holes.quoted_phrase: The argument needs horizontal datum line to mean plane. In surveying it does not.
holes.description: We miss the strongest answer available, and it is inside his own quotation - which is doubly costly because the treatment's whole rhetorical strategy is that the answer is inside his own quotation. The clause immediately BEFORE the datum clause he prints is: "That the section be drawn to the same horizontal scale as the plan; and to a vertical scale of not less than one inch to every one hundred feet". Two independently specified scales on the two axes means a railway section is not a picture of the ground at all - it is a graph of height against chainage, with the vertical exaggerated by roughly an order of magnitude. Curvature is not merely ignored in such a drawing, it is unrepresentable in it, and the straightness of the baseline carries no geometric information whatever. We spend the section on the gravity meaning of "horizontal" and on Ordnance Datum, both correct, and never make the point a reader is most likely to reach unaided.
holes.recommendation: Insert immediately after the quoted sentence: "It also needs a section to be a picture of the ground, and the clause before the datum clause - in the same quotation - says it is not. The section is drawn “to the same horizontal scale as the plan; and to a vertical scale of not less than one inch to every one hundred feet”. Two different scales on the two axes make it a graph of height against chainage, with the vertical exaggerated by roughly an order of magnitude, and on a graph the curvature of the ground is not merely ignored, it is unrepresentable. A straight baseline under a distorted profile is a drawing convention, not a measurement of the earth."

holes.field: refutation, section 1 (and advocate.best_defense, which never attacks this move)
holes.quoted_phrase: That fixed point is a benchmark, and British ordnance benchmarks of the 1860s carried heights above Ordnance Datum Liverpool
holes.description: The load-bearing move of the whole entry - the TLDR bets on it - rests on an unstated step. The order requires only that the datum "be referred to some fixed point stated in writing on the section"; it does not require an Ordnance Survey benchmark, and a railway datum is arbitrary in height and frequently a purely local mark. Our chain runs fixed point -> ordnance benchmark -> Ordnance Datum Liverpool -> mean sea level, and only the last two links are sourced (I verified the Wikipedia Ordnance datum text: "tidal observations were taken at the Victoria Dock, Liverpool, over a short period in 1844"). A defender goes here first: "a section datum is an arbitrary plane the engineer picks; nothing ties it to a tide gauge." Worse, advocate.best_defense never raises it - it attacks the curvature off-switch, the balanced-sight reinterpretation, survey closure and the correction lines, all of which section 3 and section 6 already answer - so the one move that is genuinely exposed is the one the steelman of our critics leaves alone. The fix is to stop needing the sea: what defeats the plane inference is that the datum defines a LEVEL surface, because it is set out with a spirit level, whatever its height.
holes.recommendation: Replace the quoted clause with: "That fixed point is a physical mark on the ground, and the order does not say what height it sits at - a railway datum is arbitrary in height and often purely local. What is not arbitrary is the surface it defines. The datum is carried along the work with a spirit level, and a spirit-levelled surface is perpendicular to the plumb line at every point on it, so the constant datum the order demands is a level surface by construction, whatever number is written against it. Where the fixed point is an ordnance benchmark the number is referred to Ordnance Datum Liverpool, from tidal observations at Victoria Dock in 1844; where it is not, his own Experiment 14 shows what else it tends to be - a section diagram labelled “the datum line—the Trinity high water mark”." Change the following sentence "The datum is the sea." to "The datum is a level surface, and where it is tied to a gauge it is the sea." Then add to advocate.best_defense, in their voice: "Your datum argument is a bait and switch. The order I quote requires a fixed point, not a tide gauge; engineers pick a convenient datum below the lowest cutting and it is a plane on the drawing by definition." - so that the preemptive answer above is visibly earned.

holes.quoted_phrase: list_phrasing="Surveying assumes stationary ground."
holes.description: The rendered compression box contradicts its own note. render.py maps drift_type="unsourced_addition" to the bolded label "The source does not contain this", printed directly above a note whose closing sentences read "we did not run a full-text search of either edition" and "Unreachable is not absent, and this is a statement about the passages we read, not about the corpus." The label is an unscoped absence-claim of exactly the kind the ratcheting test counts, generated by our enum choice rather than by our prose. Separately, the box pairs item 47 (a claim about motion) against a source quotation about shape, so a reader who opens "The list overstates its own source" and reads no further concludes the cluster's central item is unsourced - when item 223, the cluster's representative item, is faithful and the note says so. The harness explicitly permits saying that no drift_type fits rather than forcing one; there is no enum value for "authorship unestablished", which is what we actually found.
holes.recommendation:
Set list_phrasing="Surveying plane assumption. (item 223) - and, in the same cluster, Surveying assumes stationary ground. (item 47)" and open the note with a new first paragraph: "

Read the label above narrowly - none of the seven drift types fits what we found. The wording of item 223 is faithful. What we established about items 47, 382, 383 and 395 is that they have no ancestor in the passages we read, not that the source contains nothing of the kind: we did not run a full-text search of either edition. The drift here is one of authorship, not of wording.

"

holes.quoted_phrase: Item 382 of this cluster, “Leveling equipotential planes”, has already conceded the noun and is arguing about the adjective.
holes.description: Inverted. In the phrase "equipotential planes", the adjective is "equipotential" and the noun is "planes". The item has conceded the adjective - equipotential is our word, the geodesist's word, and it grants the gravity-field physics - and is disputing the noun, plane versus curved surface. As written the sentence says the reverse of the point it is making, in the closing line of the steelman where it is meant to land.
holes.recommendation: "Item 382 of this cluster, “Leveling equipotential planes”, has already conceded the adjective and is arguing about the noun."

holes.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, first case (and the parallel sentence in refutation section 3)
holes.quoted_phrase: the combined curvature-and-refraction term enters at 0.0675D² metres with D in kilometres
holes.description: Attributes the full curvature-and-refraction term to any imbalance. The residual after an unbalanced setup is 0.0675(Db^2 - Df^2), not 0.0675D^2: a 20 per cent imbalance at a kilometre leaves 0.0675(1.0^2 - 0.8^2) = 24 mm, not the 68 mm we quote. The figures we give are the full-imbalance bound, which is the right order of magnitude and the right rhetorical point, but a working surveyor - the reader this section is explicitly written to keep on side - will spot it, and section 3 repeats the same form ("Break the balance and the term reappears at 0.0675D² metres"). The underlying constants check out: 0.0785D^2 curvature minus one-seventh gives 0.0673-0.0675, and 0.7 mm at 100 m and 6.8 cm at 1 km follow.
holes.recommendation: "the combined curvature-and-refraction term stops cancelling and leaves 0.0675(Db² − Df²) metres for sight lengths in kilometres — at most 0.7 mm where a 100 m sight is wholly unmatched, at most 6.8 cm at a kilometre". Make the same change in refutation section 3: "Break the balance and the term reappears in proportion to the difference of the squared sight lengths: sub-millimetre at a hundred metres, up to 6.8 cm at a kilometre."

holes.field: sources[] label for the Principal Triangulation Wikipedia entry
holes.quoted_phrase: Principal Triangulation of Great Britain — spherical excess carried through the triangles;
holes.description: The label credits that page with two things it does not carry. On fetching it: it gives the survey dates (1791-1853), the 1858 report's full title, and a loose statement that surveyors allowed for "the spherical nature of the earth (meaning there were more than 180 degrees in a triangle)" - but it does not state the 289-station count, and does not mention the Airy ellipsoid. The 289 figure and both ellipsoid results are on the Alexander Ross Clarke entry, which we also cite and which confirms our numbers exactly: "a=20,927,005 ft., inverse flattening c=299.33" from British data alone, and 289 stations. So the facts are all sound; the pointer is aimed at the wrong one of our own two sources, and the Airy-ellipsoid reduction (true, and catalogued by The National Archives as "Latitudes and longitudes of the Principal Stations on Airy's 1830 Figure") is currently uncited.
holes.recommendation: "Principal Triangulation of Great Britain — the survey observed 1791–1853, the spherical excess of its triangles, and the 1858 report; the 289-station count and both ellipsoid results are on the Alexander Ross Clarke entry cited below, and the reduction on Airy's 1830 figure is catalogued by The National Archives as 'Latitudes and longitudes of the Principal Stations on Airy's 1830 Figure'"

citation_failures: galileolied.com/plane-surveying — FAILED. Fetched twice with different prompts. The page quotes textbook definitions (260 km2 / 100 sq mi / 250 km2 limits) and one arc-versus-chord line ('only 0.1 m' over 18.2 km), and performs no arithmetic of its own. The 20 m 'ignored curvature' figure we attribute to it was not located on it. See hole 1.

en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_Triangulation_of_Great_Britain — PARTIAL. Does not state the 289-station count and does not mention the Airy ellipsoid; both belong to the Alexander Ross Clarke entry (289 stations; a=20,927,005 ft, 1/299.33 British-only; a=20,926,348 ft, 1/294.26 combined), which we also cite and which checks out exactly. No change needed.

VERIFIED — Rowbotham 1865 (Gutenberg #69892) pp. 54-56: all four quoted sentences verbatim, including 'It is commonly believed that surveyors when laying out railways and canals, are obliged to allow 8 inches per mile for the Earth's curvature' and the 'obliged to interfere!' sentence. The 1865 text cites the orders as No. 6 and No. 44 with no session date.

VERIFIED — 1881 3rd ed. (sacred-texts): 'for the Session of 1862' at p. 56; 'In all these extensive surveys...' at p. 57 (Experiment 13); Experiment 14 at pp. 58-59 carries the Portlock / Precelly / Kippure 108-mile sight, 'upwards of 100 miles', and 'the datum line--the Trinity high water mark' verbatim; Experiment 9 carries the Britannica extract with 'may at a mean compensate for about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth', 'we have, therefore, made no allowance for refraction in the foregone formulae', and Rowbotham's comment 'It will be seen from the above that, in practice, refraction need not be allowed for.'

VERIFIED — Ordnance datum (Victoria Dock 1844; Dunbar-Newlyn difference 0.81 feet / 0.247 m); BLM Manual 24-mile standard parallels verbatim; Trimble Access '16" per km' and 'one-seventh of the earth curvature correction' with coefficients 0.13 / 0.142 / 0.2; Wikipedia Levelling balanced-sight sentence verbatim; USGS 'a direction perpendicular to the force of gravity' and the USC&GS equipotential-surfaces quotation; gyrotheodolite spin rate, 10-arcsecond accuracy, 15-degree polar limit and Channel Tunnel; jerrymahun 'level surfaces are irregular and converge toward the poles' and the east-west orthometric-correction sentence.

VERIFIED (arithmetic) — R^2 sin 1" = 197 km2 and 1.3" over 260 km2; 16,100^2/(2 x 6,371,000) = 20.3 m; 0.0785 x 1.609^2 = 0.2032 m = 8.00 in; D/2R = 16.2" per km; 0.0785 less one-seventh = 0.0673-0.0675. Item numbers 47, 223, 382, 383, 395 confirmed against corpus.py and assign.py, and item texts match what we quote.
reviews.summary: The verdict SELF-CONTRADICTED holds and the analysis is the strongest surveying treatment I have audited: the hedge rule passes cleanly (every Rowbotham sentence we answer, I re-verified verbatim in the 1865 Gutenberg text and the 1881 sacred-texts chapters), the steelman reaches KERNEL tier on balanced sights, and every one of the fourteen modern citations I could reach says what we say it says. Two major defects sit in the layer around the argument, exactly where the sweep predicted: the steelman credits galileolied.com with a 20 m calculation the page does not perform (our arithmetic, attributed to a named living author's site), and the cluster record still publishes all five items as "Rowbotham, Zetetic Astronomy, 1849" in five dataset rows while the treatment beside them says the text is 1865 and four of the five items are of unestablished authorship - the R06/B01/E13 pattern for the fourth time, with B01's own parenthetical fix available as the template. Four moderate holes follow: the basis line's unverified "lifted from a surveying text", a dating argument that over-concludes while leaving unread the one partial witness to the 1849 pamphlet that ARG-B01 did use (Schadewald), an unstated fixed-point-to-Ordnance-Datum step that advocate mode never attacks, and the strongest available answer left unmade - the vertical scale clause in Rowbotham's own quoted Standing Order, which makes a railway section a graph rather than a picture of the ground. Nothing here requires rewriting the argument; the marked action reflects two attribution corrections that move published dataset rows plus one added paragraph, not a defect in the reasoning.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: See the hedge_rule_ok field above for the full assessment. Additionally on THE NEW RULES: new_rules_ok=true. Absence claims are correctly scoped throughout - "we could not locate them in the Sungenis text we were able to search", with the truncation points named; "we have not read hobby flight-controller source and are not going to assert anything about what is in it". No unscoped absence anywhere in the entry. On the second rule, the treatment does not ship a to-do as prose: the cluster-split proposal lives in `verdict_challenge`, a field render.py renders as declared internal dissent, and the compression note's "Recorded here rather than acted on; the cluster record was left untouched" is a past-tense disclosure of a decision, not a recommendation in the future tense. That is the borderline case and I judged it on the right side of the line. Tone and constraint checks all pass: no adjudication of religion, no claims about motive, finances or mental state, Sungenis is handled charitably throughout (we credit him with being more careful than the list and with writing against flat-earth cosmology), the electromagnetic branch is explicitly protected from mockery, and the in-copyright excerpt is 44 words, inside the 60-word cap.

holes.quoted_phrase: a 433-day wobble driven by pressure on the Pacific sea floor
holes.description: The Pacific is our invention. Gross 2000 (Geophys. Res. Lett. 27(15):2329-2332), the paper we cite for this and name in `sources`, does not contain the word "Pacific" and localises the excitation to no basin at all: it uses a global OGCM driven by NCEP fluxes over 1985.0-1996.0 and concludes only that "the single most important mechanism exciting the Chandler wobble has been ocean-bottom pressure fluctuations, which contribute about twice as much excitation power in the Chandler frequency band as do atmospheric pressure fluctuations." The 3.45 vs 1.87 mas-squared figures and the 433.0 +/- 1.1 day period both check out; only the ocean does not. The same fabricated specificity is repeated in the body: "the rotation axis of the universe is being nudged by pressure changes on the floor of the Pacific." This is the ARG-A05 "as wide as Saturn's orbit" pattern exactly - a vivid detail added for punch, attributed to a named cited paper, and absent from it - and here it sits in the TLDR, the field most readers never expand past.
holes.recommendation: TLDR: replace "and wander in a 433-day wobble driven by pressure on the Pacific sea floor" with "and wander in a 433-day wobble whose main driver is pressure on the ocean floor". Section five bullet: replace "Under (b), the rotation axis of the universe is being nudged by pressure changes on the floor of the Pacific." with "Under (b), the rotation axis of the universe is being nudged by pressure changes on the sea floor." Amend the `sources` label to "433.0 +/- 1.1 days (period taken from Wilson and Vicente 1990); excitation dominated by ocean-bottom pressure fluctuations, about twice the Chandler-band power of atmospheric pressure".

holes.quoted_phrase: which is why the verdict is standard physics rather than refuted
holes.description: The TLDR affirmatively justifies a blanket STANDARD PHYSICS verdict over all six items while the treatment underneath it argues that a third of them are dead. The cluster name printed directly above the TLDR is "Coriolis effects reassigned to a rotating sky or to electromagnetism"; the TLDR discusses only the rotating sky, never mentions electromagnetism or the drone item, and then supplies a reason for the verdict.
