Section six of our own refutation puts the electromagnetic branch seven orders of magnitude short (I re-derived it: sigma*v*B = 3.2*0.1*5e-5 = 1.6e-5 A/m^2; j*B = 8e-10 N/m^3; /1025 kg/m^3 = 7.8e-13 m/s^2 against 2*Omega*v*sin(45) = 1.03e-5 m/s^2, a ratio of 1.3e7 - the arithmetic is sound), and our own verdict_challenge says in terms that "Holding all six under STANDARD PHYSICS reads as though the page had blessed the electromagnetic claim." The unsplit cluster is already reported and I am not re-raising it; what is unreported is that the TLDR endorses the unsplit verdict and gives a reason for it, so a reader who expands nothing carries away the blessing the writer's own challenge warns against. Recurring failure #2, and a quantifier-free version of it.
holes.recommendation: Replace "so this is not a rival to Coriolis, it is Coriolis re-derived, which is why the verdict is standard physics rather than refuted" with "so this is not a rival to Coriolis, it is Coriolis re-derived, which is why the sky-rotation half of this cluster is standard physics rather than refuted. The electromagnetic half is a different claim with a different fate - about ten million times too weak - and our own reviewer disputes holding both under one verdict, below."

holes.quoted_phrase: The six list items borrow his answer to Coriolis into a model he wrote a book against
holes.description: This sentence attributes all six items to Sungenis, in the highest-fidelity attribution field on the card, and our own compression block contradicts it: "Items 56 and 113 (electromagnetic) and 214 (drones) assert something his argument needs to be false, and we could not locate them in the Sungenis text we were able to search." Both are published. Only three of the six are "his answer"; on our own account the other three are not his and one of them cannot be, since a 2006 book cannot contain a drone claim. The cluster record compounds it by crediting all six to "Galileo Was Wrong, Vol. I", 2006. This is the ARG-R06 defect - cluster-level attribution applied to every item without checking each - and the corrections log records the agreed remedy: state the unlocatable status before refuting, not in a later collapsed block.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence with: "Three of the six list items - 6, 106 and 292 - borrow his answer to Coriolis into a model he wrote a book against; the other three do not come from him at all, and we say where we looked in the compression note below. As the refutation works out, the borrowed answer does not survive the transfer, because the whole reason a rotating frame can reverse the deflection at the equator is that the Earth is round."

holes.quoted_phrase: Items 56 and 113 replace the inertial deflection with an electromagnetic one.
holes.description: Sections six and seven refute items 56, 113 and 214 as though they were the credited originator's claims, with no scoping sentence, under a card whose meta line names Sungenis and Bennett as the source. The scoping does exist - it is in the compression block, which renders in a separate collapsed <details> after the refutation. The corrections entry of 2026-08-05 fixed exactly this in R08 by moving the disclosure to a heading ahead of the refutation. The same fix has not been applied here.
holes.recommendation: Open section six with: "Items 56 and 113 replace the inertial deflection with an electromagnetic one. We could not locate either claim in the Sungenis text we were able to search - the Vol. I archive rendering truncates inside chapter 1 and the Vol. II scan part-way through - so what follows answers a claim of unknown authorship that circulates in the list, not an argument of the cluster's credited authors, whose own version (below) contradicts it."

holes.quoted_phrase: the measured parameter matches complete dragging to the precision of ring-laser gyroscopy
holes.description: This is the quantitative hinge of our reply to the strongest form of the geocentric case, and it carries no citation - there is no ring-laser source in `sources`. It is also stated harder than the literature supports: the figure comes from large-ring-laser work where 1 part in 10^9 is a threshold recently reached, not a routine accuracy. The G Wettzell analysis (arXiv:2208.09134) opens "The absolute measurement of the Earth angular rotation rate with ground-based instruments becomes challenging if the 1 part in 10^9 of precision has to be obtained" and reports that "the Allan deviation drops below 1 part in 10^9 after an integration time of about 10^4 s". "Better than one part in 10^9" reads as an established margin; it is an integration-limited Allan deviation at the edge of the art. The argument survives comfortably at 1 part in 10^8, so the fix costs nothing.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "the measured parameter matches complete dragging to the limit of the best mechanical measurements of Earth's rotation - the large ring laser at Wettzell reaches an Allan deviation below one part in 10^9 after about 10^4 s of integration, and finds no discrepancy with the astronomical rate." Add to `sources`: {label: "Absolute measurement of Earth's angular rotation rate with the G Wettzell ring laser - Allan deviation below 1 part in 10^9 after ~10^4 s", url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09134"}.

holes.quoted_phrase: Hans Thirring showed in 1918 that inside a rotating mass shell the inertial frames are dragged
holes.description: Thirring 1918 is the single citation the STANDARD PHYSICS verdict rests on, it is named five times across the entry, and it appears nowhere in `sources`. We cite the 1985 repair and the 1966 extension - both of which I verified (Pfister & Braun, Class. Quantum Grav. 2(6):909-918, 1985, title exact; Brill & Cohen, Phys. Rev. 143:1011, 1966, title exact) - but not the paper being repaired. The Gravity Probe B numbers in the steelman are likewise uncited; they are correct (Everitt et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 106:221101, 2011: measured -37.2 +/- 7.2 mas/yr against -39.2 mas/yr predicted), but on a page whose product is provenance, an unsourced number in a steelman is the first thing a hostile reader tests. Worth adding: Thirring published a correction to the 1918 paper in 1921, which strengthens our "that result was imperfect" sentence rather than weakening it.
holes.recommendation: Add to `sources`: {label: "Thirring, 'Uber die Wirkung rotierender ferner Massen in der Einsteinschen Gravitationstheorie', Physikalische Zeitschrift 19:33-39 (1918), with the author's own correction at Phys. Z. 22:29-30 (1921) - the rotating-shell result this argument rests on, and its first repair", url: "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lense%E2%80%93Thirring_precession"} and {label: "Everitt et al., 'Gravity Probe B: Final Results of a Space Experiment to Test General Relativity', Phys. Rev. Lett. 106:221101 (2011) - frame-dragging drift -37.2 +/- 7.2 mas/yr against -39.2 predicted", url: "https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.3456"}.

holes.quoted_phrase: about 300 miles or five degrees, and it has stayed there
holes.description: Three problems in one clause, and the second is the one a defender uses. (i) NOAA AOML says "the storm must be at least 300 miles from the equator", not "about"; and 300 miles is 4.3 degrees of latitude, not five. (ii) "it has stayed there" is an empirical stability claim with nothing behind it - NOAA's FAQ is a rule of thumb, not a time series, and we have not shown the cyclogenesis exclusion latitude is stable to better than a few degrees. (iii) The comparison is therefore between quantities of the same size: Yizengaw's migration, which I verified verbatim ("latitudinal swath reaches ~3.85 degrees latitude in about twenty years or at the displacement rate of 0.2 degrees per year" at 47W), is 3.85 degrees against an exclusion belt of ~4.3 degrees whose empirical width is surely larger than that. The far stronger argument is static and we do not use it: at any single epoch the dip equator sits many degrees from the geographic equator across the South American and Atlantic sector, yet the calm belt tracks the geographic line - no time series required.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "The line first, and the decisive version needs no history: at any single epoch the magnetic dip equator departs from the geographic equator by many degrees of latitude across the South American and Atlantic sector, while the belt in which cyclonic organisation fails tracks the geographic line - NOAA's hurricane researchers state it as a distance from the equator, at least 300 miles. The dip equator also migrates, about 0.2 degrees of latitude per year over Brazil, some 3.85 degrees in twenty years; the calm belt does not follow it."

holes.quoted_phrase: because its rotation axis points the same way everywhere on it
holes.description: The stated reason does not distinguish the two cases, so as written it explains nothing. A rotation axis is a single direction; the Earth's axis also "points the same way everywhere on it". The fact that does the work - and which the steelman states correctly ("only the component of the rotation vector along the local vertical enters the horizontal deflection") - is that on a flat disc the local vertical is parallel to the axis at every point, so the projection never changes sign. Anyone who knows the physics will spot that the TLDR's reason is vacuous, and the TLDR is the field most likely to be quoted back at us.
holes.recommendation: Replace with "because on a flat disc the local vertical is parallel to the rotation axis everywhere, so the component that does the deflecting never changes sign."

holes.quoted_phrase: That qualification is not modesty, it is accurate physics history
holes.description: We quote Sungenis's hedge and then supply our own account of what it means, skipping the sentence in which he says what it means. The full passage reads: "...but not exactly. He discovered that the gravitational field inside the rotating universe was above zero. He discovered that these 'above zero' forces are caused by the centrifugal and Coriolis forces, the very ones that are deemed 'fictitious' in the Newtonian system and thus would measure zero." On his reading the inexactness is the point - it is what makes the forces real rather than fictitious - which is a claim, not an admission. Our gloss is compatible with the text but is not the only reading, and quoting the intervening sentence makes our own finding sharper, not weaker: Pfister and Braun's repair removes precisely the anomalous interior term he is celebrating.
holes.recommendation: After "...says so twice in one sentence: very much like, and but not exactly." insert: "He then says what the inexactness is - the gravitational field inside the rotating universe was above zero - and reads that as showing the Coriolis and centrifugal terms are real rather than fictitious. Note what follows: the 1985 repair removes the anomalous interior term, so the modern literature does not vindicate his qualification, it deletes it."

citation_failures: Gross 2000, GRL 27(15):2329-2332 - fetched in full. Cited in tldr and refutation section five for excitation "on the floor of the Pacific". The word Pacific does not occur in the paper; the excitation is global ocean-bottom pressure from a global OGCM over 1985.0-1996.0. The 433.0 +/- 1.1 d period, the 3.45 vs 1.87 mas^2 figures and "about twice as much excitation power" all verify; the basin does not. The period is also Wilson and Vicente 1990's, adopted by Gross, not Gross's own determination - our source label credits it to Gross.

NOAA AOML Hurricane Research Division FAQ - fetched. States "the storm must be at least 300 miles from the equator". Our text renders this as "about 300 miles or five degrees": "about" softens "at least", and 300 miles is 4.3 degrees, not 5. The additional clause "and it has stayed there" is not supported by this source or any other in the list.
Thirring 1918 - the paper the STANDARD PHYSICS verdict rests on, named five times in the entry, absent from `sources`. UNCITED, not wrong.

Gravity Probe B frame-dragging figures in the steelman - correct (verified against Everitt et al. 2011, arXiv:1105.3456: -37.2 +/- 7.2 mas/yr vs -39.2 predicted) but absent from `sources`. UNCITED, not wrong.

Ring-laser gyroscopy "better than one part in 10^9" - no source in the entry. The figure is roughly right but is an integration-limited Allan deviation recently reached (arXiv:2208.09134), stated by us as an established margin.
reviews.summary: The analysis is sound and the hedge-rule work is the best I have seen on this project: I pulled the Palm-Sungenis debate document and every quoted Sungenis sentence is verbatim, the refutation is aimed at the strong post-1985 version rather than at Thirring's 1918 approximation or at the list's fragment, and both quantitative refutations survive re-derivation (the electromagnetic branch really is ~1.3e7 short; the drone numbers - 1.03e-3 m/s^2, 0.006 degrees of tilt, ~5 m over 100 s - are all correct). Pfister & Braun, Brill & Cohen, Yizengaw, Bibnum/Ferrel and iMAR all check out exactly as cited. The defects are in the layer around the argument, as the sweep predicted: a fabricated basin ("the Pacific") attributed to Gross 2000 and sitting in the TLDR, a TLDR that supplies a reason for a blanket STANDARD PHYSICS verdict its own body and its own filed verdict-challenge dispute, and a passage gloss crediting all six items to Sungenis while the compression block says three of them could not be found in his work. On the writer's existing verdict challenge, which I was asked to assess and am not re-raising: it is right. The six items do not share a fate, the seven-orders-of-magnitude calculation genuinely refutes 56 and 113, and 214 is a 2006 attribution for a claim about consumer drones. current_verdict_holds is set false on that basis alone; my own recommended edits are sentence-level.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The hedge rule is honoured, and better than most entries on the board. The refutation explicitly refuses to beat the fragment ("Gyroscope anomalies indicating no rotation.") and is built around items 225 and 374, which it concedes are correct about deployed hardware — the first paragraph gives away the airliner-INS proof outright ("Anyone who answers this cluster by pointing at an airliner has argued in a circle... This page does not make that argument"). The steelman reaches KERNEL tier honestly: it names the specific true thing (a strapdown INS supplies the Earth-rate term from a stored latitude rather than measuring it, so the popular debunk is circular) and then shows the true thing points the other way (the latitude nut's 15·sin(lat) signature, and the gyrotheodolite finding north from nothing and failing within ~15 deg of the poles). compression.assessed=True and drifted=True are used honestly, not to avoid work, and the note refuses to score all five items as drifting the same way. ONE reservation, filed as a moderate hole rather than a hedge-rule breach: the comparison holds item 12 against a 2018 film, and the rendered drift label reads "The item states the opposite of its source" — but our own source list dates a circulating mechanical-gyroscope version of the claim to a Metabunk thread opened 20 March 2016, two years earlier. The film is the best text we can hold the item against; it is not demonstrably the text the list compressed, and the published note does not say so.

holes.field: clusters.py A07 note (renders as `basis`, in the visible summary of section 3)
holes.quoted_phrase: Knodel's own $20,000 ring-laser gyro measured a 15°/hour drift on camera — exactly 360°÷24h. He looked for ways to shield the apparatus rather than accept the result.
holes.description: The cluster note renders on the page inside the ARG-A07 block, in the collapsed summary of section 3 next to the SELF-CONTRADICTED chip, and it contradicts the entry it sits on top of, twice, about a living man. (a) The gloss states: "One line is deliberately left out. The most quoted sentence from this sequence is about what the instrument cost... it is not reproduced here, because the only use for it is to invite a reader to infer a motive." The figure is reproduced, in the same block, above the gloss that disclaims it — confirmed in the built page (docs/index.html contains `$20,000` exactly once, inside the A07 refutation summary). The page tells the reader it is withholding something it is publishing. (b) The refutation devotes a bolded paragraph to crediting the shielding run — "deserves credit rather than ridicule", "it was a control and it did its job", "That is a result. Hunting systematics after an unwelcome reading is what every laboratory does and it is not a criticism" — while this line converts the same act into refusal ("rather than accept the result"). The module docstring's claim that there is "No claim about motive, belief, finances or state of mind anywhere in the published fields" is true of the DEEP fields and false of the cluster field that renders with them. This is the highest-visibility text in the entry and the one a defender screenshots.
holes.recommendation: In scripts/clusters.py, replace the A07 note with: note="Knodel's ring-laser gyroscope read a 15°/hour drift on camera — the rate a rotating Earth produces to two significant figures, and a rate a stationary Earth puts at zero. The follow-up run enclosed the instrument against magnetic fields, returned the same reading, and the protocol had no acceptance criterion to put it in."

holes.quoted_phrase: arrives on the list under a headline asserting a result nobody in its own lineage is on record obtaining
holes.description: An unscoped absence claim about an entire lineage, published as the payoff sentence of the compression finding. Our own gloss says the opposite two sections earlier: "No write-up of this gyroscope data authored by Knodel himself was located. The GlobeBusters broadcast archive was not searched for this entry." A claim that nobody in the lineage is on record obtaining a null gyroscope result cannot be made from a corpus we state we did not search. It is also contradicted by our own steelman, which says a mechanical-gyroscope demonstration claiming exactly that result was "circulating and being picked apart on Metabunk in March 2016" — that video is somebody in the lineage on record obtaining (a bogus) null. Note that the ratcheting absence test in tests/test_provenance.py scans only tldr, refutation, untraceable and passage.gloss, and its regexes match "does not contain"-family wording, so this phrasing escapes the ratchet in two independent ways rather than being licensed by it.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "arrives on the list under a headline asserting a result that is not on record anywhere we searched for this entry — not in the film, and not in any Knodel-authored write-up we could locate. The GlobeBusters archive was not searched, and unreached is not absent. What is on record in the lineage is the mechanical-gyroscope demonstration of March 2016, whose null the steelman above explains."

holes.quoted_phrase: Transcribed here from two press accounts of the film — Newsweek, 15 February 2019, for the first sentence, and JOE.co.uk for the second — which differ in small ways.
holes.description: Three problems in the one provenance statement, on a page whose product is provenance. (1) The Newsweek article at the URL we cite carries a byline of "Feb 25, 2019 at 05:04 PM EST" (updated 3 March 2019), not 15 February 2019. The wrong date appears twice — in this locator and in the sources label. (2) The split attribution is wrong: Newsweek prints BOTH quoted sentences verbatim, including "We obviously were not willing to accept that, and so we started looking for ways to disprove it was actually registering the motion of the Earth." JOE.co.uk was not needed for the second sentence, and the two accounts do not differ on it at all; they differ only on the first (JOE prints "What we found is, when we turned on that gyroscope, we found...", dropping the "is, is" stutter and hyphenating "15-degree"). (3) The sources label puts a paraphrase inside quotation marks: the headline is "'Behind the Curve' Ending: Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves With Own Experiments in Netflix Documentary", not "Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves in Behind the Curve". Quote length is fine — 53 words, under the 60-word cap.
holes.recommendation: Locator: "Bob Knodel speaking on camera in the ring laser gyroscope sequence. Transcribed here from Newsweek's account of the film, 25 February 2019, which carries both sentences verbatim; JOE.co.uk prints the same sequence with light copy-editing to the first sentence. No timecoded viewing of the film was made for this entry and the surrounding edit was not verified." Sources label: "Newsweek, “‘Behind the Curve’ Ending: Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves With Own Experiments in Netflix Documentary”, 25 February 2019 — transcription of the gyroscope quote and the closing light-through-holes experiment".

holes.quoted_phrase: Jay L. Wile's contemporaneous review of the film describes the follow-up
holes.description: The Wile post is not contemporaneous with the film and is not from 2019. Its own dateline reads 8 August 2023, and the Goodreads syndication of the same post reads "August 08, 2023 04:27" — two independent surfaces agreeing. The film premiered April 2018 and reached Netflix in February 2019, so this is a review written four and a half years later, and "contemporaneous" is the word carrying its evidential weight in a paragraph we lean on for the entire shielding narrative (the magnetic enclosure, the dome-of-stars hypothesis, the bismuth chamber). The substance checks out — the post does read "Thus, they repeated the experiment, this time putting the gyroscope in a container that excludes magnetic fields" and "they got the same result" and "a chamber made out of bismuth" — so only the dating and the reliability signal are wrong.
holes.recommendation: Gloss: "Jay L. Wile's review of the film, posted 8 August 2023, describes the follow-up". Sources label: "Jay L. Wile, “A Really Good Flat Earth Documentary” (8 August 2023) — secondary account, written some years after the film, of the magnetic enclosure, the dome-of-stars hypothesis and the proposed bismuth chamber".

holes.quoted_phrase: built the first gyroscope in 1852
holes.description: Not supported by the source we cite for it, and wrong on the standard account. The Wikipedia "Foucault's gyroscope" page we list credits Foucault with naming the instrument ("I propose to name gyroscope the sole instrument which has served me to observe them") and makes no first-builder claim; Wikipedia's "Gyroscope" article gives the priority to Johann Bohnenberger, "who first wrote about it in 1817", with Walter R. Johnson's disc version in 1832. This is a free hit for a defender in the paragraph headed "where the evidence actually is" — the paragraph whose whole job is to be unimpeachable, since it is where the entry relocates the case so that it does not rest on the film. The argument is untouched: Foucault did build his in 1852 expressly to demonstrate the Earth's rotation and did coin the name.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Léon Foucault built his gyroscope in 1852 as a follow-up to his pendulum, for the express purpose of demonstrating the Earth's rotation, and coined the word for it — the rotating-mass instrument itself goes back to Bohnenberger in 1817, but the name is Foucault's, from gyros and skopein, to view the rotation."

holes.quoted_phrase: Position is externally updated; heading is not.
holes.description: Overstated, and overstated in exactly the place the advocate is strongest. In an aided (GPS/INS) system the Kalman filter estimates and corrects attitude and heading errors as well as position — heading error becomes observable under horizontal acceleration and is trimmed from GPS velocity. A reader with avionics knowledge answers this sentence in one line and takes the section with it. The true and much stronger claim is about INITIAL alignment: gyrocompassing derives true north from the sensed horizontal component of the Earth's rotation vector with nothing fed in, which is precisely the operation the next clause already invokes.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Position is externally updated, and in an aided system the filter trims heading error along with it. What is not supplied from outside is the initial heading: a strapdown platform obtains true north during gyrocompass alignment by sensing the horizontal component of the Earth's rotation vector, with no satellite and no star in view — the same operation a gyrotheodolite performs underground."

holes.field: clusters.py A07 note (renders in the section 3 summary)
holes.quoted_phrase: exactly 360°÷24h
holes.description: The gloss is careful to say the opposite: "the sidereal rate — the one a gyroscope actually senses, because it measures rotation with respect to the local inertial frame rather than with respect to the Sun — is Ω = 7.292115 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹, or 15.041° per hour... The figure as spoken carries two significant figures and cannot separate them, so nothing here claims that this apparatus resolved sidereal from solar." The word "exactly" in the visible summary claims the match to the solar-day rate that the body declines to claim, and it points at the wrong quantity: what the instrument senses is 360° per sidereal day, not per 24 hours. Same field as the major finding above; separable defect, and separable in its consequences, because this one is a physics slip a specialist reader catches rather than a tone problem.
holes.recommendation: Within the replacement note, use: "— the rate a rotating Earth produces to two significant figures (sidereal 15.041°/hour)" in place of "— exactly 360°÷24h".

holes.quoted_phrase: The reversal is carried by item 12 alone, and the cluster is named after it.
holes.description: drift_type="reversed" renders under the heading "The list overstates its own source" and the label "The item states the opposite of its source" — both of which assert that the 2018 film is the text item 12 was compressed from. Our own evidence says otherwise: the sources list dates a circulating mechanical-gyroscope version of the argument to a Metabunk thread opened 20 March 2016 (verified: thread start date 20 March 2016), two years before the film, and the entry's own answer to item 112 leans on that same 2016 artefact. The note is honestly scoped in one clause ("The only source text available to hold it against is..."), but the section header, the drift label and this sentence together leave a reader with a provenance claim the entry cannot support. This is the genealogy, which is the product; it also overlaps the year="2018" issue the writer reported to the parent, which the published prose does not carry.
holes.recommendation: Insert after the quoted sentence: "One caveat on what is being compared. The film is not demonstrably the text the list compressed: a mechanical-gyroscope version of the claim was already circulating and being picked apart on Metabunk by 20 March 2016, two years before the film, and no earlier text of item 12's own is in our records. The filmed statement is the best source text we can hold the item against, and the reversal is stated on that footing rather than as a claim about descent."

holes.quoted_phrase: which is the rate a rotating Earth predicts and the rate a stationary one puts at zero
holes.description: The TLDR states flat what the body is careful to qualify — the recurring failure of writing the TLDR from memory of the argument. The refutation says: "the axis geometry is unresolved: a three-axis unit reports the magnitude of the rotation vector, the full 15.041° per hour at any latitude, whereas a single-axis unit with its input axis vertical reads only Ω sin φ. Nothing in this treatment depends on which it was." But the TLDR does depend on it: 15°/hour is "the rate a rotating Earth predicts" only for a unit reading the full vector. For a vertical single-axis unit at the filming latitude (San Diego, ~32.7°N) the prediction is about 8.1°/hour, and a 15°/hour reading would then NOT be the predicted value. The verdict survives either way — any non-zero reading contradicts a prediction of zero — but the headline sentence claims a match the entry elsewhere says it cannot establish.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "which is the magnitude of the rotation rate a turning Earth produces and the rate a stationary one puts at zero".

holes.quoted_phrase: Navigation-grade units of this class are specified at bias uncertainties better than 0.01
holes.description: "of this class" quietly assigns the filmed instrument to a grade the very next sentence says we cannot establish ("No make, model, input-axis orientation or uncertainty is given in the sequences the press transcriptions cover"). The 1,500× comparison is doing rhetorical work — implying the reading is too large to be bias — on an assumption the entry disclaims one sentence later. Self-limiting, hence minor, but it is the kind of sentence the advocate's "you promoted a spoken number to an experimental result" charge feeds on.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Navigation-grade ring lasers are specified at bias uncertainties better than 0.01° per hour, some fifteen hundred times smaller than the figure reported here — though nothing available to us establishes that the filmed unit was of that grade."

citation_failures: Newsweek, 'Flat Earthers Disprove Themselves in Behind the Curve', 15 February 2019 — the URL is right and carries both quoted sentences verbatim, but the byline date is 25 February 2019 (updated 3 March 2019) and the headline in quotation marks is a paraphrase, not the title.

Jay L. Wile, 'A Really Good Flat Earth Documentary' (2019), described in the gloss as 'contemporaneous' — the post's own dateline and its Goodreads syndication both read 8 August 2023. Content of the citation (magnetic-field container, dome-of-stars hypothesis, same result, bismuth chamber next) verified verbatim.

Wikipedia — Foucault's gyroscope, cited for 'built the first gyroscope in 1852' — the page supports the 1852 date, the demonstration purpose and the coinage, but not 'first'; Wikipedia's Gyroscope article gives priority to Bohnenberger, 1817.
JOE.co.uk, cited as the source of the second quoted sentence — it does carry that sentence, but so does Newsweek, verbatim, so the stated two-source route is not what happened.

UNCHECKED, not failed: Di Virgilio et al. journal reference EPJ C 82:824 (2022). Title, author list and the substantive claim ('the Allan deviation drops below 1 part in 10⁹ after an integration time of about 10⁴ s') verified at the ar5iv URL cited; the volume/article number was not independently confirmed.
reviews.summary: The analysis is sound and the verdict holds: the steelman is genuine KERNEL tier (the INS Earth-rate term is an input, so the popular airliner debunk is circular), the refutation answers items 225 and 374 rather than the fragment, and the physics I could check is right — the Wettzell Sagnac beat recomputes to 348.6 Hz from the stated geometry, Michelson–Gale's 0.236±0.002 vs 0.230±0.005 is correct, the Metabunk thread really opens 20 March 2016, the quote is 53 words and under the cap, and the five item numbers map to the corpus exactly. The damage is all in the layer around the argument, and the worst of it is in another file: the clusters.py A07 note renders inside this entry's section-3 summary and publishes the $20,000 line the gloss says is deliberately withheld, then frames the shielding run as refusal ("rather than accept the result") in the same breath as the refutation crediting it as a control that "did its job" — a self-contradiction about a living man in the most visible field on the block. Second major: the compression note closes on an unscoped absence ("nobody in its own lineage is on record obtaining"), which our own gloss ("the GlobeBusters broadcast archive was not searched") and our own steelman (the March 2016 mechanical-gyro video) both contradict, and which slips the ratcheting test because that test does not scan compression notes. Seven moderates follow, all sentence-level: a wrong Newsweek date and a wrong transcription route, a 2023 blog post cited as a contemporaneous 2019 review, Foucault credited with the first gyroscope (Bohnenberger, 1817), "heading is not" externally updated (an aided filter trims it; the real point is initial gyrocompass alignment), "exactly 360°÷24h" against the entry's own sidereal caveat, a "reversed" drift verdict resting on a film that postdates the claim by two years, and a TLDR that asserts the axis-dependent match the body says it cannot establish.

holes.quoted_phrase: by p. 62 van der Kamp is refusing to own it
holes.description: We locate van der Kamp's disagreement in the wrong place, and the entry contradicts itself doing it. Read around scan pp. 60-64, he does not refuse the observational equivalence - he accepts it and attacks the presupposition Russell smuggles in with it (his sentence: Russell's view 'takes for granted a space pinpointing places and hence allowing motion through that space to be real, though apparently not directly but only relatively observable'). What he rejects is the deflationary half of Hoyle's formula - 'as good as anybody else's, but NOT BETTER' - because he holds the Tychonian system is better, not merely permitted. Our own compression note then quotes his conditional version of the same proposition ('If Einstein is right ...') as HIS relativistic argument, which cannot be squared with the gloss saying the proposition is other people's. The corrected reading is not softer on the list: it is a cleaner hedge_dropped, because the list turns a conditional stepping-stone into a flat proof item in his name.
holes.recommendation: Replace the gloss sentence 'But wanting a hostile witness is not the same as owning his conclusion, and by p. 62 van der Kamp is refusing to own it.' with: 'But he does not take Russell's conclusion with the quotation. He grants the equivalence - his own version of it runs under an antecedent, “if Einstein is right, neither the orbital, nor any other velocity of our Earth can be measured directly” (p. 6) - and refuses the half of Hoyle's formula that says geocentrism is therefore not better. What he objects to at p. 62 is the presupposition he says Russell carries unexamined: a real space in which real motion happens and yet cannot be observed. He wanted the question decided, not dissolved.' And in compression.note replace 'in the book the equivalence belongs to Russell and Hoyle, who are named, and van der Kamp’s sentence about them is a refusal — their claims hold only on presuppositions he rejects in the next three words. On the list the same proposition appears in his own name.' with: 'in the book the equivalence is credited to Russell and Hoyle, who are named, and van der Kamp takes it from them on terms — it holds only on presuppositions he rejects in the next three words, and he refuses the clause that makes geocentrism merely equal rather than better. On the list the proposition appears in his own name, flat, with both the crediting and the refusal gone.'

holes.quoted_phrase: His demand was reasonable when he framed it and had in substance been met by the time he published it.
holes.description: The section that answers van der Kamp's own stated demand assumes the point in dispute. Two steps: (i) 'its modern versions get the varying platform velocity for free from the Earth's own rotation and orbit rather than from an aircraft' - on the model van der Kamp defended, the Earth neither rotates nor orbits, so those experiments have no varying platform velocity and cannot be the control experiment he asked for; a defender does not need to be sophisticated to spot this. (ii) Hafele-Keating measured clock RATES, not the speed of light, which is the quantity his modus tollens is stated over ('if the speed of light measured from a fast-moving platform comes out at the earthly c ...'). So the closing verdict rests partly on an experiment that does not measure what he specified and partly on experiments whose 'fast platform' is the thing he denied. Our own advocate block already names this as the defender's best closing line and rates the objection 4, and the section does not answer it. The fix is available and is stronger than what is there: laboratory fast platforms whose speed does not depend on the Earth's state of motion at all.
holes.recommendation: Replace the final two sentences of the seventh section, from 'Clocks on fast platforms had already been flown in 1971' to the end, with: 'Be exact about one thing a defender will press: the modern Kennedy–Thorndike versions take their varying platform velocity from the Earth’s own rotation and orbit, which is the very motion in dispute, so on his own model they vary nothing. That objection is fair, and it is answered by the platforms that move fast in the laboratory frame whatever the Earth is doing. Ives and Stilwell had already flown one in 1938 — a beam of hydrogen canal rays — and the modern version stores lithium ions at 0.338c and confirms the relativistic Doppler shift to a few parts in 109 (Botermann et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 113:120405, 2014). No aircraft, no assumption about the Earth. His demand was reasonable when he framed it, the class of experiment that meets it was already running when he framed it, and what the movement did next was not to press the demand but to publish the answer he had asked to have tested.' Add the Botermann paper to `sources`.

holes.quoted_phrase: If the Earth held still, that subtraction would be a fiction
holes.description: Overstated against the model actually held. The barycentric correction removes the observer's velocity RELATIVE to the Solar-System barycentre. A neo-Tychonic cosmos - Sun circling a fixed Earth, stellar sphere carried with it, which is exactly what van der Kamp needed to keep aberration and parallax - reproduces the same relative velocity by construction, so the same correction applies with the attribution reversed and nothing is a fiction. Our own next paragraph concedes precisely this ('They are measurements of motion relative to matter'), so the sentence is not just exposed, it is contradicted two lines later by our own text, and it sits inside the paragraph the advocate block identifies as the page's most vulnerable.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'If the Earth held still, that subtraction would be a fiction, and the fiction would have to be the reason exoplanet signals stay coherent across years of observation.' with: 'The correction is not optional and not a convention: leave it out and exoplanet signals decohere across a season. A geocentric model can reproduce it, but only by carrying the Sun and the whole stellar sphere around the Earth on the same annual period — which is to say by asserting the identical relative motion under a different owner, and then owing a dynamics for it.'

holes.quoted_phrase: one universal absolute preferred frame in which c is isotropic
holes.description: A verbatim quotation of two named living authors, load-bearing for the section (it is what 'the movement's own retreat' rests on), with no entry for it in this argument's `sources` list. The reader is sent to ARG-R01 for the citation. R01 does source it - to the Internet Archive scan labelled ...Bennett4276, confirmed from its own front matter as Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II, 7th ed. 2013 - so nothing is fabricated, but on a page whose product is provenance, quoting living authors from a card that carries no citation for the quote is the move we criticise elsewhere (see the C02 entry in review/corrections.json).
holes.recommendation: Add to `sources`: dict(label="Sungenis & Bennett, Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II (7th ed., 2013) - the Earth-Centred Inertial frame named as 'one universal absolute preferred frame in which c is isotropic'; Internet Archive scan labelled ...Bennett4276, chs 7-13", url=<the same archive URL used in R01's sources>), and change 'R01 records the movement’s own retreat from this position' to 'R01 works this in full: Sungenis and Bennett name the Earth-Centred Inertial frame ...'

holes.quoted_phrase: "R03": dict(lane="A-REL", name="No experiment detects absolute motion; only relative motion is observable",
holes.description: real_source is null while our own treatment identifies the real work by name and quotes it twice - Poincare's 1904 principle of relativity, which van der Kamp himself quotes at scan p. 45. Sibling clusters in the same lane do carry the field (R04 'Einstein equivalence principle', R09 'Reichenbach-Grunbaum conventionality thesis', R05 'Godel 1949; Lense-Thirring 1918'), so R03 is the anomaly. This is not cosmetic: build.py derives the published 'two clocks' figures from this field, so R03's 8 items are currently absent from 'arguments citing a dated piece of genuine science'. IMPORTANT SIDE EFFECT, measured rather than guessed - filling it moves dated clusters 27 to 28, items citing dated work 107 to 115, and pre-1930 items 53 to 61, which turns 53/107 (49.5 per cent, 'close to half') into 61/115 (53 per cent, a majority) and breaks the passing test 'pre-1930 items are close to half, but NOT a majority - do not write most'. The prose, the test and the field have to move together or the page will assert something its own data denies.
holes.recommendation: Set real_source="Poincare, principle of relativity, 1904; Einstein, special relativity, 1905" on the R03 cluster, anchoring the edit on the cluster key rather than on a field line (see the E01/E03 misfile in review/corrections.json). Then update the Overview prose that currently says pre-1930 items are close to half but not a majority, and retarget the corresponding test to the derived value, in the same commit. Also settle originator_work/year: the treatment cites only De Labore Solis (1988) while the record credits The Heart of the Matter (1968), which was unreachable.

holes.quoted_phrase: a ring laser bolted to the ground reads the Earth's spin without looking at the
holes.description: TLDR-against-body check. The TLDR presents the ring laser as the thing that settles it - 'rotation was never inside it, WHICH IS WHY a ring laser bolted to the ground reads the Earth's spin' - while the body concedes, correctly and at length, that on a Machian rotating cosmos the compass of inertia turns with the sky and the ring laser reads 15.04 deg/h either way, and our own advocate block rates that objection 4. Readers who never expand meet the strong form with none of the qualification. The literal words are defensible (the instrument does measure rotation relative to local inertia without the sky); the implication a reader takes is the one the body declines to make on its own.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'which is why a ring laser bolted to the ground reads the Earth's spin without looking at the sky' with 'which is why the Earth's spin is measured to nine digits by a ring laser bolted to the ground, with no reference to the sky - and why answering that measurement means arguing dynamics, not coordinates'.

holes.quoted_phrase: (“Russel’s” is the spelling in the scan.)
holes.description: We publish a sic-claim about the source's orthography and carry the misspelling into a quotation of a named author. It did not replicate: two fresh retrievals of the same PDF on this pass both returned 'Russell's contention', against the writer's two passes returning 'Russel's'. All four are mediated by a summarising model over OCR, so neither pair settles it, and our own locator already says the passage was never checked against a print copy. Publishing an assertion about the spelling is a claim we cannot currently support in either direction, and the parenthetical exists only to defend an inserted error.
holes.recommendation: Set the quote's opening to 'Bertrand Russell's contention' and delete the parenthetical '(“Russel’s” is the spelling in the scan.)'. If the spelling is wanted, restore it only after page images, and word it as: 'the OCR text we retrieved is inconsistent on the spelling of Russell's name at this point; it is normalised here.'

holes.quoted_phrase: tracking the Chandler wobble and solid-Earth tides as they move it
holes.description: The single source given for the Wettzell ring laser, Di Virgilio et al., EPJ C 82:824 (2022), was checked and does support the headline number - it is 'Overcoming 1 part in 10^9 of earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data', G at the Geodetic Observatory Wettzell, Allan deviation below 1 part in 10^9 after about 10^4 s. It does not carry the wobble-and-tides claim, which comes from the Schreiber group's earlier work. True statement, source cited does not reach all of it.
holes.recommendation: Add to `sources`: dict(label="Schreiber et al., 'How to detect the Chandler and the annual wobble of the Earth with a large ring laser', Phys. Rev. Lett. 107:173904 (2011)", url="https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.173904").

holes.quoted_phrase: Poincaré, “The Present and the Future of Mathematical Physics”, St Louis,
holes.description: The Poincare wording we quote twice was verified verbatim against the cited maricourt.press page, so the quotation is sound. But that page names no translator, and the wording differs from the widely reprinted Halsted rendering ('uniform movement of translation ... we have not and could not have any means of discerning'). The entire second section of the refutation turns on the two phrases 'translation' and 'such a motion', so a defender who pulls up a different translation should not be able to suggest we chose ours.
holes.recommendation: Change the source label to: "Poincare, address to the St Louis Congress of Arts and Science, 1904 ('L'etat actuel et l'avenir de la physique mathematique'), English text as given at maricourt.press; the phrase survives in the Halsted translation as 'carried along in a uniform movement of translation ... whether or not we are carried along in such a motion'".

reviews.summary: R03's verdict (STANDARD PHYSICS) is right, its steelman genuinely reaches KERNEL tier - underdetermination, Popperian modus tollens, Russell as hostile witness - and its refutation answers the source rather than the list fragment, so the hedge rule is satisfied. Every checkable citation verified against the primary sources: Poincare's wording matches the cited page verbatim, Di Virgilio 2022 is the G ring laser at Wettzell at 1 part in 10^9, Hafele-Keating's '~10% precision' is the Wikipedia wording exactly, Planck's orbital-dipole calibration from 30 to 353 GHz and the 369.82 +/- 0.11 km/s figure are both in Planck 2018 I, Bouw's obituary carries 'went nowhere fast' and the January 1968 printing, and Faulkner's AiG article dates The Heart of the Matter to 1968 as our label says. Two majors: the gloss and compression note mislocate van der Kamp's disagreement - reading around scan pp. 60-64 he ACCEPTS the observational equivalence and rejects only Hoyle's 'not better' clause, which our own note contradicts by quoting his conditional version of the same proposition; and the seventh section's conclusion begs the question, since the modern Kennedy-Thorndike tests take their varying platform velocity from the Earth's rotation and orbit, the very motion in dispute, while Hafele-Keating measures clock rates rather than the speed of light his modus tollens is stated over. Both have concrete replacements, and the second replaces a weak answer with a stronger one (stored-ion Ives-Stilwell at 0.338c, independent of the Earth's state of motion). No hard-constraint breach: nothing adjudicates scripture, no motive or bad-faith claim attaches to any living person, and the unfalsifiable move is named rather than mocked.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Hedge rule passes, and it passes the hard way. The refutation does not beat the fragment: it answers the full-strength physical claim (sections one to five), then names the drift explicitly in section seven and in the compression block, which is the required two-products-from-one-comparison move. drifted=True with drift_type=force_upgraded is honestly earned — both Sungenis quotes verified verbatim this run. The Plait reply (isidore.co mirror, answering Plait's 14 Sept 2010 Bad Astronomy post) contains "A geocentrist appeals to Relativity not as proof or even evidence for geocentrism but merely to show" and "the geocentrist makes his case for geocentrism on solid scientific evidence that has little or nothing to do with Relativity". The Matthews interview contains "which not only supports geocentrism as a 'relative' alternative, but also modified the postulates of STR"; and the straw_man block's "This allowed the world to temporarily escape the implications of the empirical evidence" is verbatim, with "This" referring to STR, exactly as we gloss it. The one weakness, recorded as hole 2 rather than as a hedge-rule breach: neither readable Sungenis document mentions the equivalence principle, so the drift is established against the author's general speech act about relativity, not against an equivalence-principle sentence. The compression note says so in as many words ("enough to establish the speech act and not enough to establish the sentence"), which is why this is scoping debt rather than a critical hole. new_rules_ok is false on one count only: the refutation's sixth section asserts an unscoped absence over an entire literature ("nobody in this literature has produced the cosmological solution"). The existing absence-claim regex in tests/test_provenance.py does not catch that phrasing, so the ratchet passes at 4/4 while the rule itself is broken. No future-tense self-criticism was shipped: the two record issues in the module docstring (works.py title strings, cluster composition) were correctly kept out of published prose, and advocate.preemptive describes sections four and five in the past tense and both sections exist.
reviews.summary: The verdict (STANDARD PHYSICS) is right and the physics is clean — every external citation checked out verbatim, including the MICROSCOPE eta value, Will's three-part EEP with both "local" clauses, Middlemiss's 40 uGal/root-Hz MEMS gravimeter and Earth-tide measurement, Gravity Probe B's four numbers, Di Virgilio et al. EPJ C 82:824 (whose title is literally "Overcoming 1 part in 10^9 ... with the G Wettzell data"), the EarthScope 90%/El Nino sentences, and both Sungenis quotations. The arithmetic also holds: 2g/R, g/R, 0.13 m, 4.4e26 m, 27 orders, 11.3 deg/hr at Paris, ten orders of magnitude on frame dragging. The defect is in the edition layer, which is recurring failure #3: the gloss's claim that "the same chapter 10 is Vol. I in 2006 and Vol. II in 2013" is false and contradicts our own ARG-E13. I retrieved both tables of contents this run — the 2006 Vol. I chapter 10 section run reappears in the 2013 seventh edition as Volume II chapter 9 (p. 111, "Einstein's Geocentrism" at p. 126), while 2013 Vol. II chapter 10 is "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism" (p. 157), which is 2006 Vol. I chapter 12 at p. 710. Secondary: the passage block claims to have located the argument's page when the only evidence is a section heading in a chapter whose entire section list is the inertial-dragging literature that ARG-R05 answers; one unscoped absence claim over a whole literature; a noise-density-as-acceleration units slip carrying the TLDR's 13 cm figure; and one sentence that invites the reader to weigh a living named man's sincerity.
citation_failures: passage.gloss — "page citations in the critical literature to “vol. 1, 9th ed.”": no citation of a ninth edition of Volume I was located in searches for the exact string or for the book plus "9th ed"/"ninth edition". Later editions certainly exist (an eleventh, 2015, ISBN 9781939856609, and a twelfth are catalogued), so the underlying point about pagination is sound, but the specific edition and the body of literature said to cite it are unsupported as written. Recorded as not located, not as absent.

NOT a failure, recorded so it is not re-checked: every other citation verified this run — Touboul et al. PRL 129:121102 (2022) eta(Ti,Pt) = [-1.5 +/- 2.3 (stat) +/- 1.5 (syst)] x 10^-15; Will, Living Reviews in Relativity 17 (2014), both "any local non-gravitational experiment" clauses verbatim; Middlemiss et al., Nature 531:614-617 (2016), 40 microgal per hertz^1/2 and Earth tides; Everitt et al. arXiv:1105.3456, geodetic -6,601.8 +/- 18.3 vs -6,606.1 and frame dragging -37.2 +/- 7.2 vs -39.2; Di Virgilio et al., EPJ C 82:824 (2022), Allan deviation below 1 part in 10^9 at ~10^4 s on the G Wettzell ring laser; EarthScope, "shifts in zonal wind patterns and atmospheric circulation are responsible for around 90% of seasonal length of day variations" and "El Nino events are associated with longer days whereas La Nina events are associated with shorter days"; the 2006 title page (ISBN 0-9779640-0-0, "Volume I: The Scientific Evidence", completion 25 April 2006); "The Failure of General Relativity" at ch. 5 p. 334 and "The Demise of Relativity Theory" at ch. 7 p. 441; chapter 10 running 590-637 (chapter 11 opens at 638).

holes.quoted_phrase: So the same chapter 10 is Vol. I in 2006 and Vol. II in 2013
holes.description: False, and it contradicts our own ARG-E13 and ARG-E03. I read both tables of contents this run. The 2006 Volume I (archive item GallileoWasWrong) has ch. 10 "Mathematical Models of a Geocentric Universe" at p. 590 and ch. 12 "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentric Cosmology" at p. 710. The 2013 seventh-edition Volume II (archive item ...Bennett4276) has ch. 9 "Modern Science and the Acceptance of Geocentrism" at p. 111 — carrying this cluster's entire section run, with Absolute Rest versus Relative Motion at 112, Fred Hoyle's Geocentrism at 115, The Gyroscopic Effect on the Earth at 121, Einstein's Geocentrism at 126, Thirring's Geocentrism at 130, through Barbour and Bertotti's at 147 — and ch. 10 "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism" at p. 157. So the chapters were renumbered as well as rehoused (2006 ch. 8-12 map to 2013 ch. 7-10 and 12), and the 2013 Vol. II ch. 10 is a different chapter entirely: it is the one our ARG-E13 locator already cites as "Vol. II, ch. 10 'Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism'". The sentence also mis-states the standing fact it rests on: "chapters 7-13 became Volume II" is true of the seventh edition's own numbering, not of the 2006 numbering, and the 2006 ch. 7 ("What is Space?", p. 395) is not in the 2013 Volume II under that title at all. This is recurring failure #3 and it is the kind of bad edition record the harness notes reached six entries once already.
holes.recommendation: Replace the whole "Which volume this is, in which year" paragraph body with: "In the 2006 printing this material is chapter 10 of Volume I. In the seventh edition of 2013 the work was split into three volumes and that edition's chapters 7–13 form Volume II — but the chapters were renumbered as well as rehoused. The section run quoted above reappears in the 2013 Volume II as chapter 9, “Modern Science and the Acceptance of Geocentrism”, pp. 111–156, with Einstein's Geocentrism at p. 126 and Thirring's Geocentrism at p. 130. Chapter 10 of the 2013 Volume II is a different chapter, “Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism” at p. 157 — the one ARG-E13 cites — and it corresponds to chapter 12 of the 2006 Volume I at p. 710. Chapter and page citations therefore do not carry between the two editions. Ours is the 2006 first printing throughout." Then append a corrections.json entry, since this is a published edition claim that was wrong.

holes.quoted_phrase: So the volume, chapter and page of this argument are recorded here and its wording is not.
holes.description: This asserts that we have located the argument's page. We have not; we have located a section heading and inferred the rest. The evidence for putting an EQUIVALENCE PRINCIPLE argument at p. 607 is a section titled "Einstein's Geocentrism" sitting in a chapter whose section list is, from end to end, the named inertial-dragging literature — Thirring, Rosser, Bondi, Brill and Cohen, Moon and Spencer, Moller, Brown, Nightingale, Lynden-Bell, Barbour and Bertotti. That is the subject matter our own ARG-R05 ("GR admits rotating-universe solutions / frame dragging") answers, and R05 is credited to the same volume and year. Neither readable Sungenis document — the Plait reply or the Matthews interview — mentions the equivalence principle. A defender's cheapest shot at this entry is that we picked the chapter by reading its table of contents and guessing, and on the evidence published that shot lands.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "So what is recorded here is where a plausible section sits, not what it says. The identification is an inference from a heading: chapter 10's section list is a run of named inertial-dragging results — Thirring, Rosser, Bondi, Brill and Cohen, Møller, Lynden-Bell, Barbour and Bertotti — which is the material ARG-R05 answers, and the words equivalence principle occur nowhere in the front matter and contents we were able to read, nor in either of the Sungenis documents quoted below. Treat Einstein's Geocentrism at p. 607 as this cluster's most likely home, not as an established one."

holes.quoted_phrase: nobody in this literature has produced the cosmological solution
holes.description: An unscoped absence claim, and a broader one than the nine the 2026-08-09 sweep confirmed: those were about one book, this is about an entire literature, with no statement of what was searched. The rule in scripts/deep.py is 'never assert that a source does not contain something; write that X is not located in the specific text searched'. The ratcheting test in tests/test_provenance.py does not catch this because its _ABSENCE regexes match 'does not contain / never mentions / is absent from' and not 'nobody has produced', so the suite reports 4/4 while the rule is broken. The claim is also load-bearing: it carries section six's conclusion and is echoed in advocate.preemptive as 'the party asserting a cosmological solution owes the solution'.
holes.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "and the cosmological solution that would be needed to scale it to a daily rotation is not located in any of the geocentric material we were able to search — the chapter 10 section list, Sungenis's reply to Phil Plait, and the Simran Matthews interview — which is where ARG-R05 and ARG-A09 take it up." Then tighten the _ABSENCE regex list to include \\bnobody (?:has|in) and \\bno one has\\b, and re-run the ratchet.

holes.quoted_phrase: 40 µGal Hz<sup>−½</sup> (4 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup>)
holes.description: Dimensional slip, on a physics page, in the one paragraph a physicist reader will check hardest. 40 microGal Hz^-1/2 is an amplitude spectral density; 4 x 10^-7 m s^-2 is an acceleration. The parenthetical presents one as a conversion of the other, silently dropping the root-Hz. The number is recoverable — in a 1 Hz bandwidth the noise is about 40 microGal, which is where 4 x 10^-7 m s^-2 and hence 0.13 m come from — and with longer integration the figure improves, so the 13 cm is conservative rather than wrong. But the 13 cm is promoted to the TLDR ("that threshold arrives at about 13 cm of height difference"), so the whole headline number currently rests on a unit equation that does not hold as written. Middlemiss et al., Nature 531:614 (2016) verified: the abstract does say "40 microgal per hertz1/2" and does report measuring the Earth tides.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "40 µGal Hz<sup>−½</sup> — a noise density, so about 40 µGal, or 4 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup>, in a one-second measurement, and better with longer integration —" and add to the following sentence: "Thirteen centimetres, and that is the conservative figure: integrate for longer and the boundary shrinks."

holes.quoted_phrase: the chapters themselves stop being retrievable long before p. 607
holes.description: True of the fetcher used on this entry — I reproduced it, twice: the /stream/ rendering of the 2006 Vol. I djvu.txt truncates at printed p. 25, and the complete Vol. 1-3 OCR truncates at p. 34 — and ARG-A09's notes report the same limit. But our own site contradicts it in two places a reader can reach in one click. ARG-A03's passage block quotes verbatim text from "Vol. I, p. 853 of the Internet Archive scan (item GallileoWasWrong)", i.e. 246 printed pages past the point R04 says the item stops yielding; and ARG-E13 states "Full-text search of the 5.4 MB OCR of all three volumes" and quotes deep pages from it. The scan itself is fully searchable: the item metadata lists a 3.3 MB djvu.txt and a 1.1 MB hOCR search-text file over 1,160 page images. So a route to this chapter's own wording was already established elsewhere in the project and this entry did not use it. The sentence is scoped enough to pass the absence rule, but not enough to survive a critic comparing two of our own pages.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "the chapters themselves stopped being retrievable, for the fetcher used on this entry, long before p. 607 — although the same Internet Archive item yielded printed p. 853 to the route used at ARG-A03, and the seventh edition's full-text OCR was searched whole at ARG-E13. The limit recorded here is this entry's, not the scan's, and it should be closed rather than lived with."

holes.quoted_phrase: the local inertial frame is a physical thing you can go and measure
holes.description: This is the pivot the entire refutation turns on, and the one entry in the source's own section list that attacks it directly is never engaged. Barbour and Bertotti's relational dynamics — 'Barbour and Bertotti's Geocentrism', 2006 Vol. I p. 628, 2013 Vol. II p. 147 — is precisely a programme denying that there is a frame-independent standard sitting there to be read; on a relational scheme the inertial frame is whatever best fits the relative configurations of matter. We name them twice, in the passage gloss and in the steelman's SURFACE paragraph, as evidence that 'the reading behind it is not imaginary', and then argue as though relationalism were not on the table. advocate.best_defense gets close ('your gyroscope is a participant in the phenomenon, not an independent umpire of it') but answers it with frame dragging rather than with relationalism, which is the harder version. Missing the strongest available counterpoint, in a steelman we otherwise built at genuine KERNEL tier.
holes.recommendation: Insert after the sentence quoted: "The one entry in the book's own section list that bites here is Barbour and Bertotti's relational dynamics at p. 628, which denies that there is any frame-independent standard waiting to be read off: on a relational scheme the inertial frame just is whatever best fits the relative configurations of the matter, so “the Earth rotates” becomes a statement about a best fit rather than a reading on a dial. That is a serious position, and it still does not deliver a stationary Earth — because the best fit is the one Foucault, Wettzell and Gravity Probe B already measure, and it is the same 15.04° per hour. Relationalism relocates the standard; it does not abolish it, and nothing in it makes the Earth the body at rest."

holes.quoted_phrase: Decline to take him at his word
holes.description: Sungenis is living and named, and this sentence invites the reader to consider that he may not mean what he published. The dilemma it constructs is legitimate and useful — the argument is either not evidence, or it is evidence and it fails — but the axis it is built on is his sincerity rather than the argument's strength. The project's standing rule is that we make no claims about motive or bad faith regarding living people, and the straw_man block one field away states 'We take no view on anyone's reasons for holding a position', so this also reads as inconsistent with our own declared stance. The fix costs nothing: the same dilemma runs on the strength of the claim instead of on the man.
holes.recommendation: Replace the pair of sentences with: "Read the appeal at the strength his own gloss gives it and this cluster is not evidence for anything — it is a claim of respectability. Read it at the strength the list gives it and it has to be run at full force, in which case it collapses for the reasons above. Either way the list's flat “Equivalence principle validation” overstates the authority it is drawing on."

holes.quoted_phrase: Its whole content is the word local
holes.description: Small internal tension in the field readers see first, of exactly the shape the sweep's failure #2 describes. The same TLDR sentence-pair says the principle 'has been tested to about a part in 10^15' — which is MICROSCOPE, a test of the weak equivalence principle, universality of free fall — and then says the principle's 'whole content is the word local'. The body is more careful and does not make this mistake: it lists Will's three parts and says 'Both OPERATIVE clauses carry the same qualifier', tacitly conceding that WEP is not one of them. So the body distinguishes where the TLDR collapses. Not a contradiction, but a quantifier in a TLDR that does not survive contact with its own body, and per the harness those get checked.
holes.recommendation: Change to: "Its operative content is the word local:" — matching the body's "Both operative clauses carry the same qualifier".

holes.quoted_phrase: the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment
holes.description: Emphasis silently added inside direct quotation. Will's text (Living Reviews in Relativity 17, 2014, verified this run) reads 'The outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of the velocity of the freely-falling reference frame in which it is performed' with no italics; we italicise 'local' in both clauses without marking it. The same move appears in compression.source_wording, which italicises 'relative' inside Sungenis's quoted phrase and sets the whole clause 'not as proof or even evidence for geocentrism' in italics. Substantively harmless — the emphasis is on the word that is genuinely doing the work — but this is a site whose product is showing how distributors quietly alter what sources said, and unmarked emphasis is the smallest member of that family. It is also the first thing a hostile reader with a copy of Will will notice.
holes.recommendation: Append "(italics ours here and below)" after the first quoted clause, and add the same parenthetical to compression.source_wording: "… can have just as much scientific respectability as heliocentrism.” (italics ours)"

holes.quoted_phrase: page citations in the critical literature to “vol. 1, 9th ed.” will not line up with this scan’s pagination
holes.description: An unverified specific in published prose, on a page whose product is edition accuracy. Searches for the literal string "Galileo Was Wrong" plus "vol. 1, 9th ed.", and for the book plus "9th ed"/"ninth edition", returned no citation of a ninth edition of Volume I; recorded as not located rather than absent. A ninth edition may well exist — an eleventh (2015, ISBN 9781939856609) and a twelfth are catalogued, and our own works.py carries a disputed "10th ed. 2013" that ARG-E03 already showed cannot be right — but as written the sentence attributes a specific citation practice to a body of critical literature we cannot point at. The underlying point, that later printings repaginate, is true and worth keeping.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and the work ran on through at least an eleventh edition (2015) and a twelfth, so page citations to any later printing will not line up with this scan's pagination".

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The hedge rule is satisfied, and satisfied honestly. There is no upstream sentence to compress: I re-fetched the specimen (withthesun33.com/about-1) and confirmed 461 numbered items, the six item texts verbatim (429 "Liturgy calendar solar.", 431 "Sacred east orientation.", 441, 442, 446, 447), and that no item carries a citation, footnote or source. compression.assessed="no_source" with drifted=None is therefore the correct state rather than an avoidance of work, and the note's line "The hedge rule has nothing to bite on here, and that is itself the result" is the right reading. I independently probed the no_source finding against a source the treatment does not name — Sungenis's own "Sixty Ways to Refute a Catholic Heliocentrist" (27 March 2025), the movement's most recent numbered compendium — and it runs none of these six arguments; its lanes are scripture, the Fathers, the magisterium, relativity and interferometry. That is a second, independent confirmation of the verdict. IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION: one component of the search that the page publishes is wrong in the other direction (see hole 1). Hall's solar chapter does contain the "Christian feast is really solar" move; it does not contain the step to a cosmology, so no_source survives, but the sentence asserting the absence does not.

holes.quoted_phrase: none of the four is located in that chapter as retrieved
holes.description: A published absence claim about a named source is false. The text says: "We read Hall's solar chapter looking for the Christian festivals, the church calendar, eastward orientation and solar processions, and none of the four is located in that chapter as retrieved." Hall's solar chapter is The Secret Teachings of All Ages, "The Sun, A Universal Deity", sacred-texts sta11 (https://sacred-texts.com/eso/sta/sta11.htm) — NOT sta12, which our own module docstring cites and which is in fact "The Zodiac and Its Signs". Fetched 2026-08-09, sta11 contains Christian festivals read as solar in two places: "The pagans set aside the 25th of December as the birthday of the Solar Man. They rejoiced, feasted, gathered in processions, and made offerings in the temples", and the Assumption passage — "This phenomenon, which takes place every year about the middle of August, gave rise to a festival which still exists, and in which it is supposed that the mother of Christ, laying aside her earthly life, is associated with the glory of her son". So at least the first of the four (Christian festivals), and arguably the second (the dating of feasts) and fourth (processions, in the pagan case), ARE in that chapter. Either the writer read sta12 and called it the solar chapter, or read sta11 and missed the festivals; either way the sentence a reader sees is wrong, and it sits in the rendered "1 · No original to quote" block that the same paragraph invites readers to check. This is the sweep's failure pattern 1 in its mirror image — asserting an absence that is not there — and it is checkable in two minutes by anyone who wants to discredit the page. Hall is also absent from the sources list despite the prose reporting that we read him. The verdict is NOT affected: Hall infers a pagan solar origin for Christian feasts, a claim about the genealogy of religion, and draws no conclusion about the motion or arrangement of the Earth. That distinction is worth more to us than the false absence was.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence (and add a source entry) with: "We read Hall's solar chapter — The Secret Teachings of All Ages, “The Sun, A Universal Deity” (sacred-texts sta11) — and it does carry the move item 429 makes, in miniature. Hall dates the pagan “birthday of the Solar Man” to 25 December, and he reproduces Dupuis's reading of the mid-August feast of the Assumption as an astronomical event: a phenomenon that “gave rise to a festival which still exists”. What is not located in that chapter is the step this cluster needs. Hall reads a Christian feast back to a solar cult — a claim about the genealogy of a religion — and draws no conclusion whatever about the motion or arrangement of the Earth; eastward orientation and the monastic hours are not located in the chapter as retrieved. So we record the resemblance as a resemblance and stop. We are not claiming Hall or Eliade as an author here." Add to `sources`: dict(label="Manly P. Hall, The Secret Teachings of All Ages (1928), “The Sun, A Universal Deity” — read 2026-08-09 for Christian festivals, the church calendar, eastward orientation and processions: the 25 December and Assumption passages are there, the cosmological inference is not", url="https://sacred-texts.com/eso/sta/sta11.htm"). Correct the docstring's "sacred-texts sta12" to sta11 in the same edit.

holes.quoted_phrase: the earliest datable person to read the practice as solar was an outsider who was told he had misread it
holes.description: Section 2 conflates two different propositions and credits Tertullian with denying the wrong one. Apology 16 (New Advent / ANF, checked 2026-08-09) reads: "Others, again, certainly with more information and greater verisimilitude, believe that the sun is our god ... The idea no doubt has originated from our being known to turn to the east in prayer." The next sentence is a tu quoque, not a denial: "But you, many of you, also under pretence sometimes of worshipping the heavenly bodies, move your lips in the direction of the sunrise." What the outsiders assert is that the sun is the Christians' god; what Tertullian denies is that. He does not deny — and cannot deny, since east is defined by sunrise — that the practice is keyed to the sun's rising, which is all item 446 ("Liturgical eastward orientation assumes sun's path") actually says. So "he was told he had misread it" overstates: he was told his conclusion did not follow, not that his description was wrong. The treatment's own `preemptive` field already warns against exactly this hardening ("do not let §2 harden into 'the eastward turn has nothing to do with the sun'"), which is evidence the writer saw the risk and the body sentence drifted past it anyway. The point survives intact once stated precisely, and stated precisely it is stronger — the structural parallel is that a directional practice is being used to read off a doctrinal commitment.
holes.recommendation: Replace from "and the earliest datable person" to the end of the paragraph with: "and that the earliest datable reading of the practice as evidence of a solar commitment was an outsider's, answered on the spot. Tertullian concedes the description — Christians are “known to turn to the east in prayer” — and denies only the conclusion drawn from it, that the sun is the Christians' god; his reply is that pagans too “under pretence sometimes of worshipping the heavenly bodies, move [their] lips in the direction of the sunrise”. He is not denying that east is where the sun comes up. He is denying that facing it tells you what a man holds to be true — which is the inference this cluster needs and does not make."

holes.quoted_phrase: Easter runs on a reckoned table its own designers knew was drifting
holes.description: "Its own designers knew" is not supported by the evidence cited for it. The only witness given, in the TLDR and again in refutation §4 ("The designers knew the approximation was drifting and recorded it: Bede noted the equinoctial drift in 725"), is Bede — who is an expositor and user of the Alexandrian computus, not one of its designers, and who is writing roughly three centuries after 21 March was fixed. Wikipedia's Computus article, which is our source, puts it exactly that way: the Alexandrian Easter "still placed the vernal equinox on 21 March, although Bede had already noted its drift in 725". A defender who checks the one citation attached to the claim finds a man who is not a designer, and the quantifier in a TLDR is the first thing a hostile reader tests (sweep pattern 2). The substantive point — the drift was recorded and not corrected for eight centuries — is true and is better served by saying that.
holes.recommendation: TLDR: replace with "Easter runs on a reckoned table whose drift from the sky the tradition recorded for eight centuries before correcting it — Bede noted the equinox slipping in 725 — rather than on an observation". Refutation §4: replace "The designers knew the approximation was drifting and recorded it:" with "The tradition that ran it recorded the drift rather than correcting it:".

holes.quoted_phrase: Here is exactly what was searched and where it stopped, so that a reader who knows better can correct us.
holes.description: The published search log invites this test and does not survive it cleanly. Everything searched is on the geocentric side of the movement (Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I, scripturecatholic, trueorthodoxy) plus one esoteric author (Hall). The specimen is not a geocentric list — its own heading, on the page as fetched 2026-08-09, is "THE EARTH IS FLAT AND NON ROTATING" — and this project's other C-lane clusters were traced to the flat-earth-side biblical-cosmology corpus (C02's attribution history runs through Skiba; B04 and B01 through Dubay). Neither Dubay nor Skiba appears anywhere in the search account, and neither does the movement's most current numbered compendium. I checked the last of these on this pass: Sungenis, "Sixty Ways to Refute a Catholic Heliocentrist" (robertsungenis.substack.com, 27 March 2025) argues from scripture, the Fathers, the magisterium, relativity and the interferometry experiments and runs no liturgical, calendrical, orientational or horological argument — so the no_source finding holds and gets stronger by naming it. As published, though, a defender can say we searched only the half of the movement the items did not come from.
holes.recommendation:
Insert as a new paragraph after the two-compendia paragraph: "

And the movement's own most recent summary. Robert Sungenis's Sixty Ways to Refute a Catholic Heliocentrist (27 March 2025) sets out sixty numbered arguments; none of the sixty runs from the liturgy, the ecclesiastical calendar, the orientation of churches, processions or the monastic hours. Its lanes are scripture, the Fathers, the magisterium, relativity and the interferometry experiments — the same five lanes as the two compendia above. The flat-earth side of the literature is where the specimen's other Christian-tradition clusters trace to, and we name the gap rather than close it: Dubay's 200 Proofs and Skiba's biblical-cosmology compilations have not been searched for these six items.

" Add to `sources`: dict(label="Robert Sungenis, “Sixty Ways to Refute a Catholic Heliocentrist”, 27 March 2025 — searched for a liturgical, calendrical, orientational or horological argument; none of the sixty is one", url="https://robertsungenis.substack.com/p/sixty-ways-to-refute-a-catholic-heliocentrist").

holes.quoted_phrase: Council the question of revising the ecclesiastical calendar was discussed,
holes.description: The Copernicus source label prints a quotation that does not match the document it links to. The OSU PDF (Harvard Classics, Famous Prefaces) reads: "for when not so very long ago, under Leo X, in the Lateran Council the question of revising the ecclesiastical calendar was discussed, it then remained unsettled, simply because the length of the years and months, and the motions of the sun and moon were held to have been not yet sufficiently determined." Our label renders it as "when the Lateran Council the question of revising the ecclesiastical calendar was discussed, it then remained unsettled" — an unmarked elision that drops "in" and leaves the sentence ungrammatical inside quotation marks.
